The documentation absence is REAL and survives every correction; the coverage number this item quotes does NOT, and the surface the verb ranges over is much wider than this item describes.** The absence holds at HEAD `262fe51c`: `grep -rn 'api/models\.py' docs/*.md` returns only `docs/BACKLOG.md`, and `idempotency_key` occurs in ZERO `docs/*.md` files against a positive control (`max_upload_bytes`) firing in four files in the same run. But "only 24 of 451 annotated fields carry any bound" measures the wrong population. An AST walk gives 458 annotated class fields in `messagefoundry/api/models.py`, of which only **38 are REQUEST fields**; the other 420 are response models the engine EMITS, and a response field is not an input data item, so counting it as a miss manufactures a gap. All 24 constrained fields are request fields. The true reading is 24 of 38. Adding `messagefoundry/api/auth_models.py` -- which neither this item nor the residual counts, and which is the most heavily bounded file on the surface -- the operator API's request-body population is 45 of 62 bounded, and its query and path parameter population is 60 of 67 constrained. This item's research question, "whether the several hundred unbounded fields represent deliberate openness or unstated rules", therefore has no subject.

**The research pass's own surface was then narrowed the same way, and adversarial review upheld the correction.** The engine declares EIGHT inbound content types at `messagefoundry/config/models.py:73-82` (hl7v2, json, xml, text, x12, fhir, binary, dicom). The pass graded all four verb limbs verified on `docs/HL7-VALIDATION.md`, and measured: `grep -ciE 'x12|dicom|fhir|json|xml|binary|content_type' docs/HL7-VALIDATION.md` returns **0**, while the identical pattern on `docs/CONNECTIONS.md` returns **288** in the same run. The 115-line document those verified boxes rest on says nothing about seven of the eight declared formats. Also unopened: the inbound transport plane (`messagefoundry/transports/http_listener.py` is a 953-line partner-facing receiver carrying its own shipped RFC token grammars); the CLI (153 `add_argument` calls, two subcommands ingesting an arbitrary JSON blob); bare path parameters, which never appear in the 67-declaration count -- `messagefoundry/api/auth_routes.py:620`, `:670`, `:712`, `:729` each declare `user_id: str` with no `Path(...)`, no bound and no grammar; and the console's own form items, since `grep -rn BaseModel messagefoundry_webconsole/` returns zero, so "the console's rules are the engine's rules" is measurably partial.

**A second correction with a positive control, and it makes the code half load-bearing.** `grep -n 'pattern=' messagefoundry/api/models.py messagefoundry/api/auth_models.py` returns NOTHING, against a control of 35 and 25 `Field(` uses in the same run. So of the 45 bounded request-body fields, ZERO carry a structural rule -- every one is a length or numeric bound. The structural content a documentation page could transcribe from shipped code is the HL7 field-path grammar (`messagefoundry/parsing/peek.py:129-132`, enforced eagerly on the API's `field_path` parameter at `messagefoundry/store/content_search.py:89-93`) plus five trivial enum allow-lists. Everything else structural has to be BUILT, which also means a clause documenting "the engine imposes no grammar for this item" defines no rule and cannot discharge the verb for that item.

**The deciding question is a method reading, and it is unresolved.** Does 2.1.1's "data items" demand per-plane completeness, or is it discharged by documenting the application's principal data format? A sibling requirement in the same ASVS section was assessed under a documentation-only reading by the same assessor on the same date, and this one was not -- that internal inconsistency, not any code fact, separates them. `docs/ASVS-ASSESSMENT-METHOD.md` section 1.3 defaults to the worse verdict when uncertain, so the coverage reading is what the research carried, and under it the build must range over all eight content types, the transport plane, the API's request bodies AND its bare path parameters, the console's own form items, and the CLI. Settling the reading needs one fetch of the ASVS V2 chapter prose at the `v5.0.0` tag: the pinned corpus provably cannot answer it, since its rows carry requirement text and no chapter guidance. Doing the build at the narrower scope buys a bigger deliverable and the same verdict.

**The item's named trap is right, and there is a sharper reason it does not give.** Flipping `expose_docs` adds no information at all: `messagefoundry/api/app.py:1072-1079` sets `docs_url`, `redoc_url` and `openapi_url` to None when it is False, so the flag decides whether four ROUTES register, not whether the schema is generated -- and `FastAPI.openapi()` is callable in-process by anyone holding the wheel either way. The flip widens network surface and is not a documentation change. Publishing the engine-introspected connection schema instead is the same move wearing a generated-artifact hat: it inherits the code's silences and would report connector `port` as a bare `int`, which is exactly the item the divergence lives on.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the operator-surface input-validation reference, scoped to the full input surface measured above rather than to `api/`; the engine-side connection-name grammar, adopting the rule the IDE already enforces at `ide/src/connectionWizardModel.ts:103` (note it has exactly ONE call site, `ide/src/connectionQuickInput.ts:112` -- the IDE's webview authoring path applies neither it nor the port range); the email-address validation rule at its three acceptance points, where `grep -rn EmailStr messagefoundry/` returns zero against a control of 26 `Field` uses in `auth_models.py`; the connector port-range rule the IDE and `[logging].forward_port` already enforce; and an input-rule doc-drift gate in the established house style, AST-walking `transports/` and the CLI as well as `api/` and the console routes, with a planted omission that must fire. Also owed: a record correction on the denominator, and a reconciliation note on the two readings applied to one section on one date.

## 1109. research an honest pass for ASVS 2.2.1 -- positive validation that does not sacrifice the tolerance the HL7 default exists to protect

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **7/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _big bet_. Both limbs stand -- validation.strict ships False at config/models.py:667 and api/models.py carries no model_config across 84 models, against five extra=forbid declarations in config/models.py. Value 7 not 8: the 2.2.1 cell is graded at LEVEL 1, so rung 8's ASVS L3 Partial limb does not reach it, and an authenticated loopback-bound API silently ignoring unknown body keys is not rung 8's production blind spot with no workaround -- it is rung 7, a real gap an operator cannot close from outside the app. Difficulty 6 stands: two independent limbs, a method ruling on which clause binds an L1 requirement inside an L3 assessment, and an API-side positive-validation change that would reach the console and apiclient callers too. _(was 8/10 · 8/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **2.2.1** (L1) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks for positive validation of input against an allow list, or comparison to an expected structure and logical limits. What holds it short is two independent limbs: HL7 content gets only the tolerant peek because `validation.strict` ships False (`messagefoundry/config/models.py:651`), and `messagefoundry/api/models.py` carries no `model_config` at all, so API bodies run Pydantic's default `extra=ignore`.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P1. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment, an unknown or mistyped key in an operator API request body would be silently accepted and dropped rather than refused. The HL7 limb's severity is the harder question and is exactly what the research must settle, not assume.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that input is validated to enforce business or functional expectations for that input. ... For L1, this can focus on input which is used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this should apply to all input."

**What holds it short today.** The HL7 limb is a deliberate default with a stated product reason: `parsing/peek.py:9` says "real-world feeds are routinely non-conformant", and the shipped-default triage calls this "the canonical genuine product cost" -- a deploying site would start NAKing the clinical messages the engine exists to tolerate. The API limb has no stated reason at all, and the asymmetry is visible in-tree: the config models set `extra="forbid"` at `config/models.py:535` while the API models set nothing.

**The research question.** Is there a path to an honest pass that does not spend the tolerance the default protects? Named unknowns: whether the L1 clause's narrowing ("input which is used to make specific business or security decisions") covers only the fields the Router and Handlers actually read, and what a positive check on those fields would look like on top of a tolerant parse rather than instead of it; and, because the scorecard grades at L3, which clause binds a level-1 requirement inside an L3 assessment -- "all input" or the L1 focus. That last is a method question, not a code question, and it decides whether the cell is reachable at all. The API limb is a separate line of research and should not be folded into the HL7 one.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Setting `validation.strict` True. It moves the cell by making the engine reject the traffic it exists to carry -- buying the verdict with the product's stated purpose. Equally not honest: re-declaring HL7 payloads as out-of-scope "data" rather than input, which is a scope redefinition to dodge the verb. A finding that the HL7 limb cannot honestly reach pass under the L2-and-up clause, and that the cell's ceiling is partial, is a successful outcome of this item.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found these 12 V1 through V3 cells, among others, carrying no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. The finding is that this cell's CEILING IS PARTIAL and no build reaches pass -- which this item correctly anticipates as a successful outcome. Both of the item's stated limbs still hold verbatim at HEAD `262fe51c`, but its framing sentence "two independent limbs" does not, and the largest gap a first research pass claimed turns out to be FALSE.** `validation.strict: bool = False` is at `messagefoundry/config/models.py:667` (the item cites `:651`; substance unchanged), and `messagefoundry/api/models.py` carries ZERO `model_config` across 84 `BaseModel` classes, against a positive control of five in `messagefoundry/config/models.py` in the same run. What the item undercounts is the API surface -- `messagefoundry/api/auth_models.py` adds 32 more classes with no `model_config`, so it is 116 classes across two files -- and neither this item nor the record reaches the web console or the IDE at all.

**A retraction owed before anyone builds on it.** A research pass graded the non-HL7 ingress surface "no format check of any kind -- a `content_type=json` inbound accepts a body that is not JSON, an `x12` inbound accepts a body with no ISA" and called it the largest reachable gap with "shipped validators sitting unwired". That is wrong for the file-family ingress. `messagefoundry/parsing/sniff.py:63 _content_matches_declared` compares a body's leading bytes to the inbound's DECLARED `content_type` for six of the eight declared types (hl7v2 via MSH/FHS/BHS, x12 via a leading ISA, dicom via the 128-byte preamble plus `DICM`, json and fhir via a leading brace or bracket, xml via a leading angle bracket), with binary and text exempted under a stated policy. It is called unconditionally at `messagefoundry/transports/file.py:580` and `messagefoundry/transports/remotefile.py:1008`, and a mismatch is moved to the `.error` directory BEFORE the bytes reach the pipeline -- so the result changes the disposition. The absence rested on a grep confined to `messagefoundry/pipeline/`; the control lives in `transports/`, which is architecturally where it belongs per the connector-registry rule, and is named by neither that directory nor that pattern. The instrument could not have disagreed.

**The honest residual gap is real, narrower and better shaped.** The network-listener sources -- `http_listener`, `tcp`, `mllp` and the database poll -- carrying a non-HL7 content type get only the size ceiling, the declared-encoding decode and the NUL check. The build is "call the existing `_content_matches_declared` on those four sources", which is far smaller than a new dispatch layer and is better precedented, because the project has already shipped this exact check on by default.

**Why the ceiling is partial and not merely unfunded.** The binding limb is the "for L2 and up, this should apply to all input" clause over the HL7 v2 data plane. The ONLY shipped mechanism that compares an HL7 v2 message to its expected structure is hl7apy, reachable only through `validation.strict` (`messagefoundry/pipeline/wiring_runner.py:4119` into `messagefoundry/parsing/validate.py:44`). Shipping it on is this item's own named disqualifier and is correct. Every weaker route fails a test the project has already written down. Detect-and-annotate fails the enforcement limb on the project's own discriminator -- `messagefoundry/parsing/consistency.py:11-15` says of itself that it "detects, it does not decide". A mandatory validation-posture declaration at wiring load fires on a MISSING DECLARATION rather than a missing control, so an operator declares the tolerant posture and starts with no structural validation; and the bar that gave that route teeth is gone, since the owner ruled on 2026-08-17 that there is no PHI data class. A per-inbound conformance profile ships empty and a gate refusing to start without one is the shape an owner ruling already rejected elsewhere. Under the alternative level reading the cell still lands on partial: the routing-decision fields are bare `str | None` at `messagefoundry/parsing/peek.py:302-330`, and bounding them either ships empty or starts dead-lettering real feeds that send a vendor-suffixed version string or an over-long control id -- a smaller spend of the same currency the item forbids spending.

**What would NOT be an honest pass, stated so it cannot be fudged.** Wiring any codec or `consistency.py` in so an absence claim stops firing, without the validator's result changing the disposition. The discriminator: on the shipped default, with no disable knob, a body that is not its declared format must land ERROR or dead-letter under the count-and-log invariant. A log line, a warning, an annotation or a counter is detect-not-decide and earns nothing. Also disqualified: scoring the tolerant peek's carriage contract (MSH presence, size caps, expansion budget) as satisfying the verb, which requires arguing against `docs/HL7-VALIDATION.md:16`, the project's own shipped operator documentation calling that tier "only hard safety limits".

**One correction to the supporting record before anyone builds the API limb: it is not a one-line fix.** `messagefoundry/apiclient/client.py:27` and `:45` import 38 of those same classes to parse engine RESPONSES, so a blanket `extra="forbid"` would make the apiclient, the harness and the web console throw when reading a newer engine that grew a response field. The posture must be request-model-scoped, with the split recorded in a comment beside the shared base so it is not later tidied away.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** extending the existing declared-content-type sniff to the four network-listener sources -- worth doing, and explicitly NOT scoreable as moving this cell; the request-model extra-key posture, request-scoped, correcting the one-line-fix characterisation in the same change; the IDE engine-response contract, giving the success path at `ide/src/engineClient.ts:127` and `:183` the discipline the error path in the same file already has at `:211-221`; and the conformance `profile` parameter, which `messagefoundry/parsing/validate.py:48,57-58` accepts, documents and enforces nowhere -- enforce it or delete it.

**Built 2026-09-04: the API limb, and only that. The item stays OPEN.** Its closing act is
`scorecard-rescore`, which is the ASVS Tracker's act followed by the Lander's banner flip. Neither
is a builder's. The HL7 limb was not touched and the method question was not decided, so **this
build does not move the cell and must not be scored as if it did.** What it does is take the API
limb off the list of things holding the cell short.

**Both counts on this item were re-measured at HEAD `a2eef0f3` before anything changed, because
both had drifted.** `messagefoundry/api/models.py` and `messagefoundry/api/auth_models.py` carried
**zero** `model_config` across **125** model classes (93 and 32), against this item's "84" and the
2026-08-20 research's "116" -- the substance held on both readings, the counts did not, because the
files grew. Positive control in the same run: five `extra="forbid"` in
`messagefoundry/config/models.py`. The request/response split was then read from FastAPI's own
`route.body_field` at runtime rather than re-derived from source with a regex, which is a second and
silently different definition of "request model". That read reports **32** of the 125 reachable from
a request body and **93** reachable only from a response.

**What shipped.** Those 32 now subclass a new `RequestModel` in
`messagefoundry/api/request_model.py`, which sets `extra="forbid"`; the 93 stay tolerant.
`tests/test_api_request_models_forbid_extra.py` pins the split in **both** directions off that same
runtime read. The second direction is the control, not decoration: a blanket flip across all 125
passes the first assertion and breaks every client, so the test that response-only models stay
tolerant is the only thing that tells the two apart.

**The record's "not a one-line fix" correction is carried, and the defect is sharper than "a key is
dropped".** `PUT /users/{id}/channel-scope` takes `ChannelScope`, whose `channels` is optional and
whose `None` means ALL channels. A body of `{"chanels": ["IB_ACME_ADT"]}` therefore asked for one
connection, granted every one, and answered 200 -- an RBAC over-grant by typo. That is why the five
shapes carried in **both** directions (`AdGroupMap`, `AdGroupMapEntry`, `AdGroupScopeEntry`,
`AdGroupScopeMap`, `ChannelScope`) take the request rule rather than being excused as response
models, and the cost is written where it bites, in the base class and in the pinning test: adding a
field to one of those five is a client-visible wire change, and the release that adds it must ship
the client bump with it.

**No caller needed changing, and that is a measurement rather than an assumption.** The web console
constructs these models by explicit keyword against declared fields (`routes/search.py:191,240`,
`routes/core.py:682`, `routes/monitoring_writes.py:131,164`, `routes/uploaded_logs.py:312,387`,
`routes/connection_writes.py:119`, `routes/config.py:58`) and never splats a form dict into one; the
apiclient's JSON bodies are field-exact; the harness reaches the engine only through the apiclient
and imports response models alone; the IDE's three bodies (`/auth/login`, `/ai/chat`,
`/config/reload`) name declared fields only; and the approvals replay path reads its stored params as
a bare `Mapping` (`api/app.py:530-560`), never re-validating them into a request model.

**What remains, unchanged by this build.** The HL7 limb: `validation.strict` still ships `False` at
`config/models.py:667`, deliberately, and the 2026-08-20 finding that this cell's ceiling is
**partial** is untouched -- shipping strict validation on would make a deploying site NAK the
clinical traffic the engine exists to tolerate. And the method question this item names, whether
"all input" or the L1 focus binds a level-1 requirement inside an L3 assessment, is still undecided
and still decides whether the cell is reachable at all.

## 1110. research an honest pass for ASVS 2.2.3 -- whether cross-field reasonableness is shippable at all in a code-first engine, or belongs to the feed author

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **5/10** · _fill-in_. The gap is unchanged: consistency.py:11-17 still describes itself as a compose-it-yourself toolkit, its only non-test importer is samples/consistency/validated_adt.py:27, and nothing on the shipped message path calls it. The research question is genuinely open and its most likely output is a negative finding, so worth-if-built is bounded by the clean existing workaround of a Handler composing the primitives; difficulty carries the HL7-general rule-set research plus, if a set exists, a check on the message hot path with tests. _(was 5/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **2.2.3** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that combinations of related data items be checked as reasonable against pre-defined rules. What holds it short is that `messagefoundry/parsing/consistency.py` is a toolkit a Handler composes rather than a shipped check, and at `63bd55ba` a grep across `messagefoundry/`, `samples/` and `harness/` finds its only importer is `samples/consistency/validated_adt.py:27`.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P3. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no direct product effect on a first deployment. The engine does not claim to validate combined clinical items, and the config plane does refuse inconsistent combinations at construction (`config/models.py:251`); the gap is that nothing on the message path does.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that the application ensures that combinations of related data items are reasonable according to the pre-defined rules."

**What holds it short today.** The module's own docstring at `parsing/consistency.py:11` describes it as a pure toolkit of reusable checks a Handler composes -- it detects, it does not decide, and nothing in the shipped pipeline calls it. The scorecard carries an absence claim on `parsing.consistency` with a live positive control, so the negative is instrumented rather than asserted.

**The research question.** The engine ships a framework whose routing and transform logic is authored per feed, so the "pre-defined rules" for combinations of HL7 items may be feed-specific by construction. An honest pass needs a decision on whose rules the verb means -- the engine's own control plane, or the clinical content flowing through it -- and, if the content, what a shipped default could reasonably assert about combinations without a feed's context. The specific unknown: whether a non-empty set of combination rules exists that is true of HL7 v2.x generally rather than of one site's feed. If that set is empty, the honest finding is that the assessed artifact is a framework and the verb's subject is the deployment.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Wiring the existing toolkit into the default pipeline so the absence claim stops firing, without first establishing which combination rules are universally true. That would either dead-letter conformant clinical traffic or check nothing, and in the second case it would produce a green absence claim over a control that does no work.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found these 12 V1 through V3 cells, among others, carrying no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. The finding is that this cell's CEILING IS PARTIAL -- which this item names as a successful outcome -- but the reason is NOT the one this item gives, and this item's exculpatory clause about the config plane is itself only partly true.** The measured fact holds at HEAD `262fe51c`: `messagefoundry/parsing/consistency.py` has ZERO importers anywhere under `messagefoundry/`, the only tree-wide hits being a sample, a test and two docs, against a positive control (`parsing.validate`) that fires on a live engine import in the same run. What does not hold is the identification of that fact as what holds the cell short. Wiring the toolkit in would move NOTHING: it supplies no rules, and every one of its primitives is typed on a parsed HL7 `Message` (`consistency.py:84,89,99,108,121`), so it does not even apply to the `RawMessage` every non-hl7v2 content type produces. The toolkit is a symptom, not the cause.

**This item's clause "the config plane does refuse inconsistent combinations at construction" is measurably partial, and the split is executable.** The same pre-defined rule -- an outbound network destination requires a `host` -- RAISES on three connectors and silently defaults to loopback on three others. Executed at HEAD against `build_destination` with no host: `email` raises (`messagefoundry/transports/email.py:98`), `direct` raises (`direct.py:134`) and `dimse` raises (`dicom.py:500`), while `mllp` builds with `'127.0.0.1'` (`mllp.py:633`), `tcp` builds with `'127.0.0.1'` (`tcp.py:107`) and `x12` builds with `'127.0.0.1'` (`x12.py:82`). The INBOUND half of the identical rule is enforced (`messagefoundry/config/wiring.py:3829`), which is what makes the outbound half a defect rather than a design choice. A fourth connector, `remotefile`, enforces a two-field version of it (`remotefile.py:609-611`), so the honest shape is that three of thirteen destination connectors default silently, not that three enforce and three do not. Zero deployments means no migration window is warranted -- refuse outright. Note the impact is understated in one direction: where the same engine runs a listener on that port, a delivery would SUCCEED into the engine's own listener rather than stalling.

**Two of the three declared artifacts carry combination rules of their own, and adversarial review was upheld on this.** The claim that the web console "reduces exactly to the API plane" is false. `messagefoundry_webconsole/routes/admin.py:465-475` collects `ad_group` and `role` as two positional lists from a stdlib form parse and zips them with `strict=True`, dropping any half-filled row with `if g and r`; the engine model it then constructs takes an ALREADY-PAIRED list and cannot see a half-filled row, because the console never sends one. The console's own shared form helper (`messagefoundry_webconsole/routes/_common.py:24-29`) documents the hazard in its comment -- dropping blanks "shifts the positional pairing so a role from one row silently binds to a group from another - an RBAC mis-grant". Its handling of a violation is a SILENT DROP, which the pinned verb excludes: reasonableness must be ensured, not resolved by precedence. The IDE likewise carries a CLIENT-ONLY combination rule with no server counterpart: `ide/src/connectionQuickInput.ts:118-127` blocks the wizard on a required Host for an outbound MLLP or TCP, which the engine does not enforce at all per the measurement above -- and the IDE's other authoring path, the webview form, deliberately does not block, so the two paths hold different rule sets for one rule.

**The ceiling, stated with the record's reason rather than a circular one.** No shipped, vendor-supplied, non-empty rule set exists for HL7 v2 combinations that is safe to refuse on by default, and the mechanism that would evaluate a site-supplied one is gated behind a posture the record has already priced as unshippable (an ADT feed dead-lettering non-conformant messages is a patient-safety event). A first research pass instead argued that no pre-defined rule set can EXIST, because the engine's own documentation delegates combined-item consistency to the application. That argument is circular in a way that would be dangerous if reused -- it would let any assessed artifact exempt itself from any requirement by publishing a delegation -- and it is harmless here only because it points at holding partial. Carry the pricing reason, not the existence reason.

**The item's named trap is exactly right and is one line of code away.** The scorecard absence claim on this cell keys on an IMPORT STRING, so a single `from messagefoundry.parsing.consistency import check` anywhere under `messagefoundry/` -- even in a path that composes zero rules and is never called -- makes it stop firing with no change to whether any combination of any message is checked. A second, newly created by this pass's own measurement: fixing the outbound-host default and re-scoring the cell on that alone is the same trap wearing a config-plane hat, and it is also a default flip. A third: asserting that one control at the loader satisfies the verb across all three artifacts, which is true of the MECHANISM and false of the SURFACE -- the API request layer is a second seam, the console's form plane a third, and the CLI a fourth.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the outbound peer-address rule, making the three silently-defaulting connectors refuse a missing host as the others already do; the IDE conditional-required premise correction, which must land whether or not the host fix does, because `ide/src/connectionForm.ts:129-131` justifies not blocking a save with "only the engine can judge the condition, and it already does so loudly at load" -- a compensating control resting on a premise the measurement above falsifies; a structured `requiredWhen` predicate emitted by the engine, replacing the bare word-match at `messagefoundry/config/connection_schema.py:53`, consumed and enforced by both IDE authoring paths and the loader; the API and web-console request-layer combination-rule census and declaration; and a combination-rule inventory MEASURED rather than prose-grepped, so the documentation requirement and this enforcement requirement rest on one enumerated set instead of two independent word-matches.

## 1111. research an honest pass for ASVS 2.3.3 -- what a business-logic transaction boundary means where the approval gate commits before it executes

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **3/10** · _fill-in_. The audit-record defect the item was filed on is fixed (approvals.py:141-157 plus :181-208), but the pinned verb is still unmet: a partially applied executor is now recorded 'failed' with its effect landed, which app.py:537-548 exhibits concretely because config_reload swaps the graph before its audit row is written. So the remainder is the item's real research question -- the correct boundary and whether the three operations are replay-safe -- rather than only an out-of-repo re-score (value 5, difficulty 3 for a bounded API-side decision plus its tests). _(was 6/10 · 5/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **2.3.3** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that a business logic operation either succeed in its entirety or roll back to the previous correct state. What holds it short is `messagefoundry/api/approvals.py:127-133`: the row transitions to `approved` first, then `op.execute(params)` runs, and there is no compensating transition if the executor raises.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment with `[approvals].enabled` turned on, a raising executor would leave an operation recorded as approved and not performed -- an audit record that asserts something that did not happen. The pipeline's own stage handoff is unaffected.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that transactions are being used at the business logic level such that either a business logic operation succeeds in its entirety or it is rolled back to the previous correct state."

**What holds it short today.** The pipeline half is sound and documented as such: each stage handoff is a single committed transaction with rollback and startup recovery on both scored backends (`store/store.py:3872`, `:3921`). The approval half inverts on purpose -- the comment at `api/approvals.py:127` states the commit-first ordering guards a double-approve race -- and the residual notes it has no compensating transition.

**The research question.** The two orderings trade one defect for the other: execute-then-record can double-execute, record-then-execute can record an approved operation that never ran. An honest pass needs the correct boundary for an operation whose effect lands outside the row's own transaction, and a decision on whether a compensating transition, an idempotent re-drive, or a two-phase record is the right shape. Named unknown: whether the three registered operations (`api/app.py:539-541` -- dead-letter replay, connection purge, config reload) are individually replay-safe, since that decides whether a failed execute can simply be retried rather than compensated.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Re-scoring on the pipeline half alone. The staged-queue transaction is genuinely good and is the more visible half of the cell, so the tempting move is to let it carry the verdict while the approval path's gap goes unaddressed. Also not honest: leaving `[approvals].enabled` off and arguing the path is unreachable -- the scorecard scored the cell by configuration reach, and so did its sibling 2.3.4.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found these 12 V1 through V3 cells, among others, carrying no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. This item's load-bearing clause is DEAD in shipped code and the second half of its "What holds it short today" must be struck.** "There is no compensating transition if the executor raises" no longer holds: `messagefoundry/api/approvals.py:139-152` wraps the executor in an `except Exception` that calls `_compensate_failed_execution` (`:181`), which compare-and-sets the row to `failed` guarded on `from_status="approved"` (`:199-205`), audits `approval.failed` against both identities (`:206-221`) and re-raises the original (`:157`). The commit-first ordering half still holds and is deliberate (`:130`, guarding a double-approve race). The item's Severity paragraph -- "an operation recorded as approved and not performed" -- is stale with it. Line cites have drifted: the item's `:127-133` is `:130-137`, and its `api/app.py:539-541` is `:552-554`.

**What holds the cell short now is three limbs this item never names, plus a surface neither it nor the first research pass enumerated.** The compensation is best-effort and the code says so (`approvals.py:222-227` catches a failing compensating write and logs that the row "may still read 'approved' for an operation that did not run"); it moves to a NEW terminal state rather than the previous one; and the cell explicitly declines to assert the completeness of its own inventory. Two adversarial reviews both landed, on different axes, and both are upheld.

**Scope.** The multi-step-operation sweep dropped the sharpest instance of the verb in the tree, and dropped it from its own instrument's output. `messagefoundry/pipeline/dr.py:159 DrCoordinator.activate` is a four-phase control-plane operation whose phase three runs an operator-supplied VIP takeover hook (`:237`) -- an effect outside the store and outside any transaction -- and whose phase four can raise into `_record_aborted`, which audits and re-raises WITHOUT releasing the VIP. `release` (`:294`) runs the release hook FIRST (`:313`), and a raising deactivate re-raises with `self._active` still True and no released audit row. Neither disjunct of the verb holds and there is no recovery sweep. On a first deployment a failed activation would leave a box holding a virtual IP, binding no listeners, and reporting itself passive. The gate this cell is named for is also covered on one leg of three: `approvals.py:67` (guard) and `:229` (reject) are both two-write uncompensated operations, so a failed audit write after `create_pending_approval` would leave a dual-control request persisted with no `approval.requested` row. And the instrument's "two or more awaited store writes" threshold structurally hides the verb's HARDEST case -- one store write plus one effect outside the store, which cannot be inside any transaction by construction.

**Mechanism.** The proposed path was to satisfy the verb's first disjunct ("succeeds in its entirety") via durable intent plus forward recovery, on the ground that the staged pipeline already uses that pattern. That borrows the pipeline's credit and drops the precondition that makes it work: the pipeline's re-run is a no-op because the consumed row is gone (`messagefoundry/store/store.py:3963-3966`). Two of the three registered executors are NOT re-drive-safe, and the pass's own measurements say so -- `config_reload` re-reads the directory, so a re-drive can load different bytes than the request was fingerprinted against and re-bumps the cluster version, and `connection_purge` with `scope=top` re-drives onto a DIFFERENT message (`store.py:6672-6678`, `LIMIT 1` over `status=PENDING`). What a three-state chain buys for those two is DETECTABILITY, which is real, correct, and is not either branch of the verb.

**The honest path is therefore per-executor, and in this order.** Dead-letter replay already qualifies: `store.py:6620-6647` wraps the batch in one transaction with an explicit rollback, and its selection predicate makes a second pass a no-op. Connection purge needs the rollback guard its sibling has and `cancel_queued` (`store.py:6648`) lacks, AND request-time binding of the specific queue row, or no sweep can safely complete a stranded top-only purge. Config reload needs its bytes bound to the request -- capture the provenance fingerprint at request time and re-verify at execute time, refusing on drift -- so a re-drive is either the same operation or a clean refusal. Only then does a `pending / executing / terminal` chain plus a startup reconciliation sweep genuinely satisfy the first disjunct. The pipeline has such a sweep and approvals has none: `grep -rn pending_approval messagefoundry/pipeline/*.py` returns ZERO against a positive control of five `reset_stale_inflight` hits in the same directory in the same run.

**The item's named trap is now guarded in the record's own text; the live trap is different.** The cell's second re-score trigger asks for a sweep establishing that no other multi-step operation can end neither committed nor compensated, and that clause will be bought rather than earned -- a lane closes the tractable approvals limb, glances at `api/` and `pipeline/`, and writes "swept, no further instances". That sentence is false: at least 14 sequential uncompensated flows exist in `messagefoundry/auth/service.py` alone, on the SHIPPED DEFAULT path with no configuration gate, including `change_password` (`:2005`, set-password at `:2021` then revoke-sessions at `:2026`) and `create_local_user` (`:2658`, create at `:2669` then roles at `:2680` then audit at `:2681`). Also disqualified: making the compensating transition revert to `pending`, which reads as answering the residual and re-arms a re-drive of a partially applied non-idempotent operation; and adding a store transaction primitive and wrapping call sites without proving it on the SQL Server and Postgres legs, since both acquire a POOLED connection per call (`postgres.py:1332`, `sqlserver.py:3116`) so a caller-held boundary would silently span different connections -- a failure invisible on SQLite, which is the backend local pytest actually runs.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the approvals executor replay-safety and request-binding work, per executor, as the precondition for everything else; the approvals executor outcome contract with its startup reconciliation sweep, preserving the existing race guard; the config-reload success-reporting fix, since `messagefoundry/pipeline/engine.py:1598` swaps the live graph before `:1602`, `:1610` and `:1622` can raise, so a raise today reports a FAILED reload while the new graph is live and possibly already propagated; a composable write-transaction boundary on the Store protocol, proven on the server CI legs (`messagefoundry/store/base.py` exposes none -- measured zero against a four-hit positive control in the same file); wrapping the identity and authorization flows in it so an authorization change and its session revocation cannot land apart; DR activation and release recovery; and the sweep PERFORMED rather than asserted, recorded with its instrument and its false-negative limit stated.

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment, concurrent in-flight uploads would overshoot the per-uploader file-count and byte budget, and ~~N engine shards would each apply the budget separately, multiplying it~~ **[FALSE, and false in the ALARMING direction -- measured by `85fe7e85`, struck not deleted.** `_scan_metas_sync` is an **uncached filesystem read**, so shards sharing one `uploads_dir` enforce **ONE budget between them**. `config/settings.py:439` says so in the shipped code, with a live positive control: *"engine shards sharing one dir see each other's files and the budget does NOT multiply (measured 2026-08-10 -- two UploadStores over one dir, the second refused the same uploader at quota)"*. **The real remainder is far smaller than this sentence claimed:** an at-most **N-1 file overshoot**, one per competing shard caught between its scan and its file landing on disk, each bounded by `max_upload_bytes`.]**. Every other contended resource named in the residual is locked by a shipped default.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that business logic level locking mechanisms are used to ensure that limited quantity resources (such as theater seats or delivery slots) cannot be double-booked by manipulating the application's logic."

**What holds it short today.** The quota is computed by scanning file metadata and then writing, with the race documented in the source comment rather than defended against. The scorecard's absence claim pairs `_max_files_per_user` with the absence of a `Lock(` in that module, against a live positive control on the approvals path, so the negative is instrumented. The shard axis is recorded in the residual and is not covered by that claim.

**The research question.** An honest pass needs a decision point that is authoritative on both axes -- concurrent requests inside one process, and multiple engine-shard processes over the one unified store. Named unknowns: whether the quota belongs on a filesystem scan at all or on a store row that can carry the same single-transaction discipline the pipeline handoff already uses; what the correct behaviour is when the budget is reached mid-write; and whether the verb's "limited quantity resource" reading extends past uploads to anything else the engine meters per actor, which this cell has never enumerated.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Closing the visible concurrency limb only. Any control that would satisfy the scorecard's own absence-claim mutation exactly while leaving the shard-multiplication half untouched -- a control that reads as complete and is not. That is the compensating-control-on-a-false-premise shape, and on this cell it is one edit away.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found these 12 V1 through V3 cells, among others, carrying no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. This item's surviving half holds verbatim at HEAD `262fe51c`, its fix is correct and buildable, and its own named unknown -- whether the verb extends past uploads -- is now ANSWERED: it does, and further than a first research pass found.** `messagefoundry/uploads.py:487` still reads "One critical section per process", the module is byte-identical to the record's own verified commit, and nothing per-shards the directory: the supervisor forwards the same `--service-config` to every shard (`messagefoundry/pipeline/supervisor.py:116-117`), and `grep -rn uploads_dir messagefoundry/**/*.py` returns 15 lines of which none is shard-aware or warns.

**One correction to this item's suggested acceptance criterion, and it cuts helpfully.** "The quota holds across N shards sharing one `uploads_dir`, with concurrent writers on at least 2 shards" is not runnable on SQLite: `require_unified_store` (`messagefoundry/pipeline/sharding.py:81`) raises on any non-server backend for more than one distinct shard id, and `supervise` calls it at `messagefoundry/pipeline/supervisor.py:154` BEFORE spawning anything. So the demonstration needs a Postgres or SQL Server rig. The helpful consequence: the coordination point is not merely available, it is GUARANTEED PRESENT and fail-closed in exactly the deployment shape that creates the gap, so there is no SQLite multi-writer branch to design around.

**The enumeration limb of this verb is UNVERIFIED, and that is the correction this item should carry.** A first pass enumerated twelve limited-quantity resources, graded eleven as already satisfying the verb, and concluded "a pass needs one build, not a programme". At least four more exist inside the engine, and two of them fail the one-critical-section limb rather than merely the cross-process one. `messagefoundry/pipeline/cluster.py:927 _claim_or_renew_lease` is the leadership lease -- exactly one leader, cross-process, where "cannot be double-booked" is literally split-brain, and the archetype of this verb in the tree; on the merits its atomic guarded upsert plus fencing token grades verified, which is precisely the point, because a resource inventory missing the archetype is not credible. The file-processed ledger CHECKS at `messagefoundry/transports/file.py:542` (`_leave_already_ingested`, falling through to `store.is_file_processed` at `messagefoundry/store/store.py:9295`) and CONSUMES at `file.py:649` (`_leave_record`, `INSERT OR IGNORE` at `store.py:9306`) -- separated by the entire ingestion, so it is a check-then-act. `INSERT OR IGNORE` makes the WRITE idempotent; it does not make the DECISION exclusive, and a double-ingest here would mean a clinical message delivered twice. Also unassessed: DR promotion (`messagefoundry/pipeline/dr.py:145`, a second per-process `asyncio.Lock` whose own module at `:135-139` documents a sharded DR fleet activating against ONE restored store) and the account-lockout budget (`messagefoundry/auth/service.py:839-856` computes `prior + 1` off a previously fetched record and `store.py:8070-8084` writes that caller-computed value blind -- a lost-update read-modify-write).

**Why the enumeration missed them is the instrument, and it is worth recording.** The pattern was `would exceed|over quota|QuotaError|at quota|_quota`, derived from the vocabulary of the one module already known to be in play, with that same module as its only positive control -- so the control could only ever fire on the seed case. Re-run over the five missed artifacts it returns nothing, while returning 11 on `uploads.py` in the same run. An independent counterexample hunt found none, but its pattern (`per_user|per_actor|_cap`) could not have found a lease or a file ledger either. Two one-sided instruments agreeing is not corroboration. Re-do the enumeration with an instrument keyed to the VERB -- a resource with a finite quantity, a check, and a consume -- and validate it on a resource the searcher did not already know about.

**The upload fix itself stands and should be built.** Preferred end state: move the uploaded body onto the existing refcounted `attachment` / `attachment_chunk` substrate (`messagefoundry/store/store.py:1356-1385`) so the quota check and the write land in ONE database transaction and the verb is satisfied outright -- CORRECTED 2026-08-22: an earlier version of this paragraph said the substrate ships dormant and uploads would be its first consumer. That is FALSE at HEAD and is retracted. `messagefoundry/pipeline/wiring_runner.py:3933` already calls `store.put_attachment` on the ingress detach path, the method is on the protocol at `store/base.py:867` and implemented at `store/store.py:3469`, and this item's sibling 5.1.1 research names that same path. So uploads would JOIN a substrate already carrying PHI attachments rather than start one, and the refcount and prune interaction with the existing consumer is part of the work rather than absent from it. Fallback: a per-uploader store row consumed by a conditional UPDATE in the shape `decide_pending_approval` already uses (`store.py:7537`), with the reserve-then-spend discipline the AES-GCM invocation budget already proves at fleet scale (`messagefoundry/store/gcm_bound.py:11-30`), plus refund on delete and on prune and reconciliation against the directory. There is no advisory-locking precedent to copy: `grep -rnE 'fcntl|flock|msvcrt|LockFileEx|portalocker|filelock' messagefoundry/ --include=*.py` returns ZERO across the whole engine, against positive controls on `os.replace` and `import os` firing in five and three files in the same run.

**Two moves that would not be honest passes, one of them newly created by this pass.** Declaring the resource out of scope because `uploads_dir` ships unset (`messagefoundry/config/settings.py:442`) and the subsystem is therefore inert on a default install: it reads as rigour, and it is the re-declare-out-of-scope move, a built-but-off control is a partial not a pass, and an operator who turns uploads on would get the cross-shard gap with no warning emitted anywhere. And satisfying this item's acceptance criterion with two `serve --shard` processes over one SQLite file: that WORKS, because `require_unified_store` has exactly two call sites and both are the supervisor path while `serve --shard` (`messagefoundry/__main__.py:2686-2710`) never calls it and structurally cannot -- but it measures a shape the supported path refuses, so a green result certifies nothing.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the upload-quota cross-process authority work; the limited-quantity-resource re-enumeration with a verb-keyed instrument and a control that fires on an unknown instance; grades at HEAD for the leadership lease, the file-processed ledger, the WebAuthn sign counter (`store.py:8023-8037`), the DR promotion lock and the account-lockout counter; the two-shard concurrent-upload acceptance harness on a server-DB rig; and the `serve --shard` unified-store guard, either reachable from the serve entrypoint or replaced by a single-writer advisory lock at SQLite store open so a second writer fails closed -- the same defect class as this cell's, on a different resource set, and recorded nowhere today.


**RESIDUAL RECORDED 2026-08-22 BY THE DISPATCHER, AT LANDING. THE CROSS-PROCESS FIX LANDED WITH TWO OF ITS THREE BACKENDS UNEXERCISED.** The build shipped in `cf38e16a` -- one new store-protocol method across four files, graded at zero anchor FAIL risk before it landed. **All four test callers are SQLite. THE POSTGRES AND SQL SERVER PATHS SHIP WITH NO TEST TOUCHING THEM.**

## 1113. research an honest pass for ASVS 2.3.5 -- which flows in a PHI engine are high-value enough to demand a second approver, under a default that must not strand a single-operator site

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _money pit_. The code matches the item's substance: the gate ships off, three operations are registered and all three are guarded at api/app.py:2236, :2730 and :2837, and the default approvable set names only two, so no user-administration and no PHI-export flow is approvable in any configuration. Value stays mid-band because the consequence is a narrow opt-in control gap with no first-deployment product effect; difficulty is 6 because an honest pass most likely means widening the registry across API, settings, audit and console while resolving the self-approval availability cost at api/approvals.py:120. _(was 5/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **2.3.5** (L3) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that high-value business logic flows require multi-user approval. What holds it short is that `[approvals].enabled` ships False (`messagefoundry/config/settings.py:3228`) and `guard()` executes the operation inline whenever the gate is off, so no flow requires a second approver as shipped.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P3. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no product effect on a first deployment. The consequence is that a deploying site gets no second-person control on any operation unless it opts in, and the operations it could opt into are narrow.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that high-value business logic flows require multi-user approval to prevent unauthorized or accidental actions. This could include but is not limited to large monetary transfers, contract approvals, access to classified information, or safety overrides in manufacturing."

**What holds it short today.** The residual asserts "the single enabled flag is all that stands between this and a pass". The shipped-default triage explicitly rejects that and resolves to the worse answer, and the code agrees: three operations are registered at `api/app.py:539-541` and the default approvable set names two (`config/settings.py:3189-3191`, dead-letter replay and connection purge). No user-administration flow and no PHI-export flow is approvable in any configuration, so the gate cannot reach the operations a reader would call high-value.

**The research question.** The triage classifies this cell needs-owner-decision, and the constraint is concrete: `api/approvals.py:119-120` refuses self-approval, so a single-operator site with the gate on could not replay a dead letter at all -- an availability cost on a routine clinical operation. An honest pass needs the high-value set defined for this product first (is creating an administrator, exporting raw PHI, or repointing an outbound destination higher-value than a dead-letter replay?), then a default posture honest about both that availability cost and the requirement. Whether the answer is a wider registry, a different default, or a documented ceiling of partial is the owner's call, and the research should present it as a decision rather than make it.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Turning `[approvals].enabled` on. It does not reach pass even mechanically, because the approvable set does not cover the flows the verb is about, and it would trade a routine operation's availability for a scorecard cell. Also not honest: adding operations to the default list to widen coverage without deciding what makes an operation high-value.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found these 12 V1 through V3 cells, among others, carrying no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. This item asks the research to "present it as a decision rather than make it" -- and the decision has already been made TWICE.** It was scoped out on 2026-08-11 and ruled FINAL, permanently partial, on 2026-08-17, in a ruling that split the two 2026-08-11 scope-outs and returned the other one to work while keeping this one closed. This item is written as if the question were open. Its substantive claim about the code SURVIVES intact, unusually -- three operations registered at `messagefoundry/api/app.py:552-554`, two in the default set at `messagefoundry/config/settings.py:3280-3282`, `[approvals].enabled: bool = False` at `:3319`, self-approval refused at `messagefoundry/api/approvals.py:122-123` -- but every line number it cites has drifted. This research does not overturn the ruling. It records three facts the ruling did not have in front of it.

**One: the ruling's decisive availability sentence is stated over all single-operator sites, and the engine's own escalation arm cannot reach most of them.** The startup warning at `messagefoundry/__main__.py:2072` fires only when `admin_exposed and not settings.approvals.enabled and data_class is PHI`, where `admin_exposed` is an off-loopback bind or a declared TLS-terminating proxy (`:1142`, `:1988`). On a stock loopback single-operator install that arm NEVER trips. On the posture the assessment declares -- an operator console behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy on a hospital LAN -- it trips today, prints to stderr and continues (`:2080-2088`), and the shipped code names the escalation itself as an unbuilt owner fork at `:2069-2072`, including an audited `[approvals].allow_single_control` override.

**Two: the sole operator console has NO approver surface, so on a first deployment with the gate on, an operator could request a held operation and never release one.** Measured: `packaging/messagefoundry-webconsole/tests/golden/ui_routes.txt` lists 98 machine-asserted console routes and `grep -ci approv` returns **0**, against a positive control of 4 for `dead` in the same run; `grep -rn APPROVALS_APPROVE messagefoundry_webconsole/` returns nothing while the same pattern returns hits under `messagefoundry/`. Nor can a browser reach the JSON routes: `messagefoundry_webconsole/_auth.py:735-736` states the console cookie "is only ever read by require_ui on /ui routes, never by the JSON API deps", confirmed by `grep -c 'cookies|COOKIE' messagefoundry/api/security.py` returning 0 against a control of 10 for Bearer and Authorization. That is the same wiring-hole shape on which the 2026-08-17 ruling returned the OTHER scope-out to work, and it was unmeasured at the time.

**Three: a third shipped defect, in the shared engine client.** `messagefoundry/apiclient/client.py` lets a 202 through (`_request` raises only at 400 and above) and then parses it bare: `replay_dead_letters` calls `DeadLetterReplayResult.model_validate(...)` and `reload_config` calls `ReloadResult.model_validate(...)` WITHOUT the module's own decoder, on models whose every field is required while `PendingApprovalResponse` supplies none. So a correctly-working dual-control hold would raise an unhandled pydantic `ValidationError` out of the client, breaking the contract that file's own docstring says the decoder exists to preserve; `purge_connection`, which does use the decoder, would report the hold as an engine version-skew error. This joins the already-known IDE defect, where `ide/src/engineClient.ts:125` casts any 2xx body to its expected type and `ide/src/promote.ts:193-198` therefore announces a SUCCESSFUL promote -- with undefined counts -- for a reload that was only held. Both would fire in the configuration the engine's own startup warning recommends. Fix them regardless of what the verdict does.

**And one fact that sharpens the ruling rather than reopening it.** `Permission.APPROVALS_APPROVE` appears in no built-in role's explicit permission set; it reaches only ADMINISTRATOR via the full-permission frozenset (`messagefoundry/auth/permissions.py:143`) and sits in `CUSTOM_ROLE_FORBIDDEN_PERMISSIONS` (`:194-201`), so it can never be minted onto a custom role. Both default approvable operations are OPERATOR-tier. So enabling dual control today would require minting a SECOND FULL ADMINISTRATOR to release routine clinical work -- a least-privilege regression, and directly material to the availability cost the ruling turns on.

**What would still not be an honest pass.** Turning `[approvals].enabled` on is doubly dead: it does not reach pass mechanically because the approvable set does not cover the flows the verb is about, and an off-by-default control can never be graded pass under the 2026-08-16 owner ruling recorded at `docs/ASVS-ASSESSMENT-METHOD.md` section 1.1a. The LIVE trap is registering the gate against the user-administration routes so the record's "no user-administration flow is approvable in ANY configuration" sentence stops being true, and re-scoring on that: appending names to a frozenset because those names appear in a residual is reverse-engineering the record, and the tell is that two flows the record never mentions outrank one it does -- `POST /messages/{id}/edit-resend` (`api/app.py:3588`), which re-ingresses an OPERATOR-EDITED clinical body into the live pipeline on one caller's step-up, and `POST /dr/activate` (`:4964`). Building the console approver page is worth doing and moves nothing: no additional flow comes to require approval, so re-scoring on it buys a verdict with a usability fix.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the high-value-flow criterion for this product -- a written rule plus the route set it selects, ranging over the 29 mutating routes in `api/app.py` and the 24 in `api/auth_routes.py` AND the two non-route provisioning paths a route-decorator scan cannot see (`messagefoundry/auth/service.py:530` bootstrap admin seed, `:1322` AD just-in-time upsert); the approvals release-path identity re-check, since `Executor` carries no identity (`api/approvals.py:32`) and only the purge executor re-checks anything, so a held create-administrator could execute for a requester demoted inside the 72-hour window; registration of the selected flows, re-sized honestly at nine engine handler signature changes plus 13 console call sites plus their held pages plus the apiclient admin methods; a bulk-export decision, which registration alone cannot resolve because a streaming GET cannot ride the current executor contract at all; the web console approvals surface; the apiclient held-response handling; the IDE held-promote handling; and an owner question of its own -- whether the approve permission should remain administrator-only.


**OWNER RULING 2026-08-22 -- the verdict stands; both load-bearing clauses are amended.** The re-scoping found **13 distinct client call sites yielding 6 distinct shipped defects**, against the 3 the earlier pass recorded, and **1 of 6 built-in roles reachable by 3 assignment paths**. The scope-out reasoning survives intact and both dishonest moves stay dishonest, so the verdict does not move. But the ruling turns on exactly two sentences and **both are measurably narrower than the code**. First, dual control is honoured on the console only in the sense that it **stops** you, not that it **works** there: there are zero release callers and no cookie on the JSON API. Second, the second approver is not a second operator but a **second full administrator**, minted most cheaply by mapping a directory group, and asked for **less credential proof than the requester was**. Both sentences are corrected in place, because a later ruling would otherwise inherit them as descriptions of a working mechanism.
