The item's anchor is retired rather than moved -- the `setdefault` it cites does not exist, and the pair lives once at `messagefoundry/api/header_floor.py:52`, applied by `SecurityHeaderFloorMiddleware` registered LAST at `messagefoundry/api/app.py:5317`. The item's batching premise dies with it: 3.4.1 now rests on the scheme condition and 3.4.6 on a directive reaching one response family, so those three no longer share a root.

**A fifth response-emitter class exists and two prior passes missed it in the same shape.** `messagefoundry/transports/http_listener.py` is engine code in declared scope that emits HTTP/1.1 responses from its own serializer: `build_response` (`:194-227`) writes a status line, Content-Type, Content-Length, caller extras and `Connection: close`, and nothing else -- measured by calling it directly, with a positive control in the same run that the instrument DOES report an extra header when one is present. Tree-wide absence with a firing control: security-header names return zero under `messagefoundry/transports/` while the identical pattern returns seven files elsewhere. **Adversarial review found a SIXTH class and was upheld, and the build as proposed reaches only part of it.** Responses synthesised BELOW the ASGI layer by the shipped server are absent from the surface entirely. Re-read at HEAD, the class has at least three members and they are not uniform: the protocol-level 400 applies `server_state.default_headers` on `httptools_impl.py:205-207` and applies NONE on `h11_impl.py:303-319`; the app-error 500 routes through `send` (`httptools_impl.py:447-459`, prepending default headers at `:478`), so it takes them on both; and the pre-handshake WebSocket refusal is a third. `messagefoundry/__main__.py:2833-2868` passes no `headers=` to `uvicorn.run`, so none of them carries nosniff today -- measured on a real uvicorn with a well-formed request in the same run as the positive control. **The completeness gate must be described for what it can do, or it becomes the same unmeasured claim one level up.** The proposed bidirectional AST inventory gate, modelled on the crypto-inventory gate that already ships, can bound the FIRST-PARTY emitter population -- the ASGI stack, the ADR 0023 listener, and any future engine-owned protocol subclass. The pinned verb asks that the `frame-ancestors` CSP directive be used for *every* HTTP response, and explicitly refuses `X-Frame-Options` as a substitute. Where the CSP applies the directive is the strictest possible value and default-on (`messagefoundry_webconsole/_auth.py:142`, `_security.py:206`), but it is scoped to non-static `/ui` paths at `messagefoundry/api/app.py:1270`.

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** On a first deployment, practical clickjacking exposure would be low -- no shipping browser honours CSP while ignoring `X-Frame-Options`. What is real is that the control leans on the mechanism the pinned text names obsolete, and the prior pass rested on that premise.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field for every HTTP response ... Note that the X-Frame-Options header field, although supported by browsers, is obsolete and may not be relied upon."

**What holds it short today.** The attachment-download response at a `/ui` path is served `default-src 'none'; sandbox` (`api/app.py:645`, applied at `:729`), and `frame-ancestors` takes no fallback from `default-src`, so that response carries none. JSON API responses and `/ui/static` assets were likewise measured without it. The residual also records that the `X-Frame-Options: DENY` universal-carrier premise is false -- it was measured absent from the body-cap 413 and from an unhandled 500.

**The research question.** What CSP construction carries `frame-ancestors` on every response without weakening either of the two policies that are currently correct -- the attachment sandbox and the per-response nonce policy -- given that a global header and a per-route header interact rather than compose. Separately and more importantly: does "every HTTP response" admit a defensible bound for non-document responses, and if so on what authority? That answer has to come from the pinned text and the directive's own semantics, not from the observation that a JSON body is inconvenient to frame.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Re-declaring the web application as "`/ui` only" so the JSON API leaves the denominator -- the console is a browser client of that API, so the surface is not separable by assertion. Nor citing `X-Frame-Options: DENY` as coverage: the pinned text forecloses it in the requirement itself, and it was measured absent from the same error paths anyway.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is REACHABLE WITH BUILD, and this item's own trap has INVERTED: the X-Frame-Options coverage claim is now TRUE, which makes it far more dangerous than when this item was written.** The item disqualified citing `X-Frame-Options: DENY` partly because it had been measured absent from the same error paths "anyway". That "anyway" is gone. Driven at HEAD `fc54d169`, XFO: DENY appears on 11 of 11 response families including the 413, the 411 and the unhandled 500, delivered by the header floor at `messagefoundry/api/header_floor.py:54` registered last at `messagefoundry/api/app.py:5317`. Every clause of "framing is denied everywhere in every shipping browser, so score it a pass" except the last now verifies, and the refusal is not a coverage argument at all -- it is the requirement's own second sentence, which puts XFO outside the graded population by construction. All three of this item's anchors have drifted (`645` to `662`, `729` to `746`, `1270` to `1296`).

**The mechanism question this item poses is answered, and the answer disqualifies the plan a prior disposition proposed.** A global directive and a per-route policy COMPOSE, but only if a SECOND `Content-Security-Policy` header FIELD is emitted rather than merged: per CSP Level 3 each policy is enforced independently and the effect is their intersection, so a second policy naming only `frame-ancestors 'none'` cannot weaken the attachment sandbox or the per-response nonce policy. Measured on a Starlette `MutableHeaders` already carrying `default-src 'none'; sandbox`: `setdefault` is a NO-OP, `append` yields two field lines. The 2026-07-22 disposition proposed `setdefault` and argued it "cannot fight the richer policies" -- true of the two /ui policies and FALSE of the attachment sandbox, so as written it would have left this item's own headline example uncovered while reporting itself complete.

**The second half of the quantifier question is also answered, and it does not admit the bound a reader will reach for.** The pinned corpus writes "HTTP responses include" in one V3.4 requirement and "for EVERY HTTP response" in this one, and across that section the three requirements carrying a universal quantifier are exactly the three standing at partial. Borrowing a sibling cell's stated narrower denominator would read away the one word this verb adds -- it is this item's out-of-scope move wearing consistency as a hat, which is a better disguise than an unargued scope assertion. The defensible bound comes from the directive's own semantics, and it is narrow: a JSON 200, a 404, a 413, a static asset and a download are all navigable, so the "a JSON body is inconvenient to frame" argument this item pre-emptively rejects is correctly rejected.

**Adversarial review was upheld: the denominator is short by at least five families, two of them the same kind as this item's headline example.** Re-verified at HEAD, `GET /messages/export` (`api/app.py:3101`, StreamingResponse at `:3204-3207` with `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="messages-export.ndjson"`, whose own comment at `:3105` calls it the largest PHI surface in its cluster) and `GET /audit/export` (`api/auth_routes.py:933`, StreamingResponse at `:1005-1008`) carry NO Content-Security-Policy at all -- strictly weaker than the `default-src 'none'; sandbox` the record treats as its worst case -- because `AttachmentSecurityHeadersMiddleware` is path-scoped by `_is_attachment_download_path` (`app.py:711-713`) and matches neither. `GET /metrics` (`app.py:4360`), the PHI-safe 422 handler (`app.py:1251`) and the console's CSP-report endpoint (`messagefoundry_webconsole/routes/core.py:1045`) are three more. On a first deployment `/messages/export` would serve bulk raw message bodies as a browser-navigable download with no CSP whatsoever. Review also caught a substituted quantifier: "every response family the engine COMPOSES" is not "every HTTP response", and the only item touching the uvicorn-composed layer is one the finding itself labels optional and lock-fragile -- and which is already absent from a shipped first-party runner (`harness/load/ingress_probe.py:160` constructs a uvicorn config with no `headers=`).

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** adding `frame-ancestors 'none'` to the attachment sandbox constant at `api/app.py:662`, re-pointing the four tests and the one docs sentence that pin its literal value; adding it to the client-network denial page's CSP (`api/client_networks.py:191`) and giving that denial's JSON arm (`:77-88`) a CSP it currently lacks; giving `SecurityHeaderFloorMiddleware` a carrier that APPENDS a second `Content-Security-Policy` field when no policy on the response already names the directive -- append, never `setdefault` and never assign, which is what preserves last-writer-wins for the four assigning writers -- with regression tests asserting the EFFECTIVE VALUE is `'none'` per family rather than merely that the directive is present, since the requirement's posture limb is default-DENY; revising the floor module's own stated contract ("writes only names none of them own") in the same change, because appending a CSP writes a name four writers do own; adding the CSP to the unhandled-exception handler's own header dict at `api/app.py:1231`, which the floor structurally cannot reach; emitting it from `transports/http_listener.py` `build_response`, which closes the one genuinely framable uncovered document in the tree -- the sync reply at `:853` that echoes a partner's Content-Type; passing headers on the single WebSocket accept and replacing the bare pre-accept close with a headered denial; and, as a labelled belt that must never be cited as the coverage, uvicorn default headers for the protocol-level responses no application middleware can reach.

**What holds it short today.** Five bulk PHI GETs: `/messages/search` (`api/app.py:2968`), `/messages/export` (`:3057`), `/messages/{message_id}` (`:3166`), `/uploads/{file_id}/messages` (`:3803`) and `/search/layered` (`:4068`). Two session mints on a safe method: `GET /ui/sso` (`messagefoundry_webconsole/routes/sso.py:87`) and `GET /ui/oidc/callback` (`routes/oidc.py:258`). The second arm cannot rescue them -- `Sec-Fetch` is read in six console files and nowhere in the engine, and both console shapes fail open on an absent header (`_auth.py:341-347`; `sso.py:64`, `oidc.py:182`, `oidc.py:226`).

**The research question.** Bounded by a recorded ruling the research must respect: the scorecard states that a future assessor must not upgrade this cell on the strength of `oidc_enabled` or `kerberos_enabled` shipping False, consistent with the owner's 2026-08-05 correction that a default-off feature scores partial rather than pass. Within that boundary, two things need establishing. Is bulk PHI retrieval "sensitive functionality" under this verb, given that it mutates nothing but streams the corpus? If it is, what would an honest pass require -- a POST twin for read endpoints changes caching, logging and client contracts, and a `Sec-Fetch` validator on the engine surface has to decide what to do with requests that carry no such headers at all, which is every non-browser client the product ships (the harness, `apiclient/`, an operator with curl). "Cannot honestly pass without breaking non-browser API clients, and here is the cost" is a valid finding.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Counting the two session-minting GETs as out of scope because SSO and OIDC ship off -- the ruling forecloses exactly that move. Nor declaring the JSON API a non-browser surface so a browser-origin requirement does not reach it, while the shipped console is a browser calling that API.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is REACHABLE WITH BUILD, it requires a MIXED-ARM build because the two surfaces have opposite answers to this item's own blocking question, and the engine half is an owner funding decision across roughly fifty routes rather than the handful this item enumerates.** Two of this item's sentences fail at HEAD `fc54d169`. Its list of "five bulk PHI GETs" drops the record's own "at least five" hedge into a bare enumeration; the repo's tested predicate (`tests/test_no_store_phi_coverage.py:104`) run over the built app finds ELEVEN PHI-read routes, all GET, none with an unsafe-method twin, and all five cited line numbers miss at HEAD. And its premise that "the shipped console is a browser calling that API" is false: `mount_ui` registers every `/ui` route onto the engine's own FastAPI object and the `/ui` handlers call the engine handlers in-process, which `require_ui`'s docstring states verbatim. The CONCLUSION -- do not declare the JSON API out of scope -- survives on a better ground: a sibling V3.5 cell already adjudicated the identical scoping question on the identical surface inclusively, so re-litigating it here is forum-shopping a boundary already decided.

**The header-less problem this item names as global is true of the JSON API and false of the console, and that asymmetry is what forces the split.** Measured across the whole first-party tree, the console has exactly ONE non-browser HTTP client -- `messagefoundry/tray/probe.py:102`, a tokenless liveness GET of `/ui` -- against a positive control of eleven JSON-API call sites in `messagefoundry/apiclient/client.py`. So a fail-closed fetch-metadata gate is shippable on `/ui` and is not shippable on the JSON API. Conversely, arm B is DECORATIVE on the JSON API: `require()` resolves identity solely through `bearer_token()` (`messagefoundry/api/security.py:216` calling `:165-171`), which reads only the Authorization header with no cookie fallback, and `require_service_cert` raises at app-construction time for any PHI-view permission (`api/security.py:420-426`), so no browser-initiated cross-origin call or resource load can carry authority there. Wiring a `Sec-Fetch` validator onto those routes would fire this cell's own recorded re-score signal while rejecting only requests already destined for 401 -- the disqualified no-op wearing a fetch-metadata hat.

**Adversarial review was upheld and the engine limb is four times larger than the build that was scoped for it.** The enumerating instrument filtered `isinstance(route, APIRoute)` and then selected with a PHI predicate, so it was blind twice over -- to non-`APIRoute` route objects (four anonymous docs routes and the `/ui/static` mount) and to sensitive non-PHI GETs -- and every stated control ran inside that blind set, so no reading of any of them could have contradicted the enumeration. Re-measured by the synthesizer over the built app: **50 safe-method route rows on the JSON API, against a positive control of 54 unsafe-method rows in the same run**, of which 40 paths carry only safe methods. The 38 the proposal never touches include the identity and authorization administration reads (`/users`, `/users/{user_id}/permissions`, `/roles`, `/ad-group-map`), the audit reads (`/audit`, `/audit/export`), the approvals queue, session and second-factor state, and the posture reads. Because arm A is a NEGATIVE limb, those boxes would be covered by NEITHER arm after the full funded build -- and the record's only stated reading of this section's sensitivity scope (auth requests, state changes, resource-demanding operations) sweeps them in rather than out.

**The console build is well-founded but carries a build-blocking correction and an unstated cost.** A `Sec-Fetch-Site` rule refusing cross-site outright would break BOTH federated-login legs, which are cross-site BY DESIGN and recorded as such in shipped comments (`routes/oidc.py:230`, `routes/sso.py:60-63`, citing ADR 0068). The fix stays inside arm B and is the verb's own navigation sub-limb: permit cross-site only when `Sec-Fetch-Mode` is `navigate` AND `Sec-Fetch-Dest` is `document` AND `Sec-Fetch-User` is `?1`, on those two paths only. The build is also load-bearing rather than decorative, for a reason the finding under-argued: on the shipped loopback default another local port is SAME-site, so `SameSite=Strict` does not stop an injected image load against `GET /ui/messages/{id}/attachments/{aid}` (`routes/core.py:495-509`), which is the verb's own named resource-load case. And the honest cost list must include the hundreds of shipped `/ui` test call sites that send no fetch-metadata headers and would red under a fail-closed middleware, alongside the tray probe and the missing supported-browser matrix.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the console fetch-metadata validator as pure-ASGI middleware registered inside `mount_ui` -- which also fixes the recorded defect that the console's checks are per-handler rather than middleware -- enforcing `Sec-Fetch-Dest` in {document, empty}, refusing `Sec-Fetch-Mode: no-cors`, refusing cross-site and same-site, and FAILING CLOSED on an absent header, with three written carve-outs (`/ui/static/**`, `POST /ui/csp-report`, and the two federated-login legs under the narrow navigation rule); inverting the three navigation gates (`routes/sso.py:64`, `routes/oidc.py:182`, `:226`) from `if mode is not None and mode != "navigate"` to a strict test plus a `Sec-Fetch-Dest: document` requirement, so the two session-minting GETs (`routes/sso.py:87`, `routes/oidc.py:258-259`) are closed by being FIXED rather than counted out; the tray console-liveness probe fix, the only non-browser `/ui` client in the tree; deleting the GET and moving criteria into the body on the query-bearing bulk PHI reads, which doubles as the fix for the PHI-needle-in-query-string defect; the safe-method conversion across the remaining engine reads, gated on the owner's funding decision and priced as "the JSON read API becomes POST-only" rather than as seven property-neutral reads; a fetch-metadata check on `GET /service/identity` (`api/app.py:4845-4859`) regardless of that fork, since it is the engine's only ambient-credential GET and writes an audit row per hit; a route-table drift guard built on the repo's whole-surface route walk (which emits WebSocket rows, mounts and plain routes rather than dropping them) with a sensitivity classifier on top, demonstrated failing on a planted non-PHI sensitive GET; and the supported-browser matrix, without which a fail-closed console gate cannot honestly ship.

**Progress 2026-09-04 -- the console limb is BUILT and this item stays OPEN. The fail-closed arm is DECLINED WITH A MEASUREMENT, and it is a browser-support decision rather than a code change.** Everything below was verified by execution against the built app with a positive control in the same run, never by reading.

**Re-measure first, and the largest correction is that this item's own proposed console build had already half landed.** A `UiFetchMetadataMiddleware` has been on `main` since commit `829ed98f8` under **#1371**, which scoped it to the `/ui/static` Mount that a route dependency cannot reach. So the middleware, its `mount_ui` registration and eight tests already existed; what did not exist was the tightening this item asks for. Two of the arms in the paragraph above were therefore already shipped and are struck here rather than rebuilt: refusing `Sec-Fetch-Mode: no-cors` and refusing cross-site and same-site both hold on `main` today.

**The load-bearing case this item names was ALREADY CLOSED, and saying so is the honest result.** The injected image load against `GET /ui/messages/{id}/attachments/{aid}` from a sibling local port returns **403** on unmodified `main`: `same-site` is a member of `_auth._CROSS_ORIGIN_FETCH`, and an image load is `no-cors`, so it never reaches the navigation carve-out. The argument that `SameSite=Strict` does not stop it is correct and the middleware does.

**What was actually still open were two holes in the carve-out, both measured before the fix.** First, `Sec-Fetch-Dest` was a **denylist** of `object` and `embed`: a cross-site `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` carrying `Sec-Fetch-Dest: iframe`, `frame`, or **no destination header at all** was served 303 in the same run where `object` was refused 403. `frame-ancestors 'none'` does not cover that gap, because it is emitted only on the /ui HTML surface and `/ui/static` -- the tier this middleware exists to reach -- carries no CSP at all. Second, the carve-out was granted to `same-site` on the same terms as `cross-site`, and the two are not alike: `SameSite=Strict` strips the cookie from every cross-site request but not from a same-site one, and a site ignores the port, so a page on `http://127.0.0.1:9999` could script `window.open` at a /ui URL and arrive **with the operator's session cookie**.

**Built:** the destination check is now an **allowlist** of `document`, and a **`same-site` navigation must additionally carry `Sec-Fetch-User: ?1`** -- the header a browser sets only for a user-activated navigation, which a scripted `window.open`, a `location =` assignment and a `<meta http-equiv=refresh>` all lack. Both live in a named `_is_safe_top_level_navigation` predicate in `messagefoundry_webconsole/_security.py`. Five mutations, each a change someone would plausibly propose as an improvement, are killed by exactly one distinct test each: the denylist restored; the activation clause dropped as dead code; `?1` demanded on both halves; every same-site navigation refused outright; and absence made to fail closed. A row for the whole control, which #1371 never added, is now in `docs/SECURITY.md` Table A.

**`Sec-Fetch-User` is demanded of the same-site half ONLY, and the asymmetry is deliberate.** The IdP's redirect back to the OIDC callback is a server-driven 302 that carries no user activation once the IdP session is established, so a `?1` requirement on the cross-site half would refuse silent re-authentication -- a broken login that every hermetic test in the tree still passes, which is how a first cut of this middleware shipped a 403 on every real SSO login once already. The proposed narrowing of the carve-out to the two federated-login paths is likewise **not** built: a cross-site navigation arrives with no cookie, so refusing an operator's intranet link into the console would cost usability and buy no authority.

**DECLINED, with the number: failing closed on an absent header.** Measured by inverting that one condition and running the console suite: **231 of 408 tests go red**, and the shipped Windows tray's own tokenless `GET /ui` liveness probe (`messagefoundry/tray/probe.py:102`) is refused with it. The deeper reason it cannot ship is not the test cost: `docs/SYSTEM-REQUIREMENTS.md:135` promises only "A modern browser", and no supported-browser matrix exists anywhere in the tree, so refusing a browser that omits the header family is an undeclared support decision. Every rule this item did build is reached **only after `Sec-Fetch-Site` has arrived**, which is precisely what lets those ship without that matrix and what an absence rule could not claim. The matrix stays a named precondition.

**NOT DONE, and named rather than started: the three route-level navigation gates.** `routes/sso.py:64`, `routes/oidc.py:182` and `:226` still read `mode is not None and mode != "navigate"`, which carries both defects fixed above. They are not shadowed by the middleware -- they also catch same-origin non-navigation fetches, and they **audit** the reject, which middleware cannot -- so changing them alters an audited reject shape and belongs in its own change. Unifying all four sites behind the one predicate is the natural follow-on and is unallocated.

**THE ENGINE LIMB IS AN OWNER FUNDING DECISION AND WAS NOT STARTED.** Re-measured over the built app: **50 safe-method route rows against a positive control of 54 unsafe-method rows**, of which 40 paths carry only safe methods. The 38 the original proposal never touches include the identity and authorization administration reads, the audit reads, the approvals queue, session and second-factor state, and the posture reads. Priced honestly it is "the JSON read API becomes POST-only", not a handful of endpoint twins. Note also that arm B is **decorative** there and must not be wired as a consolation: `require()` resolves identity solely through `bearer_token()` (`messagefoundry/api/security.py:216` calling `:165-171`), which reads only the Authorization header with no cookie fallback, so a `Sec-Fetch` validator on those routes would fire this cell's own re-score signal while rejecting only requests already destined for 401.

**Two corrections to this item's own text, neither propagated.** Its "five bulk PHI GETs" is a bare enumeration that dropped the record's own "at least five" hedge -- the repo's tested predicate (`tests/test_no_store_phi_coverage.py:104`) run over the built app finds **at least eleven** PHI-read routes, all GET, none with an unsafe-method twin, and all five cited line numbers miss at HEAD. And its premise that "the shipped console is a browser calling that API" is false: `mount_ui` registers every `/ui` route onto the engine's own FastAPI object and the `/ui` handlers call the engine handlers in-process, which `require_ui`'s docstring states verbatim. The conclusion it supports -- do not declare the JSON API out of scope -- survives on the better ground already recorded here, that a sibling V3.5 cell adjudicated the identical scoping question on the identical surface inclusively.

**Status unchanged, deliberately.** The closing act is a vault scorecard re-score plus a banner flip, neither of which is a Builder's to make; shipped code beside an open item is the correct outcome here.

## 1123. research an honest pass for ASVS 3.5.5 -- what a trustworthy postMessage origin check is inside a VS Code webview

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P3.** Value **4/10** · Difficulty **3/10** · _fill-in_. No PHI and no engine surface, the interface exists only in the VS Code extension, and the platform-limits finding is already written down and test-enforced, which leaves value in the polish band. Difficulty 3 is the vault record plus the SDS-3.7 discharge, and that discharge is not a formality: webviewMessaging.ts claims every panel is served script-src nonce, while stepsView.ts:959 emits a CSP of default-src none plus style-src unsafe-inline with no script-src at all, so the blanket claim has to be checked panel by panel. _(was 5/10 · 5/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **3.5.5** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that messages received by the postMessage interface be discarded if the origin is not trusted, or if the syntax is invalid. All eight receivers in the shipped IDE extension discard on an unexpected discriminator; none of the eight reads `event.origin` or `event.source`.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** No PHI effect and no engine effect -- the interface exists only in the VS Code extension, not in the web console or the engine. On a first deployment the exposure would be bounded by each webview's `default-src 'none'` CSP with a per-render nonce, so the only poster in a webview's frame tree would be the extension host itself.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that messages received by the postMessage interface are discarded if the origin of the message is not trusted, or if the syntax of the message is invalid."

**What holds it short today.** Eight `window.addEventListener('message', ...)` receivers under `ide/src/` -- `alertEditor.ts:321`, `codeSetEditor.ts:527`, `connectionEditor.ts:639`, `home.ts:175`, `securityEditor.ts:326`, `sourceControl.ts:518`, `testBench.ts:790`, `wiringMap.ts:403` -- each with no else branch for an unrecognised `command`/`type`, and an origin/source scan over `ide/src` and `ide/media` returning nothing but unrelated property accesses. The residual reads the clause conjunctively and argues the grammar decides it, so the origin arm is required, not optional.

**The research question.** What a *verifiable* origin or source check even is in this runtime. A VS Code webview's host origin is a generated `vscode-webview://` value rather than a fixed string, so research has to establish what a receiver can compare against that is both stable across VS Code versions and not supplied by the sender, and whether `event.source` identity is usable there at all. Two outcomes are legitimate: a check that genuinely holds, or the finding that the platform exposes no verifiable origin, in which case the honest record is that the named control cannot be built and the webview CSP is what actually bounds the risk. If it goes that way, SDS-3.7 binds -- the CSP claim has to be verified as a real enforcement property, not asserted as a compensating control.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Reading the requirement's "or" as two alternative compliance routes so the existing discriminator check alone carries the cell. The scorecard already rejected that reading and gives its grammatical reasoning; re-adopting it would drain the requirement of content by letting an application that never inspects origin claim conformance.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is REACHABLE WITH BUILD, CONTINGENT on one platform measurement nobody has taken, and this item's implicit premise that the origin question is untouched is dead -- it has been built, graded, and rejected as a verdict-mover.** This item's two measurement sentences still hold at HEAD `fc54d169` (eight receivers, none reading `event.origin` or `event.source`), established by two independent instruments -- a line-based grep and a multiline-tolerant scan over 109 files -- both returning 8, against a positive control of 98 `addEventListener` occurrences. All eight of its anchors are stale by exactly five lines (`ide/src/alertEditor.ts:316`, `codeSetEditor.ts:522`, `connectionEditor.ts:634`, `home.ts:170`, `securityEditor.ts:321`, `sourceControl.ts:513`, `testBench.ts:785`, `wiringMap.ts:398`). On 2026-08-17 the extension gained `ide/src/webviewMessaging.ts`, a marker above each receiver, and three pinning tests; the record has ruled that a documented rationale is not a discard, by analogy to the neighbouring warning-is-not-a-refusal ruling. A reader coming to this item cold will re-propose that move first.

**The shipped rationale's load-bearing sentence is over-general, and the false step is identifiable.** `webviewMessaging.ts:15-17` argues that "anything this script could compare with would have to be read out of the incoming event or out of its own document at runtime -- that is, supplied by the very sender the check is supposed to authenticate." Those are two different things fused by an em dash. A value read out of the INCOMING EVENT is sender-supplied; a value the document resolves from its OWN browsing context (`window.parent`, `window.origin`) is not -- the embedder fixed it and no poster can change it. The file is right that `event.origin` has no bakeable constant and right that a prefix test on the webview scheme would be theatre; it over-generalises from those two to "no comparand exists", and it asserts that without recording any measurement of what actually arrives.

**The measurement is the gate, and it should run before anything is designed.** Add one probe to the integration leg that already exists, open a panel, post from the host, and echo back `ev.source` identity against `window.parent`, `ev.origin`, `window.origin`, `location.origin`, and whether `window.parent === window`. The discriminating question is whether the webview scheme yields a TUPLE origin or an OPAQUE one: if tuple, `ev.origin === window.origin` is a genuine same-origin check with a self-read comparand and is per-panel unique; if opaque, both sides read the string "null" and the comparison is vacuous while looking exactly like a passing origin check -- the sender-supplied-comparand trap wearing the best disguise available. Under the opaque outcome the named control is unbuildable, the acceptance criterion is unreachable, and whether a host-minted token satisfies the origin limb becomes an owner ruling that the default-to-the-worse-verdict rule says should be expected to stay partial.

**The census guarantee is claimed wider than the instrument that enforces it, and that matters because the pass would rest on it.** All three pinning tests filter on `/window\.addEventListener\(\s*['"]message['"]/` applied to ONE trimmed line. Measured against candidate spellings: `window.addEventListener('message'` matches, while `globalThis.`, `self.`, a bare `addEventListener('message'`, `window.onmessage =` and a two-line split ALL evade. The corpus helper feeding those regexes is narrow one layer earlier still -- it reads `ide/media` non-recursively and filters `.js`, so a receiver added under `ide/media/walkthrough/` or spelled `.mjs` never reaches the regex at all. Nothing is wrong today, since a spelling-agnostic census also returns 8; but a pass whose completeness limb rests on that pin would rest on an instrument answering a narrower question than the one asked.

**One record correction that does not move the verdict.** The residual says data handling inside the receivers is not an additional defect, on the strength of checking one receiver's escaping. That is broader than what was measured: `ide/src/testBench.ts` has five `innerHTML` assignments (`:679`, `:700`, `:723`, `:759`, `:790`) and several message-derived values reach them unescaped (`:689-693`, `:629-639`, `:659-661`, `:717`, and at least three more). Those are safe today only because the host generates them, which is exactly the trust this requirement says must be established -- and CSP bounds the sink to markup and UI spoofing rather than script execution, because `script-src` is nonce-only on all eight receiver-bearing panels and no policy in `ide/` sets `frame-src` or `child-src`, so nested frames fall back to `default-src 'none'`.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the webview message-delivery probe on the existing integration leg, kept afterwards as a standing regression test and run BEFORE any origin or source check is designed; a per-panel channel object that mints the CSP nonce and a SEPARATE 144-bit message token together (never reusing the CSP nonce, which is a script-execution capability), embeds the token through the existing JSON-into-script helper, stamps all 33 host-to-webview sends, and regenerates with every one of the 16 `webview.html` assignments so a stale token cannot silently kill the channel, with the buffered-post race designed against; a fail-closed source or origin rejection at all eight receivers, conditional on the probe's answer, with the silent-breakage cost carried rather than engineered away; widening the receiver-census instrument -- BOTH the three regexes and the corpus helper -- worth doing on its own merits whether or not the guard is built; guard pinning with jsdom unit tests proving the guard discards a no-token, a wrong-token and a wrong-source message and ACCEPTS the right one, the accept case being the positive control without which a guard that rejected everything would pass vacuously; rewriting `webviewMessaging.ts` from a documented absence into a statement of what the check is and what it still does not cover, correcting the fused sentence and updating the pinning test that requires that file to keep naming its three tokens; and escaping the message-derived values that reach `innerHTML` in the test-bench webview.

## 1124. research an honest pass for ASVS 3.7.5 -- deriving a supported-browser matrix rather than authoring one that fits

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P3.** Value **4/10** · Difficulty **3/10** · _fill-in_. SYSTEM-REQUIREMENTS.md:135 still offers only a modern browser, the web-console plan still carries the matrix as open question 1 at 11-web-console.md:446, and SECURITY-DOCS-POLICY.md:5 still withholds the operator-facing copy while the behavioural half ships in _security.py and _html.py, so the antecedent the requirement grades against remains undefined. Value 4 because this is documentation completeness over a working control set with no exposure and no product effect; difficulty 3 because the deliverable is a table derived from the shipped feature floors plus two owner rulings, touching no code, no mypy surface and no test. _(was 4/10 · 5/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **3.7.5** (L3) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that the application behave *as documented* when the browser does not support the expected security features. The behavioural half is built and substantial; what holds the cell short is that the requirement's antecedent -- the expected browsers and versions -- has no shipped definition (`docs/testing/master-test-plan/11-web-console.md:446` records it as an open question).

> **SHIPPED-BUT-OPEN 2026-08-22 -- PR #497, same [ADR 0165](adr/0165-a-builder-pr-satisfies-the-ledger-gate-with-a-paired-commit-authored-by-the-dispatcher-or-lander.md) pairing.** The degrade-contract guard is split so its CODE half runs in a public checkout: `messagefoundry_webconsole/_security.py`, `packaging/messagefoundry-webconsole/tests/test_ui_csp_canary.py`.
> **WHAT THIS FIXES IS A GUARD THAT PASSED WITHOUT RUNNING.** Its assertions had teeth -- a planted mutation flips them -- but the whole module skipped on a vault-only document absent from every public checkout, reporting `19 passed, 3 skipped`, silently, under `-q`. The split lands an announced absence that prints in the warnings summary even under `-q`, an env pointer to repoint the comparison, and an env flag making absence a hard failure. Against the real vault copy the suite runs **25 passed with ZERO skips**, so the runbook and the in-code enumeration agree today -- which was assumed and is now known.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore
**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P3. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** No product effect and no exposure. This is a documentation-completeness gap sitting on top of a working control set, and it should be described that way.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that the application behaves as documented (such as warning the user or blocking access) if the browser used to access the application does not support the expected security features."

**What holds it short today.** Four active degrade detects ship on a startable configuration, gated on a bound per-response nonce (`messagefoundry_webconsole/_html.py:186` onward), and the complete 15-row per-feature degrade contract ships inside the wheel as the `_security.py:51-159` module docstring. Two things carry the partial: `docs/SYSTEM-REQUIREMENTS.md:135` says only "A modern browser", so no minimum versions exist anywhere in the shipped tree; and the operator-facing copy of that degrade contract is deliberately withheld by `docs/SECURITY-DOCS-POLICY.md:5`.

**The research question.** Both halves are owner calls, and the research exists to put the options in front of the owner rather than to decide them. First: what would a supported-browser matrix be *derived from*? The shipped features have real floors -- nonce-based CSP with `strict-dynamic`, `window.isSecureContext`, `PublicKeyCredential`, COOP/CORP, `Clear-Site-Data` -- and the honest matrix is whatever those floors imply, not whatever currently works. Second: can "as documented" be honestly satisfied while the operator-facing degrade copy stays withheld, given the in-wheel docstring already states the contract per feature? Whether that docstring counts as the documentation the verb names is itself an open reading.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Writing a browser matrix chosen to match observed behaviour, with no derivation from the feature floors. This requirement measures the application against a document, which makes authoring the document to fit the single cheapest way to buy the cell and the one to refuse. Publishing the withheld runbook copy purely to move a score, against a standing docs policy, is the same move in a different file.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is REACHABLE WITH BUILD, and the cheap move this item forbids would not work even if it were permitted.** The withheld operator-facing copy was read: its section headed "Supported browsers and the defined fallback" names ZERO versions and no matrix at all -- it is a prose mirror of the same fifteen rows. Publishing it verbatim would close the delivery limb and leave the antecedent limb exactly where it is. So the honest restatement of the trap is narrower and sharper than this item gives: the disqualified move is publishing the vault copy as a batch, verbatim, without reading it against the project's own withholding test. That test is public: `docs/SECURITY-DOCS-POLICY.md:11-18` withholds a document only if it describes an open, un-remediated weakness in enough detail to act on or names a customer, site or deployment. The policy states a LOCATION fact (the security-posture set is maintained privately); it is the WITHHOLDING RULE that does not reach this content, and the 2026-08-17 publication decision calls itself "a judgement, not a ruling", nominates that same public test as the decider, and carves out in terms that work closing a cell "by writing prose from public code" is unaffected and should proceed.

**The behavioural half is built and substantial, and the currency claim behind it is false in every tree that exists.** The fifteen-row contract at `messagefoundry_webconsole/_security.py:79-156` re-counts exactly at HEAD `fc54d169`: four rows DETECTED and WARNED, eleven DEGRADES SILENTLY each with a named compensating control, and 19 shipped tests pass covering the canary's emission, its lack of a nonce, its ordering and the server-rendered banner. But `_security.py:73-78` tells every reader a CI guard enforces the enumeration, and it does not run: `pytest packaging/messagefoundry-webconsole/tests/test_ui_csp_canary.py -q -rs` returns 19 passed, 3 skipped, and the three skips ARE the bucket-drift guard, skipping at `:513` on a vaulted path -- with the skip firing BEFORE the docstring-side loop in all three, so the artifact that ships in the wheel is unchecked. The cell's own 2026-08-08 amendment is over-stated on exactly this: the testpaths change moved the MODULE into collection, it did not un-skip the guard. Fixing that is the PRECONDITION for any re-score, and it is worth doing whether or not the cell ever moves.

**There is a shipped conformance gap on a startable configuration, which is this cell's own subject rather than the neighbouring documentation cell's.** Setting `MEFOR_WEBCONSOLE_DISABLE_BROWSER_HARDENING` (`_auth.py:77`) binds no nonce, so ALL FOUR detects vanish -- `messagefoundry_webconsole/_html.py:155` says so in the emitting module. The shipped contract does not: its only statement about the opt-out (`_security.py:24-30`) is that the middleware binds no nonce and mutates no header, which describes header emission rather than the disappearance of the warnings. An operator reading the shipped contract would believe the CSP-not-enforced banner still fires. The variable appears in no operator document -- zero hits in `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`, `docs/SECURITY.md` and `docs/SYSTEM-REQUIREMENTS.md`, against a firing seven-hit tree-wide control.

**Adversarial review was upheld on the IDE, and the IDE limb is a build rather than the one paragraph proposed for it.** The limb that IS this cell's subject -- conformance -- was never instantiated for the extension. And its claimed zero is not zero: `ide/src/stepsView.ts:284-287` arms a 3-second handshake and `:400-411` surfaces a user-visible error when the webview script fails to initialize, with the client half at `ide/media/stepsWebview.js:10-12` -- the same class as the console's own script-execution row. The finding's absence came from a vocabulary grep controlled only on the CONSOLE's vocabulary, which could never have found a detect written as a ping. Re-measured at HEAD: 13 files assign `webview.html`, 12 carry a CSP meta, and `ide/src/configEditors.ts` (three assignments at `:59`, `:140`, `:306`) is absent from the enumeration entirely, with `:59` a CSP-less shell. So exactly 1 of 13 shells detects the inert-script state, every editor webview is script-only, and an unmet host expectation would leave a rendered but inert form with no notice. `ide/media/` was never opened at all, even though the shipped static webview script lives there -- and the extension's own hardening suite already carries a control test written because a source-only scan "would report a clean media/ directory whether or not they ever opened one".

**What would still NOT be an honest pass.** Writing a browser matrix chosen to match observed behaviour -- this cell measures the application against a document, and the document is the movable part, so authoring it to fit buys the cell and verifies nothing. The falsifiable test of whether the derivation was done: does the floor rest on CSP NONCE-SOURCE support (the feature whose absence blocks every script including the watchdog) or on `'strict-dynamic'` (which a CSP2 browser ignores harmlessly)? Both browsers look fine in a smoke test, so only a derived matrix distinguishes them. Also not honest: re-pointing the dormant guard's accessor at a newly-authored page written to satisfy it; shipping a `/ui` page and re-scoring while the IDE limb stays absent; and writing the IDE paragraph to match today's behaviour, which is the authored-to-fit trap one artifact down.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the derived browser-support floor, enumerating the relied-on set FROM THE CODE with the derivations the bucket-drift guard already implements and resolving each member to a per-engine minimum from a PINNED, CITED compat dataset, producing a floor plus a per-engine table of permanent documented degradations rather than a single supported-at-version-N row (two of the fifteen rows are not simultaneously satisfiable by any one browser, and the contract already says so for one); the operator-facing browser-support surface rendered from the in-code source of truth and served as a `/ui` page so it ships in the console wheel and is reachable at the moment of degradation, linked from the three banner texts that today say only "Use a current browser" (`_html.py:377`, `:397`) and mirrored into `docs/SYSTEM-REQUIREMENTS.md:135`; the bucket-drift guard split so the docstring-side assertions execute unconditionally and only the runbook comparison skips; the opt-out degrade disclosure plus documenting the variable in an operator document; generalising the inert-webview notice across the remaining shells BEFORE any IDE paragraph is written, plus a decision on `configEditors.ts:59`; the IDE client-support statement placed where the VSIX carries it (`.vscodeignore` keeps `docs/` out of the package), reconciling `ide/package.json` `engines.vscode ^1.95.0` with `docs/SYSTEM-REQUIREMENTS.md:136`; repairing the 17 shipped string literals that send an operator to a `docs/security/` path no installed or cloned tree contains, including the console auto-degrade message at `__main__.py:1835`; and a boundary statement on the opt-in `[api].expose_docs` surface.


**TWO FILED CLAIMS ARE WRONG, CORRECTED 2026-08-22 BY THE CLAIMING LANE AND RE-VERIFIED HERE. THE FIRST WOULD SEND A FIXER TO A NO-OP.**

**CORRECTION 1 -- "the bucket-drift guard DOES NOT RUN" is the wrong mechanism with the right conclusion.** It **does** run: `ci.yml` carries a *Web console tests (pytest)* step firing on every code pull request and push, and `pyproject` `testpaths` collects the suite locally.

***THE REAL DEFECT IS A SKIP, NOT AN ABSENCE.*** All three enforcement tests call `_runbook_contract()` **before** their loops, and it `pytest.skip`s when `docs/security/OFF-LOOPBACK-DEPLOYMENT.md` is missing -- **which it is on `main` BY DESIGN**, deny-listed to the vault (`git ls-files docs` returns 487; `git ls-files docs/security` returns **0**). **So the code-side half of the check is held hostage to a vault-only document it does not need.**

**Why the distinction costs real work rather than being pedantry:** acting on *"does not run"* means wiring it into CI. **It is already wired.** That fix is a no-op, it goes green, and all three enforcement tests still skip. The assertions were shown to have teeth -- tampering the docstring flips the check -- **they are simply never evaluated.** And the step runs `pytest ... -q` with **no `-rs`**, so three skips render as three `s` characters and nothing surfaces.

**This is a SEVENTH instance of the class ADR 0156 records for six `*_doc_drift` modules, now in the console package.** `ci.yml` already carries an explicit warning about exactly this for the **engine** suite -- *"89 of these tests SKIP here and that is structural... do not read the skips as coverage"* -- and **the console step has no equivalent note.**

**CORRECTION 2 -- the count is FOURTEEN literals, not seventeen, and the cited line is dead.** An AST pass gives `LITERAL=14`, `DOCSTRING=2`, `COMMENT=2`, plus one YAML comment: **19 references on 19 lines**. The 17 is reachable only by counting two module docstrings and a YAML comment as string literals.

***THE CONSOLE AUTO-DEGRADE CITATION AT `__main__.py:1835` POINTS AT A COMMENT.*** The literal is at **`:1854`**; it drifted when an unrelated commit inserted 19 lines above it. **A fixer opening `:1835` today finds a comment and may conclude the item is already done.** The citation was correct when written -- which is the argument for symbols over line numbers, not against the original author.

**TWO LINES A NAIVE FIX WOULD BREAK, both confirmed here:** `config/retention_classification.py:13` is an **anti-instance** -- its whole point is that `docs/security/` **is** gitignored, and deleting the path destroys the reasoning anchoring the PHI retention drift test to the tracked `docs/PHI.md`. And `auth/identity.py:39-40` is the already-fixed case from `#1151`. *Counting that second one in or out without saying which is how three sessions derive three different totals from one tree.*

**Honest restatement: 14 literals -- 13 runtime operator messages plus the scaffolded CI template -- at `:1854`, not `:1835`.**

**CROSS-REFERENCE, ADDED SO THESE TWO RECORDS DO NOT DRIFT APART: the skip mechanism above is ALREADY RECORDED ON `main` UNDER `#1116`, down to the same numbers** -- 19 passed, 3 skipped, naming `_runbook_contract` at `test_ui_csp_canary.py:502-517`. **The claiming lane re-derived it independently, which is corroboration rather than a new discovery, and this item should not be read as the first place it was found.**

*Two items describing one mechanism is the shape that produced a duplicate allocation twice tonight. It is tolerable here only because the two are now explicitly joined; whoever closes either should check the other.*

**AND `#1116` CARRIES A HALF THIS ITEM LACKS, WHICH IS AN SDS-3.7 CASE.** `messagefoundry_webconsole/_security.py:72-77` tells the reader the canary **derives all three sets from the code and fails on an unbucketed member.** **That sentence is false in every shipped tree** -- the derivation is exactly what the skip prevents from running. *A comment asserting a guard's behaviour, in the file the guard protects, while the guard is unreachable, is a compensating control resting on a false premise: the reader who checks the code finds reassurance instead of the gap.*
## 1125. research an honest pass for ASVS 4.2.1 -- what a single component can claim about request smuggling when the chain is not its own

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **6/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _big bet_. The two intake surfaces still disagree exactly as filed -- exact equality at http_listener.py:318 against substring containment at api/app.py:1323 and :1339 -- so a legal Transfer-Encoding of gzip, chunked is classified differently by the engine's own two parsers. Value 6 is rung 6, and a fact the filing does not record bounds it further: http_listener.py:202 ships one-request-per-connection with no keep-alive, so the listener half cannot be pipelined into a following request and the desync is reachable only against an operator-chosen upstream. Difficulty 6 for the unmeasured half -- exercising both parsers across the RFC 9112 grammar, settling what all application components binds to, and re-verifying a cell whose last_verified is the oldest here. _(was 6/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **4.2.1** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that *all application components* determine HTTP message boundaries by the mechanism appropriate to the HTTP version, and that in HTTP/1.x a present `Transfer-Encoding` makes `Content-Length` ignorable. What holds it short is that the engine's two HTTP intake surfaces do not agree on how they detect chunked framing.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** On a first deployment behind a front proxy, a desync between two components about where a message ends is the classic smuggling primitive. The engine parses with one h11 instance on the API side, which bounds it, but the disagreement between its own two surfaces is real and unremarked.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that all application components (including load balancers, firewalls, and application servers) determine boundaries of incoming HTTP messages using the appropriate mechanism for the HTTP version to prevent HTTP request smuggling."

**What holds it short today.** `messagefoundry/transports/http_listener.py:316` tests `head.headers.get("transfer-encoding", "").lower() == "chunked"` -- exact equality -- while the ASGI middleware at `messagefoundry/api/app.py:1294` substrings `"chunked" in transfer_encoding`. A legal `Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked` passes one and not the other. Two record facts matter for whoever picks this up: the cell is among the thinnest in the scorecard (`last_verified = "2026-08-01"` at `f8d11685`, no `reviewed_by`, no re-score trigger), and its only ledger mention anywhere is a *closed* item listing it under `**Closes (ASVS 5.0 L3):**` at `docs/archive/backlog/BACKLOG-CLOSED.md:4293` while the scorecard scores it partial.

**The research question.** The verb's subject is "all application components", and the engine ships behind an operator-chosen proxy it does not control and cannot test. So: what can shipped software honestly claim on its own -- is the assessable unit the engine's own parsers (uvicorn/h11 plus the hand-rolled `http_listener`), or does the verb reach the whole chain, in which case an honest pass may be unreachable for a product rather than a deployment and the right outcome is a recorded deviation? Underneath that sits a plain measurement nobody has taken: what the two parsers actually do across the RFC 9112 grammar -- repeated `Transfer-Encoding` fields, a list with a trailing empty element, obs-fold, and case and whitespace variants. Re-verifying the cell is part of this item, not a precondition for it.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Aligning the two string tests and scoring pass on that alone -- it would fix one known input shape and leave the grammar unmeasured, which is a completeness claim rather than a result. Nor re-declaring the proxy out of scope so that "all components" quietly becomes a sentence about the engine by itself.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. The cell cannot honestly pass today under either reading of its scope, the build is unconditional and larger than this item describes, and the ceiling turns on an owner ruling this item does not frame correctly.** This item's bounding sentence is measurably FALSE: "the engine parses with one h11 instance on the API side, which bounds it". At HEAD `fc54d169`, `AutoHTTPProtocol` resolves to `uvicorn.protocols.http.httptools_impl.HttpToolsProtocol` -- httptools 0.8.0 sits in `requirements.lock:377` with no environment marker under `uvicorn[standard]`, so a hash-locked install always gets llhttp. The same false premise is written into shipped source at `messagefoundry/api/app.py:1320-1321` ("Our single h11 parser doesn't desync") and repeated across the assessment lineage. It is not cosmetic: llhttp and h11 have MATERIALLY DIFFERENT acceptance sets on exactly the smuggling grammar, so the sentence that "bounds it" names the wrong parser and asserts a different bound. Driven across 14 cases, llhttp rejects CL+TE, duplicate CL, duplicate TE, a TE list not ending in chunked, `identity`, space-before-colon, obs-fold and bare-LF head termination, and correctly frames `gzip, chunked`; h11 diverges on four of those, and `uvicorn/protocols/http/auto.py:6-10` selects between them on a bare, unlogged `ImportError`.

**The hand-rolled intake reader accepts eight shapes both library parsers reject, and the item's two named surfaces are not where the sharpest violation lives.** Driven directly through `_read_request` at HEAD: `Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked` (the exact-equality test at `transports/http_listener.py:318` misses it, so `:334-336` falls to read-to-EOF and chunk framing is ingested as clinical payload), `chunked,`, `identity`, `Content-Length : 3` with whitespace before the colon (normalised away at `:279`, where RFC 9112 requires a MUST-reject), `Content-Length: +3` and `1_0` (`:325` uses `int()`, which accepts a leading plus and PEP 515 underscores, so `1_0` frames ten bytes), a bare LF inside a header value that fuses two framing headers into one and defeats both guards, and a bare-LF request line where `:263`'s split leaves the parsed header dict EMPTY while the body is still read. The sharpest measured violation of the verb's own second sentence is on a surface neither this item nor the record names: Python's `http.client`, reached from twelve first-party modules, returns `chunked=False, length=3, body=b'3\\r\\n'` for a response carrying `Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked` and `Content-Length: 3` -- Content-Length CONSULTED while a Transfer-Encoding field was present, with a plain-CL positive control reading correctly in the same run.

**Adversarial review was upheld on three heads, and the first means the proposed listener fix closes nothing on the listener's least credentialled path.** Re-verified at HEAD: `_read_body` short-circuits GET and HEAD at `http_listener.py:313` BEFORE the chunked refusal at `:318`, and the read-to-EOF fallback is gated to POST/PUT/PATCH, so `GET` and `HEAD` carrying `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, `gzip, chunked` or a `Content-Length` are all ACCEPTED with an empty body and their declared bytes unconsumed -- on the health-probe path that `_authorize_head` (`:624-625`) exempts from intake auth. The shipped docstring at `:305-311` calls that ordering deliberate and warns that hoisting the refusal "would read as hardening and would in fact be a silent behaviour change", so closing it is a decision to state rather than an edit to fold in. Second, the outbound family is fourteen modules and not twelve: the enumerating grep could not match `import httpx`, missing `messagefoundry/tray/poller.py:25` and `tray/probe.py:47`, and it missed `messagefoundry/transports/soap.py` (urllib at `:52-54`, `:759`, `:797`, reading responses at `:764` and `:823`), which returns `(body, status, headers)` into the pipeline as a captured downstream reply -- so there the truncation would corrupt engine-held message CONTENT rather than mis-read a discarded response.

**Third, and it re-frames the ruling: the chain limb has an engine-owned half.** The scope argument is built on an ingress-only premise -- the engine ships behind an operator-chosen proxy it does not control. On EGRESS the engine ships and configures a per-connection forward/egress web proxy (ADR 0126; `transports/rest.py:885`, `:903`, `:917`, `:1123`, threaded through `rest.py`, `fhir.py`, `soap.py` and `dicomweb.py`) with a bypass list and proxy authentication, and zero framing treatment anywhere: measured, ADR 0126 returns 81 hits for proxy and 0 for smuggling, chunked or framing, and `docs/CONNECTIONS.md` returns 10 and 0. The standard's "configuration is outside the application's responsibility" lever is materially weaker against a chain component the application resolves per host and authenticates to, so the ruling must be taken with both proxies on the table. Relatedly, the structural bound "urllib forces `Connection: close`, so response-queue poisoning is unavailable" reasons only about the engine's own socket; `Connection` is hop-by-hop and constrains nothing about a proxy's reuse of its upstream pool.

**What would still not be an honest pass.** Aligning the two string tests and scoring on that alone -- and the measurements make it worse than this item argued, since alignment would leave the reader accepting space-before-colon, a bare LF that hides a second framing header, a bare-LF request line, and `1_0` as ten, and would leave the fourteen-module outbound family untouched. QUIETLY re-declaring the proxy out of scope so "all components" becomes a sentence about the engine by itself; an EXPLICIT owner ruling with the reasoning written on the cell is a different act, and the two produce the same verdict and are told apart only by whether the reasoning is recorded.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the inbound listener's RFC 9112 grammar hardening, with framing DECIDED IN THE HEAD PARSE for every method before method dispatch runs, so the GET/HEAD short-circuit can only discard a body already proven absent -- refusing the PRESENCE of Transfer-Encoding (the narrow fix already written up in engine issue #98, OPEN), plus the four gaps that issue does not cover: whitespace before the header colon, bare LF anywhere in the head, a non-token HTTP-version, and a strict `1*DIGIT` Content-Length; pinning and reporting the API HTTP parser by passing an explicit protocol class on the default serve path (the seam already exists at `messagefoundry/api/tls_client_cert.py:87`, swapped in at `__main__.py:2857`) and surfacing the resolved parser on the security-posture read-out, deleting the false single-parser comment in the same change; a shared inbound-response framing guard across the fourteen-module urllib family, refusing only AMBIGUOUS framing (a Transfer-Encoding present that the client did not honour, or duplicate Content-Length values that differ) and never merely sloppy responses, with the SOAP captured-reply path treated as the priority; the real-socket framing test leg that does not exist today, since every current framing assertion drives a hand-composed ASGI scope and never reaches a wire parser; framing agreement written into BOTH the ingress reference proxy configurations and the egress proxy documentation, which today contain zero words on the subject; and re-verification and record repair of the cell itself, whose residual names one surface out of at least six.


**OWNER RULING 2026-08-22 -- grade by ownership, in four grades. The packet's binary does not survive the surface.** The re-scoping found **23 distinct files, 37 call sites and 4 framing implementations, plus 5 intermediary components that are not call sites at all**. The packet asked whether the graded unit is the operator's deployed chain or the engine's own HTTP components; on egress that split does not exist. A **loopback TLS-terminating sidecar whose contract this project itself wrote** defeats the narrow reading's central lever, and an **ambient environment proxy that attaches with no engine involvement** defeats the broad reading's mirror lever. Two of four ownership grades therefore have no home in the binary. The ruling replaces it with the grades the surface actually contains -- engine-authored, engine-contracted, operator-deployed, ambient -- and grades each hop by which one it is. The narrow reading was rejected specifically because the sidecar defeats it: the boundary would be drawn where the evidence says it does not hold.

## 1126. research an honest pass for ASVS 4.4.1 -- WSS everywhere from an engine that deliberately declines to terminate TLS

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **6/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _big bet_. The default still ships no certificate (settings.py:758) and exposure_protected still resolves from an operator declaration about the far side of the hop (:834), so in the assessed proxy posture the proxy-to-engine WebSocket leg would be plaintext on first deployment with nothing refusing or warning. Value is the awkward-workaround band rather than no-workaround because tls_policy.py:299-300 short-circuits on proxy_terminated before the attestation test and no validator forbids setting tls_cert_file alongside tls_terminated_upstream, so an operator CAN encrypt that hop today without tripping the revocation refusal. Difficulty stays high because any gate is fenced by a refusal stated in shipped code and must not make the assessed posture unstartable. _(was 7/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **4.4.1** (L1) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb is one sentence and admits no partial reading: WebSocket over TLS for all WebSocket connections. What holds it short is that `tls_cert_file` ships `None` (`messagefoundry/config/settings.py:712`), so the proxy-to-engine WebSocket hop is plaintext `ws` and no gate refuses it.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P1. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** On a first deployment in the assessed posture -- console behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy on a hospital LAN -- the browser-to-proxy leg would be `wss` and the proxy-to-engine leg would be cleartext on the wire, carrying live operational and potentially PHI-bearing stream data. Nothing in the engine would refuse or warn about that hop.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that WebSocket over TLS (WSS) is used for all WebSocket connections."

**What holds it short today.** `tls_cert_file: str | None = None` at `settings.py:712`; `exposure_protected` resolves true from an operator's *declaration* that a proxy terminates TLS (`settings.py:779`), which is an assertion about the far side of the hop, not a property of it. The scorecard's own anchors for this cell predate the current tree (`last_verified = "2026-08-01"` at `f8d11685`, no `reviewed_by`), and its only ledger mention is a *closed* item listing it under `**Closes (ASVS 5.0 L3):**` at `docs/archive/backlog/BACKLOG-CLOSED.md:4293` while the scorecard scores it partial.

**The research question.** Bounded by a deliberate default that research must respect rather than route around: the shipped-default triage classifies this same setting as deliberate under 12.3.3, with the reason stated in shipped code -- the engine refuses off-loopback in-process TLS because it performs no certificate revocation check, stdlib `ssl` having no OCSP or CRL fetch (`messagefoundry/__main__.py:1677-1683`). So the question is whether a component that deliberately declines to terminate TLS can honestly claim WSS on all connections. Unknowns: whether the revocation objection that blocks in-process TLS for a browser-facing hop applies with the same force to a proxy-to-loopback hop; whether a startup or handshake gate could refuse a non-loopback plaintext `ws` without making the assessed proxy posture unstartable; and what the operator attestation path (`MEFOR_TLS_REVOCATION_ATTESTED`) can honestly certify about a hop the engine cannot observe. "Cannot honestly pass without either terminating TLS or refusing plaintext off-loopback, and here is what each costs" is a valid and useful finding.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Shipping a certificate path so the default reads TLS-enabled: a private key cannot be a shipped default, and the engine's own refusal exists for a stated reason. Nor re-declaring the proxy hop out of scope so that "all WebSocket connections" means only the browser-to-proxy leg the engine does not serve -- that is scope re-declaration to dodge the verb, and the residual's whole finding is about the leg it would exclude.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is REACHABLE WITH BUILD, conditional on one scope fork, and the surface this item and the record both describe is missing the limb that actually decides the verdict.** The item's load-bearing sentence survives -- `[api].tls_cert_file` still ships `None` (`messagefoundry/config/settings.py:758`) and nothing has re-verified the cell. But both this item and the residual name only the proxy-to-engine hop, and THE SHIPPED DEFAULT HAS NO PROXY. On a stock `serve` (`[api].host` = `127.0.0.1` at `settings.py:724`, `[api].serve_ui` True at `:732`) the browser opens a plaintext WebSocket DIRECTLY to the engine, because `messagefoundry_webconsole/static/app.js:113-114` derives the scheme from `location.protocol`. That is the product's only WebSocket connection on a stock serve, and a build fixing only the proxy hop would leave the cell partial. A retired assessment did name it and it was lost when that framing collapsed.

**This item's stated boundary does not reach the topology that holds the cell short.** It asks research to respect the engine's refusal of off-loopback in-process TLS for want of revocation checking. That refusal is real, but `in_process_tls_revocation_refused` opens with `if not (tls_enabled and not is_loopback): return False` (`messagefoundry/config/tls_policy.py:296-298`) -- it SHORT-CIRCUITS ON LOOPBACK. So in-process TLS on the shipped default's own bind is already permitted today, and the revocation objection is INAPPLICABLE to the posture at issue. This answers the item's first named unknown outright, in shipped code, in the negative: the recorded reason the loopback bind ships plaintext is not revocation but the lockstep client migration ADR 0143 sizes as an XL. Two smaller drifts: the item's severity says the proxy-to-engine leg "would be cleartext on the wire", but on the topology the runbook RECOMMENDS it is cleartext on the loopback interface, not a NIC; and the ledger citation is off by eight lines.

**The lever is the transport, and it satisfies the verb by construction.** A TLS listener cannot be reached over a plaintext WebSocket scheme, so no scheme inspection, attestation or header appears anywhere in the path. The build is the first-run self-signed certificate work already filed and owner-authorised as #1276 (`docs/BACKLOG.md:10428`, "The owner has authorised the override (2026-08-16)"), plus three things that item does not say. FIRST AND MOST IMPORTANT: the mint must fire under `[api].tls_terminated_upstream` TOO. That is the whole cell, and it is the obvious thing to suppress in order not to break the reference proxy configuration -- and suppressing it leaves the proxy-to-engine hop plaintext forever while the sibling cookie cells move without it. Since there are zero deployments, the back-compatibility cost of that is vacuous, so the correct end state is unconditional and the runbook flips to an https upstream with verification in the same change set. Second, `messagefoundry/pki.py:157-159` emits DNS SANs only, so a certificate whose SAN is the string "127.0.0.1" is not valid for `https://127.0.0.1`; either add IP-address SAN support or standardise every first-party client default on a hostname, which independently fixes an RP-ID defect. Third, the reference proxy configurations contain NO WebSocket upgrade directives at all (`proxy_http_version`, `Upgrade`, `Connection`) against a positive control that `proxy_pass` and `reverse_proxy` are both present, so on the recommended posture the console has no WebSocket at all today and degrades silently to HTTP polling (`app.js:141-151`) -- a real product defect independent of any cell.

**Two of the finding's own evidence boxes were struck on refutation and had to be re-measured.** The enumeration box names "engine plus web console, whole route table" and its instrument was `route_gates.route_rows()`, which builds `create_app()` -- and `create_app` defaults `serve_ui=False`. Re-run by the synthesizer at HEAD `fc54d169`: 105 rows, **zero** of them `/ui`, one WebSocket row. On the shipped-default app (`_serve` passes `serve_ui=settings.api.serve_ui`) the table is 210 rows, 101 of them `/ui`, plus one mount, and still exactly one WebSocket. The conclusion is right and the evidence cited for it excluded the artifact it named. Separately, the absence claim "no transport check exists anywhere on a code path that demonstrably does have refusal machinery" is false at HEAD -- `messagefoundry/api/security.py:449-470` `enforce_phi_read_hop` refuses on a transport-derived disposition computed from `phi_read_hop_secure = is_loopback or exposure_protected` (`__main__.py:2810`, `config/tls_policy.py:643-685`) -- and its stated positive control (`close(code=1008)` firing three times) proved refusal machinery exists on the WebSocket route while proving nothing about whether the token-shaped pattern could have found a transport check. The narrow true statement is that no transport check exists ON THE WEBSOCKET PATH: `authorize_ws` (`api/security.py:737-773`) and `authorize_ui_ws` (`messagefoundry_webconsole/_auth.py:691-725`) check Origin, credential, MFA and permissions and never the scheme.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Booking the cell on a `websocket.url.scheme == "wss"` check: uvicorn's proxy-headers middleware rewrites that scheme from `x-forwarded-proto`, so the check is TRUE TODAY on the very posture the cell is open for -- it measures the proxy's CLAIM, and the tree's only `wss` assertion drives exactly that middleware over a hand-built ASGI dict. Booking it on the operator attestation path, which certifies something about the operator's PKI rather than about a hop, and whose siblings the shipped code itself disclaims (`settings.py:811`: "They are NOT runtime enforcement"). Deleting the stats WebSocket and falling back to polling, which buys the verdict by removing a capability. Re-declaring the proxy hop out of scope. And a request-time close on a non-TLS upgrade is not a substitute for a startup gate.

**Proposed work, by subject, all unallocated:** the ruling and the code for whether the first-run mint fires under a declared upstream terminator, which is the difference between this cell moving and not moving; IP-address SAN support in the self-signed minter, or standardising first-party client defaults on a hostname; the reverse-proxy runbook flip to an https upstream with verification, landed in the same change set as the mint; the missing WebSocket upgrade directives in that runbook; a startup refusal on a plaintext API listener as the regression backstop behind the mint, explicitly not a request-time close; concurrency-safe first-start minting under engine sharding, since `supervise` spawns one `serve --shard` subprocess per shard over one certificate path while the only key writer refuses to overwrite (`__main__.py:3658-3665`); client scheme agreement across tray, `apiclient`, harness and IDE, since `messagefoundry/tray/config.py:204-218` infers the scheme from `[api].tls_cert_file` in the service TOML; and re-verification of the cell itself, whose three anchors are stale by tens of lines, which carries no reviewer field, and whose residual names only the proxy hop.

## 1127. research an honest pass for ASVS 5.1.1 -- a per-feature file inventory that stays true, against a doctrine that treats enumerations as liabilities

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P3.** Value **4/10** · Difficulty **4/10** · _fill-in_. Both concrete defects are fixed in shipped text: the SCP is enumerated as the fourth file surface and the 16 MiB inflate ceiling the item said appeared nowhere under docs/ is now documented. The remainder is the half the item was actually filed for -- an inventory that stays true as connectors are added -- since the block states it is hand-maintained and the drift test pins tokens rather than deriving the surface list from code (value 4, difficulty 4). _(was 5/10 · 4/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **5.1.1** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that documentation define permitted file types, expected extensions and maximum size *including unpacked size* for *each* upload feature, plus how files are made safe. The shipped block at `docs/CONNECTIONS.md:716` opens with a completeness claim -- "MessageFoundry's file surface has three parts" -- that omits a fourth.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
