**Severity:** No exposure; this is a documentation and inventory gap. On a first deployment an operator reading the file-handling policy would not learn that the DICOM C-STORE SCP accepts remote-pushed files at all, nor what bounds them.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that the documentation defines the permitted file types, expected file extensions, and maximum size (including unpacked size) for each upload feature. Additionally, ensure that the documentation specifies how files are made safe for end-users to download and process."

**What holds it short today.** The three enumerated parts are the directory sources, the opt-in HTTP uploaded-logs upload and the attachment download. The DICOM C-STORE SCP is a fourth receiver of remote-pushed files, and its unpacked-size ceiling -- `guard_part10_deflate`, 16 MiB, on by default, called from `messagefoundry/parsing/dicom/dataset.py:77` and `peek.py:85` -- appears nowhere under `docs/`.

**The research question.** The verb demands per-feature completeness; CLAUDE.md section 11 (SDS-3.6) holds that a completeness claim is a liability and prefers "at least" to an enumeration. Those pull in opposite directions and resolving that tension *is* this item. Three unknowns underneath it: what the actual inventory of file-accepting surfaces is, since C-STORE was found by inspection rather than by any sweep and no one has measured whether it is the last one; whether "upload feature" in the pinned text reaches a DIMSE receiver and a polled drop directory at all, or only a user-initiated upload; and what would keep such a document true as connectors are added, given that a hand-maintained list decays silently.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Deleting the "three parts" claim, or softening it to "at least three parts". That would satisfy SDS-3.6 and evade the requirement's per-feature verb in the same edit, and it is precisely the shape the owner ruled out -- editing the document the requirement measures against so that it fits. The requirement is not asking for a defensible sentence; it is asking for the surfaces to be documented one by one.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is reachable, but by a derived inventory with a build gate rather than a better sentence -- and this item's framing no longer holds.** Both halves of "What holds it short today" are false at HEAD `262fe51c`. Commit `10ed7a77` (2026-08-19, PR #435) replaced "three parts" with "at least four parts", named the DICOM C-STORE SCP with an ADR 0025 link at `docs/CONNECTIONS.md:718-729`, and documented the unpacked-size ceiling in two places: the drop-directory bullet at `docs/CONNECTIONS.md:756-760`, which quotes 16 MiB and names `guard_part10_deflate`, and the connector row at `:1624`, which documents `max_object_bytes` as both the object cap and the pre-decode inflate ceiling with its counterintuitive 0/None-tightens-to-16-MiB fallback. The item's code anchors (`parsing/dicom/dataset.py:77`, `peek.py:85`) are still exact; the conclusion drawn from them is not.

**The second-order drift is the live subject.** The residual named one omission and that commit repaired exactly that one, while the omission a prior assessment named in writing -- `GET /messages/export`, a bulk raw-PHI NDJSON download at `messagefoundry/api/app.py:3207`, sitting immediately above a downloads-are-made-safe clause scoped by its own first sentence to one of three `Content-Disposition` emitters -- is still unrepaired. The enumeration has now been wrong three times and each fix chased only the last assessor's finding.

**Measured over the block slice** (`#### File handling & quarantine policy (ASVS 5.1.1)` to the next level-3 heading, lines 716 to 863, 148 lines), with `at least four`, `max_file_bytes`, `uploads_dir` and `_safe_attachment_content_type` PRESENT in the same run as positive controls: `/messages/export`, `audit/export`, `/ui/static`, `zip_decompress` and `.mfbak` all ABSENT. Also ABSENT, and this surface was found only under adversarial review: the attachment / embedded-document **ingest** path -- `pipeline/wiring_runner.py:3890` `_detach_documents`, gated by the per-inbound `stream_threshold_bytes` (`config/wiring.py:3166`), with permitted types accepted as declared outside six magic-sniffable families (`parsing/sniff.py:104-111`, `:134`), a download extension derived by `mimetypes.guess_extension` (`api/app.py:701-707`), and ceilings that are the per-inbound `max_message_bytes` plus the aggregate `[inbound].stream_inflight_budget_bytes`, whose documented default is `0` meaning unlimited (`docs/CONFIGURATION.md:315`). That is the one surface whose ceiling is engineered to exceed every ceiling the block quotes, and the block states none of it. Separately, `docs/adr/0123` gives the decompressor signatures at `:51`, `:52`, `:55` and `:64` as an optional `max_output_bytes=None`; at HEAD all three are keyword-only with no default, so the only shipped documentation of that API states the opposite of the shipped policy, in the direction that understates the control.

**The doctrinal tension dissolves rather than needing adjudication.** SDS-3.6 objects to a hand-maintained list decaying *silently*; a claim a build gate re-derives on every commit cannot decay silently, because its decay is the build failure. The instrument is not hypothetical -- `tests/test_communications_inventory.py` already does this over the same document against the same connector registry for the communications requirements, and `tests/test_security_doc_drift.py:61`/`:706` supplies the route-axis half. **The correction found under review is that two derived axes are not enough:** a per-inbound wiring knob and an `[inbound]` service setting are neither a connector type nor an entry in `create_app().routes`, so built as first proposed the guard would ship with the silent-decay property intact on exactly the surface it missed.

**The trap this item named has half-fired.** `docs/CONNECTIONS.md:718` now reads "at least four parts ... not a closed set", which is true whether the real number is four or fourteen. Re-scoring on the strength of that hedge is the live trap: a hedge that cannot be falsified is not a per-feature inventory, it is the absence of one phrased so no assessor can catch it. So is a token-presence guard -- `tests/test_asvs_file_surface_doc_drift.py:14` says of itself "this guards TEXT not code", which is why the block was still wrong on 2026-08-19 with a green suite.

**Work, by subject, all unallocated:** the derived file-surface inventory table above a stated one-sentence inclusion criterion that decides the `Http()`/`X12()`/`TCP()`/`MLLP()` receivers rather than leaving them unaddressed; the code-derived drift guard on three derived axes with planted-omission self-tests; the attachment / embedded-document ingest documentation row including the aggregate budget's unlimited default; the ADR 0123 signature correction, which is free and should not wait; the unenumerated-surface rows; the downloads-made-safe clause widening; the DICOM SCP malformed-object behaviour sentence; the ADR 0065 stale-class correction at `docs/adr/0065-web-ops-dashboard.md:41`; and the support-bundle scope disposition. Owner rulings needed on the inclusion criterion for "upload feature", on whether the verb reaches the IDE's two local file pickers, and on whether the embedded-document detach is a distinct upload feature -- the last changes the documentation's shape but not the requirement that its two ceilings be pinned somewhere.

## 1128. research an honest pass for ASVS 5.2.2 -- file-content validation that does not sacrifice payload-agnostic ingress

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **6/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _big bet_. The residual holds: the sniff still dispatches on the connection's declared type, binary and text are accepted unchecked at the catch-all arm, and zip_decompress is a Handler-facing export with no transport call site, so archive members reach Handler code unsniffed. Difficulty is 6 rather than lower because the permissiveness is ADR 0004 design, so the research must find a control that does not sacrifice payload-agnostic ingress and any build reaches two transports plus a new archive-member seam. _(was 6/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **5.2.2** (L1) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that an accepted file -- on its own or inside an archive -- have its extension checked against an expected extension and its contents validated as corresponding to that type. The engine validates leading bytes against the *connection's declared* content type, which is a different check, and two declared types are unchecked by construction.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P1. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** On a first deployment, a drop-directory or remote file whose declared type is `binary` or `text` would enter the pipeline with no content check at all, and archive members handed back by `zip_decompress` would reach Handler code unsniffed. The L2 clause "all files being accepted" would be unmet.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that when the application accepts a file, either on its own or within an archive such as a zip file, it checks if the file extension matches an expected file extension and validates that the contents correspond to the type represented by the extension ... For L2 and up, this must apply to all files being accepted."

**What holds it short today.** `_content_matches_declared` (`messagefoundry/parsing/sniff.py:63`) dispatches on the connection's `content_type`, and its own code comment records the shape: hl7v2 to MSH/FHS/BHS, x12 to ISA, dicom to preamble plus DICM, json/fhir to `{`/`[`, xml to `<`, and binary/text unchecked (`sniff.py:94`). It runs on both file sources (`transports/file.py:514`, `transports/remotefile.py:889`) and quarantines rather than dropping. No path sniffs archive members.

**The research question.** This is 2.2.1-shaped, and the constraint has to lead. The permissiveness is a design property, not a switch: payload-agnostic ingress (ADR 0004) exists so that any declared content type routes without HL7 parsing, and `binary`/`text` are the escape hatch that makes it work. So the question is whether a path to an honest pass exists that does not sacrifice the property that default protects. Unknowns: what "expected file extension" even means for a drop directory whose glob is operator-declared (default `*.hl7`), and for a receiver that has no filename; whether the declared-type arm the engine already has can honestly stand in for the extension arm or is a materially different control; and what an archive-member check would cost when the members are produced inside Handler code rather than at the transport. A finding that L1's business-and-security-decision scoping is reachable while L2's "all files" is not without giving up the escape hatch would be a successful outcome, recorded as such.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Narrowing `content_type=binary` and `content_type=text` out of the assessed surface -- that is re-declaring scope to dodge the verb, and those are the two types the residual is about. Nor inventing a magic-byte check for `binary`, which by definition has none: a control that cannot discriminate is a compensating control resting on a false premise, which SDS-3.7 forbids.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. The outcome is CONTESTED and needs a decision, not more research -- and the reasoning that would have justified a permanent ceiling here does not survive either way.** Two independent adversarial reviews reached opposite headlines and both are partly right, so this is recorded as a genuine contest rather than resolved by preference.

**Item-framing drift, load-bearing.** The item pairs `binary` and `text` as "unchecked by construction" and reasons only about `binary`. `text` is not unreachable: `nontext_upload_reason` (`messagefoundry/parsing/sniff.py:159`) ships, rejects a NUL-bearing or control-dense body and the six magic-byte container families, is called on the upload route (`api/app.py:3842`), and is simply never called from either file transport. That is a coverage gap with a shipped fix in the tree, not a structural ceiling. Second, the item's line citations are stale: `transports/file.py:514` is inside `FileSource.stop()` and `transports/remotefile.py:889` is inside a `validate_startup` docstring at HEAD `262fe51c`; the live sniff call sites are `file.py:580` and `remotefile.py:1008`.

**Where the contest sits.** The first review holds the verdict at partial on the ground that `content_type = binary` (`config/models.py:81`, "opaque byte payload") declares the payload's type unmodelled, so the contents-correspond limb has nothing to confirm. The second review shows that argument is keyed on the wrong thing: the pinned verb asks that contents correspond to the type represented **by the extension**, not by the connection's declaration -- and the finding itself pins the limb that way and then grades every structured type against the declaration. On a file source declaring `content_type = binary` with `pattern = "*.pdf"`, the type represented by the extension is PDF, which has a signature, and the engine already ships the discrimination: `_MAGIC_PREFIXES` at `parsing/sniff.py:104-111` covers six opaque container families and `attachment_mime_agrees` already applies it to opaque bytes. There is no plumbing obstacle -- `path.name` is a live local inside the sniff block at `transports/file.py:594`. **The stated ceiling reasoning is therefore withdrawn regardless of the destination.**

**A separate defect both reviews expose, and it is uncontested.** The surface behind any residual sentence was never censused. Measured at HEAD: `messagefoundry/auth/policy.py` `_operator_corpus` opens the operator-configured `password_breach_corpus_file` (setting at `config/settings.py:1826`, consumed at `auth/service.py:269`) with `errors="ignore"` and the format auto-detected from the first non-empty line -- no extension consulted and no content shape that can fail, on a file that makes a security decision, which is the verb's own narrowest example category. And `config/code_sets.py:419-427` checks the suffix against an expected set, refuses an unexpected one loudly, and dispatches the parser **from** the extension, with `load_code_sets` at `:485` filtering the directory the same way; `pipeline/retention.py:84-88` plus `:91-125` is a second such surface. So the claim that the uploads chokepoint is the one place in the tree where the verb is met literally is false at HEAD, and any terminal residual must prefer "at least" to an enumeration (SDS-3.6) rather than assert a universal into the record.

**The decision to be taken.** May a file inbound's accepted-extension set be constrained to extensions the engine can validate, refusing at build time when the set names one it cannot? If yes, pass is reachable with a build larger than a coverage patch, and `binary` stops being special: a `*.pdf` glob gets a `%PDF-` check, a `*.zip` glob gets a `PK` check, a `*.bin` glob does not start, and payload-agnostic ingress is untouched because the constraint is on a filename policy, not on pipeline handling. If no, the terminal state is a recorded partial -- but the written deviation must be keyed on the extension question, not on "binary is opaque". There is nothing deployed, so the compatibility argument against the constraint is vacuous; equally, that fact cannot be spent to justify a ceiling.

**Still disqualified, and one move this item did not anticipate.** Narrowing `binary`/`text` out of the assessed surface, and inventing a magic-byte check for `binary` as such, both stand. The move to watch is the one that argues from the standard's own text: reading the requirement's L1 relaxation into this cell because a relayed payload makes no business or security decision. Every clause of that is individually true and it never touches the surface; it fails on the assessment's declared Level 3 target, which is scope re-declaration wearing the standard's clothes. Deleting `deflate_decompress`/`zip_decompress` from the public surface would also improve the verdict and make the engine worse, since Handler authors would fall back to bare `zlib`/`zipfile` with no ceiling and no PHI-safe error.

**Work, by subject, all unallocated:** the declared-extension binding at both file transports, including a build-time refusal when a `binary` or `text` inbound's glob constrains no extension at all; the extension-keyed content check, gated on the decision above; the text-arm content check wiring the already-shipped `nontext_upload_reason` into `_content_matches_declared`, updating the deliberate-policy assertion at `tests/test_asvs_phase0.py:350` that currently pins the gap, and explicitly not extending it to the binary arm; the archive-member extension policy on `zip_decompress`; the dry-run message-reader hardening at `pipeline/dryrun.py` `read_messages`, which covers the IDE Test Bench, the Steps live-values sample, `messagefoundry dryrun` and `messagefoundry check` from one place; the operator breach-corpus file discipline; and the file-accepting-surface census that any "every" sentence depends on. The residual correction separating `text` from `binary` is cheap, factual and independent of any build, but must be written without a universal.

## 1129. research an honest pass for ASVS 5.2.3 -- a literal before-uncompressing check when the declared size is attacker-controlled

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P3.** Value **4/10** · Difficulty **3/10** · _fill-in_. The permissive Handler-facing default the item re-scoped itself onto is gone: a caller must now pass max_output_bytes or an explicit None, so the severity paragraph no longer describes the code, and the file-count clause is met on the default. What remains is a method question, whether the pinned verb admits incremental per-member enforcement or wants a recorded deviation, with no code change indicated, which prices both numbers in the record-accuracy band. _(was 5/10 · 5/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **5.2.3** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that compressed files be checked against a maximum uncompressed size *and* a maximum file count *before* uncompressing. The engine's readers enforce their ceilings incrementally instead, deliberately, and the Handler-facing archive reader ships its size ceiling off.
> ⚠️ **AMENDED 2026-08-13 -- THE CENTRAL PREMISE IS FALSE. A literal before-uncompressing check DOES ship, DEFAULT-ON, and it cites this very cell in its own source.** The item stays OPEN, but on a much narrower question than it was filed with.
> **What ships:** `parsing/dicom/_inflate.py` provides `bounded_inflate_or_error(compressed, *, max_bytes)`, which inflates in `_INFLATE_CHUNK`-bounded chunks, **discards the output**, and raises `DicomBombError` the instant the cumulative uncompressed size would cross the cap -- so a small compressed bomb with a huge inflated size **never materialises in memory**. `guard_part10_deflate(data, *, max_bytes=DEFAULT_MAX_INFLATED_BYTES)` runs it **before any `dcmread`**, and the default argument is what makes it **default-on** rather than opt-in.
> **And the code names this cell.** `parsing/dicom/peek.py:81` reads: *"ASVS 5.2.3: a Deflated Explicit VR LE object inflates unbounded inside dcmread ... Pre-check the inflate in bounded memory and reject an over-cap object ... BEFORE dcmread ever touches it."* **The module knew about this cell while this item did not know about the module** -- the same shape recorded on #1114.
> **THE STRUCK CLAUSE, and why it is not a small correction.** The item's ground is that the engine enforces ceilings *incrementally instead* of checking before uncompressing. That is the pinned verb's exact distinction, and it is **false for the DICOM path**: this is a literal before-uncompressing check, which is the thing the verb asks for. The `zip_decompress` half stands unchanged.
> **RE-SCOPE:** the live question is whether the Handler-facing `zip_decompress` default (`max_output_bytes=None`) is an honest gap **given** that the transport-facing DICOM path already does the literal check -- and whether "maximum number of files" is answered anywhere. That is narrower and harder than "does a before-uncompressing check exist", which is answered.
> **SECOND ITEM FROM THE 2026-08-08 SWEEP WITH A FALSE CENTRAL PREMISE**, after #1131. Both failed the same way: **the absence was asserted from plausible shapes rather than from the state.** #1131's regex could not match `admin_reset_password`; this one looked at the archive reader and did not look for a bounded inflate elsewhere. **If a third turns up, the sweep's METHOD is the defect and wants its own item, not another amendment.**
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** On a first deployment a Handler author calling `zip_decompress` without passing `max_output_bytes` would get no total-size ceiling. Bounded in practice by the transports' own ceilings on the bytes that reach a Handler, but the helper is re-exported and its default is permissive.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that the application checks compressed files (e.g., zip, gz, docx, odt) against maximum allowed uncompressed size and against maximum number of files before uncompressing the file."

**What holds it short today.** `zip_decompress` at `messagefoundry/parsing/compression.py:180` defaults `max_output_bytes=None`, so its total-size ceiling is off unless the caller passes one. Reading that file at `63bd55ba` adds a correction the residual (`last_verified = "2026-08-01"`, no `reviewed_by`) does not carry: the sibling parameter `max_entries: int = 1024` ships on and is tested against the central-directory member count at `compression.py:196` before any member is extracted, so the file-count clause appears met on the default. Re-measuring this cell against the current tree is part of the item, not a precondition for it.

**The research question.** The literal "before uncompressing" can only be satisfied for *size* by trusting the archive's own declared uncompressed size, which is attacker-supplied -- and the code says so, choosing per-member bounded reads so that "a lying central-directory size cannot force full expansion" (`compression.py:184-187`). So the question is whether an honest pass exists for a reader that is deliberately more correct than the verb as written: does the pinned text admit incremental enforcement as satisfying the check, and if it does not, is the right outcome a recorded deviation rather than a weaker control? A second, smaller unknown: what a Handler-facing helper can honestly default to when the ceiling is properly the caller's to choose.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Two moves. Changing the `None` default alone and scoring the cell -- it would be a genuine improvement and would still leave the "before uncompressing" clause exactly where it is. And, worse, adding a pre-check that reads the declared uncompressed size from the archive header so the code matches the verb literally: that trades a control which cannot be lied to for one which can, buying a cell with a weaker defence.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. The size axis needs an owner ruling that cannot be derived from code or from the standard; the file-count axis is open, buildable today, and gated on nothing.** Both halves of the item's ground are now stale, including the 2026-08-13 amendment.

**Item-framing drift.** The central fact is dead: `zip_decompress` no longer defaults `max_output_bytes=None`. Measured at HEAD `262fe51c`, `inspect.signature(gzip_decompress)` returns `(data: 'bytes', *, max_output_bytes: 'int | None')` and `zip_decompress` returns `(data: 'bytes', *, max_output_bytes: 'int | None', max_entries: 'int' = 1024)` -- keyword-only, no default on the size ceiling, `TypeError` on omission. That shipped under #1237 in `96c9a860` (2026-08-13), which also corrects this item's severity sentence: the gap is **not** bounded by the transports, because the File connector decompresses single-stream gzip only (`transports/file.py:90`) so no transport ceiling ever sees a zip expansion, and `transports/file.py:73` bounds the *compressed* input at 16 MiB. The amendment's re-scope asks about a default that had already gone the same day it was written, and its bolded headline is contested by the later record rather than confirmed by it: the guard it names is a bounded trial inflate that discards output, not a declared-size read, which is exactly the distinction the amendment struck. Line anchors also drifted -- `compression.py:180`/`:196` are now `:195`/`:196` and `:217`.

**The size axis, and why no build settles it.** Decomposed by container format: ZIP carries a declared uncompressed size per member so a literal pre-check is buildable; gzip carries ISIZE mod 2^32 so a partial one is, evadable above 4 GiB; and zlib (RFC 1950) and raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951) carry no uncompressed length at all. Raw DEFLATE is not a corner case here -- it is the format on a live ingress path, the DICOM Deflated Explicit VR LE Data Set that `parsing/dicom/_inflate.py:84` inflates. So on the axis actually exercised at ingress, the only construct that can put a check ahead of the real decompression is the one already shipping. The question, answerable yes or no: does a bounded, output-discarding pre-pass that refuses an over-cap stream before the real decompression satisfy "before uncompressing the file", or does any construct that must itself inflate to learn the size count as uncompressing, so that only a declared-size read -- which raw DEFLATE does not carry -- would satisfy the verb? The OWASP V5 chapter was fetched at tag `v5.0.0` and read in full: there is no assessment guidance for this requirement anywhere in it, and the glossary contains zero occurrences of compress, archive, zip or bomb against an 89-line positive control. That is a measured negative result, and it is what makes this a ruling rather than an assessor's call.

**The count axis needs no ruling, and this item's framing hides it.** Measured by execution with a two-sided control: a 500-member concatenated gzip (16,500 compressed bytes) passed to `gzip_decompress(blob, max_output_bytes=64*1024*1024)` is ACCEPTED, 6,500 bytes out, with no member-count check; the same blob at `max_output_bytes=10` raises `CompressionError`, so the function was live and its size cap works. `gzip_decompress` carries no member-count parameter at all and `gzip.GzipFile` joins concatenated RFC 1952 members transparently (`parsing/compression.py:109`). Because `transports/file.py:572` is the only shipped ingress decompressor and it is the gzip path, the verb's second conjunct is unsatisfied on the one exercised surface. Whether an RFC 1952 member is a "file" for that limb has never been decided; if it is, this is buildable today, and if it is not, the rationale needs writing down so the next sweep does not re-open it.

**Surface correction found under review.** There are three `dcmread` call sites in the tree, not two: `parsing/dicom/peek.py:88`, `parsing/dicom/dataset.py:80`, and `transports/dicom.py:611` inside the outbound C-STORE SCU -- with a fourth inflate-guard call at `transports/dicom.py:597`. That path is guarded, so it opens no hole, but it is a decompressing path no anchor carries. Related, and stated in the shipped code: `transports/dicom.py:591` records that a deflated Part-10 file-drop "passes the File source's DICM-magic-only sniff and reaches this `dcmread` unparsed, where it would inflate UNBOUNDED", so `_SUPPORTED_COMPRESSION = frozenset({"gzip"})` bounds what the File connector *decompresses*, not what reaches it.

**What would not be an honest pass.** This item's first trap already fired and was caught -- #1237's banner says in bold that it closes no ASVS cell. The live successor is citing that landing as the reason to re-score: the residual closes the defect it named and then holds on a different, untouched ground, so anyone re-scoring must quote the deciding sentence rather than the closure sentence. The second trap is right but stated too broadly: a declared-size pre-check that **substitutes** for the incremental one trades a control that cannot be lied to for one that can, while one added **in front of** it trades nothing -- the in-tree precedent is `pipeline/dr_backup.py:927` rejecting the declared tar-header size before streaming plus `:938-944` capping the streamed bytes, with the docstring at `:917-920` stating the point. Re-wording that trap is the owner's call, and any additive filter must ship with a test proving a lying central directory is still caught incrementally. Also disqualified: making the engine refuse compressed feeds, either by dropping `decompress="gzip"` or by refusing a standard DICOM transfer syntax, which satisfies the verb by never uncompressing anything and buys the verdict with the product's purpose.

**Work, by subject, all unallocated:** the owner ruling on the pre-pass reading, which is cheap and decides the size axis; the gzip member-count decision and, if a member is a file, the member cap, which should not wait behind it; the discarding bounded pre-pass for the compression codec, gated on the ruling and cheaper than it looks since `compression.py:150` `_bounded_inflate` is already the shared helper and the work is adding a discard mode; the additive ZIP central-directory pre-filter, contested and to be put to the owner alongside the ruling rather than built unilaterally; the outbound DICOM SCU evidence row; the apiclient response-decompression bound, since the shared httpx client sends `accept-encoding: gzip, deflate` by default and decodes transparently with no size bound while the nine urllib egress modules get `identity` by omission; and the falsy-off switch at `transports/file.py:391`, where an operator writing `0` for `max_decompressed_bytes` would get an unbounded gunzip on an ingress path on a first deployment -- different in kind from the helper-side explicit `None`, which is a deliberate greppable caller act, and the two should be decided separately.

## 1130. research an honest pass for ASVS 5.3.2 -- containment for filenames a remote SFTP or FTP server chooses

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P3.** Value **4/10** · Difficulty **3/10** · _fill-in_. The security-material half shipped: a hostile listing name is refused at the source (remotefile.py:955) before the pattern filter and before the join, so the traversal primitive the item priced is gone and its founding sentence is false in the code. Value 4 on the remainder, which is a census across the file-path-constructing transports plus the record work to move the cell; difficulty 3 because the guard and its both-polarity tests exist to copy and any further sites are the same shape. _(was 7/10 · 5/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **5.3.2** (L1) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that file paths be built from internally generated or trusted data, and that where user-submitted names or file metadata must be used, strict validation and sanitization be applied. The remote file source joins a server-supplied listing name straight onto the configured directory with neither.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P1. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** On a first deployment, a malicious or compromised partner SFTP/FTP server could return a listing entry that escapes the configured directory, and the engine would retrieve, move or delete at that path. It needs a hostile server rather than mere drop-directory write access, which bounds it -- it does not remove it.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that when the application creates file paths for file operations, instead of user-submitted filenames, it uses internally generated or trusted data, or if user-submitted filenames or file metadata must be used, strict validation and sanitization must be applied. This is to protect against path traversal, local or remote file inclusion (LFI, RFI), and server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks."

**What holds it short today.** `messagefoundry/transports/remotefile.py:857`, `path = posixpath.join(self._remote_dir, name)`, where `name` comes from the server's own directory listing; that path then feeds retrieve, move and delete with no containment check, and the default `pattern` of `*.hl7` matches `../../etc/passwd.hl7`. The local `File` source has the guard the remote one lacks (`transports/file.py:737`, `_within_root`), and the HTTP upload surface is the opposite posture entirely -- internally generated ids, a 32-hex id regex and an explicit parent check (`messagefoundry/uploads.py:50`, `:313`, `:389`).

**The research question.** First, a reading question that decides the shape of everything else: is a name returned by an SFTP or FTP listing "user-submitted data" under this verb? The engine authored the connection and the operator chose the partner, but the bytes are chosen by a remote party. Second, and protocol-shaped: what containment is even expressible over SFTP and FTP, where the client cannot canonicalize remotely, the server resolves symlinks on its own, and a syntactic check on the returned name may be the only control available -- whether that qualifies as "strict validation and sanitization" under the verb needs establishing rather than assuming. Third, what the threat model should assume about a partner file server; that one is likely an owner call and the research should surface it as one.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Declaring the remote server trusted infrastructure so its listing stops counting as user-submitted data. That re-declares scope to dodge the verb, and the product already refuses exactly that trust one layer over: the local source treats its own drop directory as untrusted and guards it.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is reachable with a named build, but not by re-verifying the box this item names -- and the completeness sentence that would carry it must be struck first.**

**Item-framing drift.** The sentence the item rests on is false at HEAD `262fe51c`. There is a containment check on the remote listing name: `_is_contained_name` at `messagefoundry/transports/remotefile.py:98`, wired at `:955` at the loop head, **before** the `fnmatch` filter at `:971` and before the join at `:973`, so it dominates every consumer -- retrieve, the oversize move, the error move, the `after_read` disposition and the leave-mode dedup key. It landed in `f27509f5` (2026-08-13) under #1238, the build half of this item, and both polarities are pinned: `tests/test_remotefile_transport.py:1185` refuses empty, NUL, newline and the drive-relative `C:evil.hl7`, while `:1195` accepts `file with spaces.hl7` and `unicode-e.hl7`, with the test's own comment recording that a check refusing everything is not a control either. The item's line citations (`remotefile.py:857`, `file.py:737`) are stale; the banner still reads "not started".

**On the reading this item left open** -- whether a syntactic check meets the verb's "strict validation and sanitization" language -- the answer is yes, on three checkable grounds. The verb's construction is a treatment pair for a name that must be used, and a refusal is the strictly stronger member: it is what strict validation means when the accept set is a single path component. The sanitizing alternative was ruled actively harmful on measured grounds under #1238, because `posixpath.basename` aliases onto a real file and hands a hostile server a move-or-delete primitive, so demanding mutation would demand a worse control. And the accept side is narrow rather than degenerate. The residual limit #1238 recorded honestly -- resolved-path containment is not in our power, since the server resolves its own symlinks -- is not a limb this verb ranges over: the verb governs how the **application** creates the path. Note one unverified peer claim carried rather than adopted: `SSH_FXP_REALPATH` may make an advisory server-side canonicalization buildable over SFTP with no FTP analogue, so the bound written on the record should say "advisory only" rather than "not expressible".

**Two boxes of the same class are absent, and both were live at the assessment's own verified_at commit** -- sweep misses, not regressions. `messagefoundry/corepoint_import.py:422` takes the export JSON's `channels[i].inbound.name` verbatim (`module_name = _opt_str(inbound, "name") or f"IB_{ident.upper()}"`) and `:1942`/`:1943` then write `(out / f"{module_name}.py")`; the module's own `_sanitize` is applied to the fallback stem and to handler names at `:454`, and `_lit`/`_comment_text` harden export values against code injection, so the one export value that becomes a filesystem path is the one left unguarded. Here mutation is the right fix rather than the aliasing trap, because the importer writes into a directory it created rather than selecting an existing file, and the count-and-log leg is already handled by the writer's `assigned` set, which deterministically suffixes a colliding stem and records `renamed_from`. Separately, `messagefoundry/config/codeset_edit.py:176` runs `src = _existing_path(codesets_dir, old)` **before and without** `_validate_name`, which is only applied to `new` at `:177`, so `os.replace(src, dest)` at `:194` would move a file resolved outside `codesets/` into it; the three sibling entry points all validate first, and `tests/test_codeset_edit.py:435`/`:557` carry the show and remove traversal tests with no rename-source equivalent. That entry point has a second caller beyond the CLI -- `ide/src/codeSetEditor.ts:117`/`:177` shells `codeset rename --name <old>` from a webview message -- which bears on whether the operator-authority counter-reading holds.

**The instrument must be re-keyed.** The recorded absence claim is keyed on `_within_root`, a symbol belonging to the local source. Re-run over the verifier's own 412-file corpus it matches zero files with its recorded positive control matching `remotefile.py` in the same run, so the gate is green and not blind, and is nonetheless certifying a stale residual, because the guard that shipped is named `_is_contained_name`. No reading of that claim could have proved the residual wrong.

**What the research does NOT license, and this is the correction found under review.** A sentence asserting that all four limbs are satisfied across the engine, the web console and the IDE is a completeness claim over a surface that was never censused. Measured at HEAD: a path-construction grep over `messagefoundry --include=*.py` returns 162 sites across 49 files (267 `.py` files in the tree as the positive control), against roughly fifteen files named. `scripts/` is one of the four roots the verifier scans and gets no grading, no exclusion and no rationale -- 39 `.py` files. `harness/` carries nine name-into-dir joins, several taking a CLI-supplied name, not the one site the research sizes its fix for. The claim that the remaining IDE joins are workspace-relative settings paths is false at `ide/src/extension.ts:214`, which joins a value arriving as a command argument, and at `hl7schema.ts:39`, which joins a module constant -- and since no `.py` instrument can ever cover `ide/` under `scripts/asvs/scorecard.py:1181`, a hand-read row is the only evidence that limb will ever have, so its accuracy is the whole control. Two independent reviews also found the same unenumerated site, `messagefoundry/config/environments.py:107`, which is safe only because of `_valid_environment_name` at `config/settings.py:2406` gating on a character set with no separator -- a verified box whose safety nothing in the research had traced. Two reviewers landing on the same missed site is evidence that the matrix method, not the site, is the defect.

**Also disqualified.** This item's stated trap is moot -- the build took the opposite position and refuses the listing name. The live traps are re-scoring on the strength of that build alone, and adding a `_within_root` alias in `remotefile.py`, which changes zero behaviour and mechanically makes the recorded absence false. The correct response to a stale absence claim is to re-key the claim to the control that shipped, never to rename the control to match the claim.

**Work, by subject, all unallocated:** the Corepoint-import module-name sanitization work, with a test asserting an export naming `../../../evil` writes inside the output directory and nowhere else; the codeset-rename source-name validation work plus the mirroring traversal test; the file-path-construction census over the verifier's roots, with the command and its positive control recorded, as the precondition for any residual sentence containing "every"; the absence-claim re-key with a mutation that bites; the IDE surface row correction; the harness file-drop filename sanitization work and the eight sibling joins beside it, contingent on scope; and the record correction that router and destination names from a Corepoint export are **not** sanitized (`corepoint_import.py:445`, `:432`), contrary to the contrast clause offered for the module-name omission. One owner ruling is needed and it is broader than this cell: are `harness/` and `scripts/` inside the assessed scope? The method doc names three artifacts while the verifier scans four roots, and that mismatch affects every requirement that writes an absence bound.


**SHIPPED IN `#488` AT `cf38e16a`, AND STILL OPEN ON PURPOSE. DO NOT REBUILD IT.** The build landed; the banner has not moved because closing it is a judgement this seat cannot make alone -- the building lane witnessed the code, and this seat did not.

**The merge commit touched ZERO ledger lines,** so nothing in this entry would otherwise say the work exists. That is the gap this note closes: a lane arriving here reads an open item with no marker and rebuilds shipped code, which is the double-build this project already pays for elsewhere.

**Before working this item, read it as: code on `main`, banner open, closure pending.** The remaining question is whether anything is left, not whether to start.
## 1131. research an honest pass for ASVS 6.1.1 -- what the anti-automation documentation must say about malicious account lockout

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **3/10** · _fill-in_. > Research: done 2026-08-20

> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **6.1.1** (L1) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that application documentation make clear how the anti-automation controls are configured and prevent malicious account lockout. > **1. THE REMEDY IS STRONGER THAN THIS ITEM CREDITS, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS LOAD-BEARING.** `api/auth_routes.py:753` routes `POST /users/{user_id}/reset-password`, and `:757` takes `Depends(require_step_up(Permission.USERS_MANAGE))` -- **the admin RE-AUTHENTICATES; it is not a plain permission check.** ~~This item's own research question says an unlock route is *"a candidate with its own abuse surface, not an answer"*, and the step-up is a partial answer to exactly that abuse surface, which nothing in the record credits.~~
> ⚠️ **THAT SENTENCE WAS WRONG IN BOTH HALVES AND IS CORRECTED HERE 2026-08-13. It was mine, and I landed it.** **(a) The record is NOT silent** -- cell **6.3.8** already describes *"the only reset is administrator-initiated behind a step-up gate"*. So **6.1.1 OMITS it; the record does not LACK it** -- a narrower and different defect. **(b) THE SIGN IS INVERTED. It is not a credit on 6.1.1's axis, it CUTS THE OTHER WAY.** 6.1.1 is about **malicious lockout**, and a stronger gate on the *sole* administrative remedy makes **RECOVERY HARDER**, not easier. **Record the step-up as a CONSTRAINT on the remedy, not as a mitigating control** -- it is part of why the sole-administrator case is a dead end, now filed as **#1236**.
> **How the error happened, because it is the reusable part:** the step-up's EXISTENCE was verified at `auth_routes.py:757` and is real. Its INTERPRETATION -- that it mitigates 6.1.1 -- was inherited from the report and never checked against the cell's axis. **Measuring the fact and adopting the framing are two acts, and only the first was performed.** Coverage is uniform, so this is not a partial-surface finding: all three backends clear the lock in `set_password` (`store.py`, `postgres.py`, `sqlserver.py` -- `failed_attempts=0`, `locked_until=NULL`, two sites each).
> **2. THE `docs/SECURITY.md:1474` CITATION IS STALE and will cost the next reader time.** At engine `9d98f339` that line is an unrelated **AD** row in the comparative-properties table. The disputed parenthetical is now at **`:1544`**, in the three-limiter anti-automation table. **Cite the greppable phrase, not the line number.**
> **AND THE DISCLOSURE GAP IS NOT ONE PARENTHETICAL -- it is a CONTRADICTION a reader hits FIRST.** `docs/SECURITY.md:59` reads *"never auto-disabled, so **a single-admin deployment can't be locked out**"*. In context that sentence is about auto-retirement, but **its words flatly deny the thing this item is about**, and it sits **1,485 lines BEFORE** the known parenthetical at `:1544` -- it is the one a reader greps for and stops at. Two further collisions on the same word: `:741` *"AD operators are never locked out"* (true, and for a reason worth stating) and `:782` *"admin is never locked out"* (scoped to the enroll/confirm routes). **A documentation fix that edits only `:1544` leaves the contradiction that is read first.**
> **3. WHY THIS ITEM GOT IT WRONG -- RECORDED AS METHOD, NOT MERELY AS A CORRECTION.** The filed absence claim searched `def admin_unlock|unlock_account|clear_lockout`. Measured on `main`: that regex returns **0 hits** in `auth/service.py`, a file containing exactly **1** `def admin_reset_password`. **The regex CANNOT STRUCTURALLY MATCH THE THING THAT SHIPS.** So the zero was a **true answer to a question nobody asked**, and this item's conclusion -- *"no dedicated administrative unlock exists"* -- is **literally true and materially misleading**: an unlock ships, as a side effect of a forced password rotation.
> > **THE PRESCRIPTION: an absence claim over a CAPABILITY must be written from the STATE, not from plausible function names.** *"Find every write to `locked_until`"* would have found it; *"find every function called something-unlock"* never could.
> **RE-SCOPE:** the live question is the **adequacy and disclosure of a step-up-gated forced-rotation reset as a remedy for a MALICIOUS lockout** -- not whether an unlock affordance exists. That is a harder question than the one filed, and it is why this stays open rather than closing on the route's existence.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P1. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no product effect on the control itself; on a first deployment an operator reading the documented protection set would not learn that a known local username can be held refused by repetition at roughly five requests per fifteen minutes, ~~nor that no dedicated administrative unlock exists.~~ **[STRUCK -- an unlock DOES ship, step-up-gated, via forced password rotation; see the 2026-08-13 amendment above.]**

**The pinned verb.** "The documentation must make clear how these controls are configured and prevent malicious account lockout."

**What holds it short today.** The scorecard grants the rate-limiting and configuration clauses "unusually well" and names the malicious-lockout clause as the sole ground. In the current tree the lock is tested and audited at `messagefoundry/auth/service.py:665-668`, ahead of the credential comparison at `:669`; the threshold is five failures for fifteen minutes (`messagefoundry/config/settings.py:1773-1774`); and a lapsed window only restarts the counter, so re-locking is available indefinitely. The cell's absence claim for `def admin_unlock|unlock_account|clear_lockout` returned zero files against a live positive control.

**The research question.** Two unknowns, and the first decides the second. (a) Does the verb grade the document alone, or does "prevent malicious account lockout" name a property the control must hold and the document must explain? On the second reading an honest pass needs an affordance that does not exist, and its shape is open -- anything that clears a lock is itself a control an attacker wants, so an unlock route is a candidate with its own abuse surface, not an answer. (b) What disclosure is both true and useful, given the cell's own re-score trigger says a rewrite of `:1474` alone would resolve it. Constraint to respect: 6.3.8 records the lockout transition as an enumeration signal, so anything changed here must be checked against that cell.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** The move available here is a documentation edit that deletes the falsifiable sentence rather than resolving what it misstates -- striking the word "indefinitely", or softening `:1474` into a claim nobody can test, would move the cell and leave the reader exactly as uninformed. Setting `lockout_minutes = 0`, which the same table presents as the effective opt-out, also does not count: it removes the anti-guessing control rather than preventing its misuse.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. Outcome: an honest pass is reachable with a build, and the enumeration limb is wider than this item measures. One reading question decides whether the build is needed at all.**

**THE ITEM'S "WHAT HOLDS IT SHORT" NO LONGER HOLDS ON THE DOCUMENTATION HALF.** Commit `2a6693f3` (2026-08-19, an ancestor of `origin/main`) rewrote both sites this item names. The disputed parenthetical is gone; the control-1 row at `docs/SECURITY.md:1600` now states in terms that **repetition is unbounded**, with four paragraphs following at `:1610-1647` (the lock is bounded and the campaign is not; the signal; recovery; arrange in advance), and the reader-hits-first contradiction the 2026-08-13 amendment named is repaired at `docs/SECURITY.md:66-68`. **The cell's own first re-score trigger has fired.** Note how invisible that was: the rewrite kept the phrase the evidence anchor quotes, so the anchor still resolves through a **meaning change** and every gate stayed silent.

**A NEW FINDING, AND IT CUTS AGAINST THE RESEARCH RATHER THAN FOR IT.** The claim that no adaptive-response control ships anywhere in scope is **false**. `[auth].admin_new_ip_step_up` ships at `messagefoundry/config/settings.py:1808` (default `false`), is implemented at `messagefoundry/auth/service.py:1950`, is charged from `messagefoundry/api/security.py:566/598/651/681`, and is documented as forcing a fresh step-up at `docs/SECURITY.md:1157` and `docs/CONFIGURATION.md:589` -- while being **absent from the graded protection-set section** (`docs/SECURITY.md:1592-1766`, scanned with a control that fires three times outside it). Whether it belongs in this requirement's protection set is an assessor ruling to write down; the categorical sentence is not defensible either way, and re-running the cell's absence claims and reporting them green would stamp it into the record.

**THE HONEST PATH.** Re-verify the cell first -- record the disclosure ground as discharged, replace **both** absence claims (the first is a true zero to a question nobody asked; the second is false), and re-anchor the five drifted lines. Then enumerate the shipped anti-automation surface **from code** per artifact and reconcile it against the nine-control table, repairing the route-to-limiter enumerations, which omit at least five console routes (`messagefoundry_webconsole/routes/account.py:214/:274/:333/:347/:444`) and `POST /alerts/test-email` (`messagefoundry/api/app.py:2515-2519`). If the second sentence carries implementation content, the control half also needs the **always-evaluating per-identifier authentication throttle** work: delay-not-refuse so a correct credential still gets in, keyed on the presented username, applied before any verify and outside the argon2 semaphore at `messagefoundry/auth/service.py:287`, covering both failure feeders (`:746`, `:2205`) and the passkey lock check at `:2529`, shipping on. The **control-1 documentation rewrite** lands with it, restricting rather than deleting the advance-mitigation paragraph and repairing the three dangling code citations at `docs/SECURITY.md:1665-1667`.

**THE READING DEPENDENCY, NAMED RATHER THAN GUESSED.** Whether "prevent malicious account lockout" grades the document alone or names a property the control must hold decides the whole build. The pinned corpus cannot settle it; the deciding artifact is the OWASP V6 chapter prose at tag `v5.0.0`, fetched and quoted. Under the documentary reading this is reachable today on the landed documentation plus the enumeration repair.

**AND THE TRAP HAS MUTATED.** The delete-the-falsifiable-sentence trap is spent -- the commit did the opposite. The live trap is its mirror image: **re-scoring on the strength of that landed disclosure alone**, buying the verdict by adding a sentence you can defend while the shipped control is byte-for-byte what it was.

The shipped documents name four of the twelve terms enforced at `messagefoundry/auth/policy.py:38-53` and hedge them with "like" and "e.g.".

> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no product effect on the screen, which ships on (`messagefoundry/config/settings.py:1765`) and rejects hard (`auth/policy.py:134`). On a first deployment a reader could not determine from documentation which terms are enforced, and a site could not add its own organization or codename terms at all.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that a list of context-specific words is documented in order to prevent their use in passwords. The list could include permutations of organization names, product names, system identifiers, project codenames, department or role names, and similar."

**What holds it short today.** `docs/SECURITY.md:1371-1372` and `docs/CONFIGURATION.md:549` give a category description with four illustrations; at least eight of the twelve enforced terms appear nowhere as members. The scorecard also records that the documented characterization ("app/vendor/HL7 terms") mis-describes five generic members, and that no operator-supplied context-word setting exists in the scanned trees against a live positive control.

**The research question.** (a) Whose list is the subject? The requirement's own examples are organization names, project codenames and department or role names -- none of which a vendor constant can contain -- so establish whether an honest pass is a published enumeration of the shipped twelve, or requires the deploying organization to be able to supply its own terms at all. (b) If publication is the answer, what keeps the published list in step with `auth/policy.py:38-53`; an enumeration written once into Markdown with no gate is a claim that decays silently and would re-open this cell without anyone noticing.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Pasting the twelve terms into `docs/SECURITY.md` and re-scoring, if research finds the requirement's subject is the deployment's list rather than the vendor's -- that satisfies the sentence while leaving a site unable to ban its own name. Equally, an enumeration adopted with no mechanism tying it to the constant buys the verdict for exactly as long as nobody edits `policy.py`.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. Outcome: CONTESTED -- the verb is satisfied at HEAD but the two adversarial lenses contradict each other on whether the verdict may move before a parity gate is green. Recorded as a decision rather than resolved by preference.**

**THE ITEM'S CENTRAL FACTUAL CLAIM IS FALSE AT HEAD.** Commit `10ed7a77` (2026-08-19) replaced the illustrative sentence with a verbatim enumeration of all twelve terms at `docs/SECURITY.md:1465-1471` under a heading that says "in full", and **retracted the mis-description in place** at `:1472-1478`, naming the five generic members. Set equality against the imported constant was measured in both directions with a negative control: twelve terms, both differences empty. The cell's own first re-score trigger has fired. The item's surviving clause -- that no deploying site can add its own terms -- re-measures true, but the cell already records it as supporting context that would not resolve the cell on its own, so this item's title frames the research around a limb that was never decisive.

**WHAT IS SETTLED, UNDER EITHER READING.** The finding's premise that `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` "links rather than repeats, so the coordination risk is retired by construction" is **wrong**: `docs/CONFIGURATION.md:565` republishes the cardinality ("The **twelve** terms"), a sub-count ("five of the twelve are generic credential words"), the substring semantics, and a tunability claim. And the module the finding names for the gate cannot read that file -- `tests/test_security_doc_drift.py:46` is a single path, and `grep -c CONFIGURATION` on it returns **0** against a control of **20** for `SECURITY.md`. A one-file gate would red on a thirteenth term for one document while the other kept asserting "twelve": this item's own named decay, one file over, under a green check. `tests/test_security_doc_rate_limits.py:43` already carries a second document path, so a two-file vehicle exists and needs no new CI plumbing.

**THE CONTEST.** One lens holds this is a re-verification with the durability assertion landing in the same pass; the other holds the gate must be green **first**, because the trap this item states ("an enumeration adopted with no mechanism tying it to the constant buys the verdict for exactly as long as nobody edits `policy.py`") carries no condition. Both agree the gate must be built; neither is factually wrong. Nothing ties the two together today -- `CONTEXT_WORDS` returns no lines under `tests/` or `scripts/` against a live control at `messagefoundry/auth/policy.py:38` and `:134`. **The deciding artifacts are (a) a ruling on whether a documentation cell may pass on a shipped, tracked document with no CI gate, and (b) a precedent check on whether any already-passing documentation cell rests on a hand-mirrored enumeration.**

**THE HONEST PATH, WHICHEVER WAY THAT GOES.** The **context-word documentation-parity gate**, covering **both** published files, asserting set equality in both directions against `CONTEXT_WORDS`, asserting the spelled cardinality at every publishing site, guarding the retired phrase, pinning the "no setting adds a term" absence, and carrying a planted-mutation self-test so a parser extracting zero terms reds rather than passing vacuously. Plus the **stale-anchor repair**: one anchor is ambiguous and one has its expect string **gone from the whole docs tree**, and the gone one must be **retired as gap-closed**, not silently re-pointed. Plus the **divergence-authority sentence rewrite** -- `docs/SECURITY.md:1477-1478` currently tells the reader the code wins if the two diverge, which with no gate behind it is the sentence a later reader uses to excuse a divergence rather than fix one. Re-verify with the sibling context-word cell off one reading of the same block.

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment a reader would draw the local pathway weaker and the delegated pathways laxer than the code makes them, and an operator following the pathway table would meet a configuration-load refusal, because the table names `[auth]` keys the loader rejects.

**The pinned verb.** "...these are all documented together with the security controls and authentication strength which must be consistently enforced across them."

**What holds it short today.** `docs/SECURITY.md:1454-1455` says `require_mfa` scopes to local Administrators and is a step-up boundary; the shipped default is `every_local_account` (`messagefoundry/config/settings.py:3624`) enforced as an access gate on every non-exempt authorized route (`messagefoundry/api/security.py:227`). `:1459-1460` misstates how the federated second-factor grant is decided. `:1393` and `:1454` instruct the reader in relocated `[auth]` keys. The same document contradicts each of the first two elsewhere in its own tables.

**The research question.** Correcting three sentences is an edit, not research. The research is whether truth is sufficient and what keeps it true. The clause reads "strength which must be consistently enforced across them", and the sibling 6.3.4 records that it is not: AD and Kerberos mint sessions MFA-verified at `messagefoundry/auth/service.py:794` and `:824`. So does an accurate document describing a known inconsistency satisfy 6.1.3, or does this cell inherit 6.3.4's outcome and become unpassable until that one moves? Second unknown: three defects in one section suggests the artifact has no gate -- what mechanism would make a five-row pathway table and a settings-key reference falsifiable in CI.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Rewriting the three sentences, re-scoring, and never answering whether a documentation cell can pass while the enforcement it documents is inconsistent. Also not honest: deleting the disputed paragraph so nothing contradicts anything -- a document that stops saying which strength is enforced has stopped documenting strength, which is the thing the verb asks for.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 83 of the partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. Outcome: an honest pass is reachable with a build, and the build is a documentation corpus wider than this item or the finding scoped it. The item's own trap was half-sprung on 2026-08-19.**

But the identical retracted framing is live at `docs/SECURITY.md:788-793` -- 760 lines above the gate's window in the **same file**, and the corrected paragraph at `:1572` cross-links the reader **to** it -- and, measured, in at least four further tracked documents: `docs/FEATURE-MAP.md:142`, `docs/EARLY-ADOPTER-GUIDE.md:89` and `:400`, `docs/Secure_Development_Standards.md:629` and `:705`, plus loader-rejected key spellings at `docs/CONTAINER-EXPOSURE-EVALUATION.md:56/:146/:387`. The conclusion still holds; the stated ground does not, and a researcher who checks the ground and finds it false would be wrong twice over. The grounds that hold are the method's rejection of the vacuity argument and the recorded triage inversion.

**THE ITEM'S QUESTION ANSWERS NO: this cell does not inherit the sibling enforcement cell's outcome.** The pinned corpus sites the two requirements in different sections with different verbs, and reading this one's relative clause as an enforcement obligation makes it a strict duplicate of a clause OWASP wrote out separately; the same assessor in the same pass graded this cell on documentation defects and the sibling on the enforcement gap. **THE HONEST PATH.** The **MFA-section correction** at `docs/SECURITY.md:781-807`, stating the fact once and linking rather than restating it a fourth time. The **corpus-wide retired-key and retracted-framing sweep** across every tracked operator document plus the API contract and the CLI help text at `messagefoundry/__main__.py:1970`. The **corpus-scoped documentation-drift gate**, deriving its forbidden set by **importing `_RELOCATED_TO_SECURITY`** from `messagefoundry/config/settings.py:4096-4112` (all fifteen entries, not the four the finding names) so it cannot fall out of step, reading every tracked `docs/**/*.md`, with planted-mutation self-tests. Plus the **IDE authentication-claim correction**, the **console posture-row derivation**, and a **client-reachability row** naming which pathways each shipped client can drive.

**THE LIVE TRAP is re-scoring on the green gate.** `tests/test_docs_security_pathways.py` names this requirement in its own docstring, derives its rows from live code, carries planted-mutation discipline and passes 17/17 -- and its window is one `###` section of one file.
