BEFORE performing", and the project has already written the principle down in its own source -- ADR 0077's Context states that a login-seeded window means every step-up-gated action is unlocked with no fresh proof, and `auth/service.py:1826-1827` comments that a broad login-seeded window can never authorize a factor-binding action.

**The path reuses machinery that is already built, already default-on, and already refuses.** Add one action constant beside the six at `auth/service.py:119-124`, swap `api/auth_routes.py:481` and `:493` to the action-bound reauth-only factory (keeping `mfa_gate=False`), swap `messagefoundry_webconsole/routes/account.py:338` and `:351` to the console twin, and add the `action=` tag to the two registered continuations at `account.py:93-94`. No further plumbing: `routes/core.py:914` already forwards the purpose into `reauth()`, so the console re-auth mints the matching single-use grant and the registered auto-retry re-POSTs the terminate. This is not a dormant toolkit being wired for effect -- the mechanism is consumed by nine route dependencies today, the grant is minted ONLY inside `reauth(purpose=...)` (`auth/service.py:1825`, guarded by a non-None purpose, so login and `verify_mfa` mint nothing), and `has_action_step_up` POPS it, so it is single-use and TTL-bounded on a monotonic clock. Decide deliberately whether one action name or two: two means a ceremony gathered to drop one device cannot silently unlock the mass terminate, which is closer to ADR 0077's own rationale.

**Two surface rows in the research were false and are corrected here, because a later reader would act on them.** The extension DOES ship a terminate: `ide/src/statusBar.ts:816` registers `messagefoundry.engineSignOut`, offered as a Sign out item in three engine states, calling `signOut()` (`ide/src/auth.ts:86`) which POSTs `/auth/logout` with the bearer at `:92` -- and the extension's own docstring says dropping only the local copy is not signing out. The instrument that missed it searched the token `sessions`, which cannot match `signOut` or `/auth/logout`, while its positive control proved only that the tree was readable. Likewise "exactly four self-service terminate entry points exist, no fifth path" was measured over two API subtrees on five method names and so could not see `POST /me/password`, which reaches `change_password` and calls `revoke_user_sessions(identity.user_id)` at `auth/service.py:2026` -- a self-service mass terminate of every session the caller holds. That one cuts in the finding's favour: it is the one self-service mass terminate in the tree that ALREADY satisfies the "again" clause, because `api/auth_routes.py:306` demands the current password before the revoke. State the enumeration as "at least", not as a closed set.

**Still not an honest pass, and the trap has moved somewhere worse than the item names.** The item disqualifies flipping `seed_reauth` on the password leg, and that stands -- `has_recent_step_up` is read at six call sites governing 26 engine and 33 console step-up dependencies, so a flip would silently change the freshness posture of a neighbouring requirement's entire scored surface. But on the shipped default the password leg ALREADY passes `seed_reauth=False`, so the move actually tempting today is deleting the single `mark_session_reauthed` line inside `verify_mfa` -- a one-line change that moves the cell, looks like a tightening, and is worse on three counts: it would force a fresh password step-up on all 59 step-up-gated routes immediately after every MFA login; the line is not a seeding line at all, its own comment at `auth/service.py:2196-2198` says it re-anchors the session to the address that completed the second factor so a roamed administrator clears the new-client-IP signal with one proof, so deleting it breaks a control belonging to a different requirement; and it would be invisible to a reviewer reading only the diff against the residual's stated mechanism. Also disqualified: gating `GET /me/sessions` so the whole surface "looks protected", since the pinned parenthetical binds terminate only and friction on viewing buys no limb; and treating the login-supersession question on `GET /ui/sso` as verdict-neutral -- it is not, because declining it leaves the terminate limb unmet on one of the three cookie-minting login legs. Proposed work, all unallocated and named by subject: the session-terminate action-binding build across the four self-service routes; the test inversion, since the two currently-passing immediate-terminate tests are the instrument that measures the gap; the ADR 0077 amendment recording the session-terminate action, since that ADR scopes the vocabulary to durable-takeover factor-binding routes; the `docs/SECURITY.md:1418-1434` session-inventory documentation gap, which enumerates all four routes and never mentions the password re-proof gate that already shipped; the current-session revocability correction at `docs/SECURITY.md:1433`, which says the current session is only revocable via sign-out while `revoke_own_session` accepts it; the stale in-source docstring at `pages/account.py:508` asserting the sessions page carries no step-up; and the residual and anchor repair, including the reviewer attribution and re-score trigger the cell has never carried.

## 1150. research an honest pass for ASVS 7.6.1 -- bounding time since the IdP authentication event without forcing a credential prompt every round trip

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **5/10** · _fill-in_. With federation enabled a first deployment could not bound time since the IdP authentication event at all, and the one shipped lever destroys single sign-on, so there is no acceptable workaround. Difficulty 5: an owner ruling plus one setting, a max_age parameter on the existing authorize call and an auth_time comparison at the id_token seam, with a fallback for IdPs that omit the claim. _(was 5/10 · 7/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **7.6.1** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that session lifetime and termination between relying parties and IdPs behave as documented, requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached. The engine cannot see or bound that interval: it sends no `max_age` on the authorize request and never reads `auth_time`.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment with federation enabled, an IdP holding a long-lived SSO cookie could re-issue id_tokens indefinitely without any fresh authentication event, and the engine would never know -- it bounds how long the token is good for, not how long ago the user actually authenticated.

**The pinned verb.** "...requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached."

**What holds it short today.** The lifetime limb is fully satisfied by shipped defaults: `_issue_session` caps at `min([auth].session_absolute_hours, id_token.exp)` at the single `create_session` call site (`auth/service.py:1450`), documented at `docs/SECURITY.md:1240`, with `[auth].oidc_session_max_hours` able only to tighten. The re-authentication limb is not, and the one control that would force it ships off: `[auth].oidc_prompt` is None (`config/settings.py:1905`), so `prompt=login` is never requested. Termination is partial too -- with no back-channel logout receiver (10.5.5 is `na`), an IdP-side sign-out does not end the engine session.

**The research question.** The shipped-default triage classifies this cell `needs-owner-decision` and states the boundary the research must respect: setting `prompt=login` forces a fresh IdP credential entry on **every** authorize round trip, removing the one benefit a hospital enables OIDC to get. It also records that the surgical control does not exist -- an `oidc_max_age_seconds` setting plus an `auth_time` check would be a build, not a flip. So: what is the smallest honest construction that bounds time-since-IdP-authentication without collapsing single sign-on, and does it hold when the IdP omits `auth_time` (which OIDC permits unless `max_age` was requested)? A finding that no construction satisfies both is a successful outcome and belongs in front of the owner.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Setting `oidc_prompt = "login"` to move the cell. That trades away the product property federation exists to deliver, and "it can be configured" is never a pass under the method in any case. Nor rescoring `na` because `oidc_enabled` ships off -- the scorecard already endorsed scoring this cell on its merits, following the method's 3.7.3 worked example, and `na` stays reserved for conditionally-worded cells.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 80 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no item naming them in `docs/BACKLOG.md`. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. The construction this item asks for EXISTS and is fully determined; the cell NEEDS AN OWNER RULING, and the build does not settle it either way.** Every load-bearing sentence in this item still holds at HEAD, including the parenthetical, which I verified against fetched spec text rather than from memory: OIDC Core section 2 says `auth_time` is REQUIRED whenever `max_age` is requested, and section 3.1.2's Authentication Request subsection says the OP MUST attempt to actively re-authenticate only IF the elapsed time exceeds the value. That single conditional word is the whole difference between the move this item disqualifies and the honest one, and it is why single sign-on survives untouched for every user inside the window. All seven of the record's anchors are line-drifted -- `auth/service.py` 1035 to `:1125` and 1450 to `:1563`, `docs/SECURITY.md` 1317 to `:1330` and 1329 to `:1342`, `config/settings.py` 1977 to `:1985`, 1982 to `:1990` and 1896 to `:1904` -- and no expect string failed to resolve, so only the navigation aids rotted.

**The absence is real and re-measured with the recorded positive control live.** Zero hits tree-wide for the recency pattern across the engine, the packaged console, the extension, the harness and the vendored relay, while the control `params["prompt"] = prompt` fires at `messagefoundry/auth/oidc/flow.py:220` in the same run. `build_authorization_url` (`auth/oidc/flow.py:193-224`) carries nine fixed parameters plus optional `acr_values` and `prompt` and no `max_age`; `FederatedPrincipal` (`auth/oidc/claims.py:92-112`) carries no recency field; and the core-claims check (`:207-274`) reads expiry, issued-at, not-before, issuer, audience, authorized party, nonce and subject, and never `auth_time`. The one knob that would force a fresh IdP authentication ships unset (`[auth].oidc_prompt = None`, `config/settings.py:1985`).

**The build is five parts and needs no lab, which matters because the owner ruled 2026-08-20 that there is none.** A non-zero `max_age` default with NO off switch and a validator clamp -- ship the strict position, because at zero deployments a staged opt-out is a real cost paid to protect users who do not exist; the parameter appended in `build_authorization_url`; VERIFICATION in the claims ladder, which is the half that turns a request into a control -- require `auth_time`, refuse a stale one, with two new closed-set reason slugs so the browser error mapping and the audit stay closed-set, and carry the value as a typed field on `FederatedPrincipal` exactly as the expiry already is; the recency bound folded into the minted session's deadline at `auth/service.py:1125-1129` alongside the existing `min()`, which is REQUIRED rather than belt-and-braces because `/ui/reauth` (`messagefoundry_webconsole/routes/core.py:792-870`) verifies a password and a local second factor on every branch and never returns to the IdP, so a login-time gate alone would let the interval drift unbounded for the session's whole life; and the CI riders, each of which reds if skipped -- the offline verifier asserts every reason slug maps to exactly one rung, and the doc-drift test's contextual name markers include the bare `oidc_` prefix, so the new setting must be classified into the documented input table or the suite fails.

**Two rulings are needed, and one of them makes this a permanent partial if it goes the other way.** First: does "Identity Provider" include the on-prem KDC consumed through browser Kerberos SSO, or only the OIDC issuer? If only the issuer, the build above closes the cell. If both, the ceiling is partial permanently -- `authenticate_kerberos` passes no lifetime cap, ADR 0079 records that pyspnego discards the ticket timing, and SPNEGO gives a relying party no `max_age` equivalent with which to ask a KDC for a fresh authentication, so no build reaches it. The evidence leans toward both: ADR 0079's own title calls the directory the IdP, and the record already credits the directory leg for this cell's termination limb, which is hard to do while denying the directory is an IdP for the re-authentication limb. Second, on termination: NIST SP 800-63C-4 section 4.7, which this ASVS section names as its derivation, says a relying party and an IdP MAY communicate end-session events and that the relying party's session validity is independent of the assertion's -- MAY, not SHALL -- so documenting that independence properly may satisfy the limb outright, where the conservative answer costs a second build AND creates applicability where none exists today, moving more than this cell. Note also that scope review found two of the five authentication pathways the product's own documentation enumerates at `docs/SECURITY.md:1500-1501` were never graded or excluded, that `POST /auth/negotiate` (`api/auth_routes.py:261`) is a SECOND Kerberos mint route with a different freshness posture from the browser leg, and that "structurally unreachable without a fork" is true of the Windows provider and only approximately true of the GSSAPI one -- all of which enlarge rather than shrink the surface a control would have to cover.

**Still not an honest pass:** setting `[auth].oidc_prompt = "login"`, disqualified twice as a shipped-default flip re-scored on its own and as a purchase of the verdict with the very property federation exists to deliver, since it throws away the conditionality above. Nor re-scoring not-applicable because federation ships off. And a third the item does not name, which is the most convincing wrong move available: tightening `[auth].oidc_session_max_hours` (`config/settings.py:1990`) and calling the interval bounded. That knob only tightens the `min()` at `auth/service.py:1126-1129`; it bounds how long the TOKEN is good for and says nothing about how long ago the human authenticated -- and it is actively counterproductive, because shortening the session multiplies authorize round trips, every one of which an IdP holding a long-lived cookie can answer silently with no fresh authentication event. A real knob, a real tightening, a real number that moves, aimed at the wrong quantity, and no gate would catch it. Sending `max_age` and not checking what comes back is the same failure in the other direction, which is why the verification half is not optional. Proposed work, all unallocated and named by subject: the federated recency bound, co-landed with the sibling recentness arm as one change set per the designated resolution of their knob-name and missing-claim collision; the relying-party session-independence statement replacing the bare out-of-scope list entry at `docs/SECURITY.md:1342`, which is docs-only, small and worth doing regardless of every ruling above because that list entry is the artifact the verb's "as documented" clause is currently measured against; the Kerberos-leg written ceiling, stated once in the mechanism-comparison table rather than living only in an ADR amendment, since the shipped documentation states the OIDC session cap explicitly and says nothing about the Kerberos leg's session-versus-ticket relationship; and, only if the termination ruling comes back conservative, the OIDC back-channel logout receiver, priced with its coupling.

## 1151. research an honest pass for ASVS 8.1.1 -- documenting the data-specific access rules where a reader can actually find them

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **5/10** · _fill-in_. The code enforces more than the documentation describes, so there is no product effect and the residual is silent drift rather than exposure, which caps this below the surfaces that would misbehave on a first deployment. Difficulty 5 holds because the deliverable is not prose: the item requires establishing whether a drift gate over data-scoping claims is constructible at all, plus the public-versus-vaulted split the dangling docs/security pointer is a symptom of. _(was 6/10 · 5/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **8.1.1** (L1) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that authorization documentation define rules for restricting function-level AND data-specific access, based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. The function axis is exhaustive and CI-pinned in both directions; the data axis is where it falls short.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no direct product effect -- the code enforces more than the documentation describes, not less. The exposure is that an operator or reviewer reading the shipped documentation cannot learn the data-scoping rules, and undocumented rules drift silently.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes."

**What holds it short today.** Saved-search presets are strictly owner-scoped in code on list, get, delete and layered compose (`api/app.py:3960`, `list_search_presets(identity.username)`), and that rule appears nowhere in `docs/SECURITY.md` -- all four `/search/presets` route rows carry empty Extra-constraints cells. Separately, `auth/identity.py:37` points the reader at `docs/security/PHASE-8C-RBAC.md` for the per-channel scope rule, and there is no `docs/security/` directory in the engine tree at all (verified 2026-08-08 at this checkout). The scorecard's own note: every doc claim on this cell is prose, unchecked by the drift gate that pins the function axis.

**The research question.** What must "authorization documentation" contain to satisfy a data-specific rule, and where can it live? The second half is the real constraint: security documentation is deliberately kept out of the public engine repository, so the dangling pointer is a symptom of a standing decision rather than an oversight, and the research must ask what a public-repo reader is entitled to see about data scoping versus what belongs in the private record. The other unknown is enforcement: the function axis is credible because a CI gate fails when the map drifts from the routes, and there is no equivalent instrument for data-scoping claims -- so the research should establish whether one is constructible before any prose is written.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Adding sentences to `docs/SECURITY.md` describing the preset and channel scoping and calling the cell closed. That is prose no gate can check, on a cell whose residual specifically names unchecked prose as the defect; it would move the verdict while leaving the documentation free to drift back out of truth at the next commit. Deleting the dangling `docs/security/PHASE-8C-RBAC.md` pointer instead of supplying what it points at is the same move in a smaller package.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 80 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no item naming them in `docs/BACKLOG.md`. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is REACHABLE with a build, and this item's STATED BLOCKER does not exist.** The research question assumes security documentation is deliberately kept out of the public engine repository, so a dangling pointer is a symptom of a standing decision. `docs/SECURITY-DOCS-POLICY.md:12-15` is narrower than that: a document is withheld only if it details an open un-remediated weakness in enough detail to act on, or names a customer, site or deployment -- and `:23-25` records the rule moving documents INTO the open. A description of shipped, working data-scoping rules meets neither test. The pointer is not dangling either: the target exists, and `docs/SECURITY-DOCS-POLICY.md:5-8` states in terms that such a citation names a real maintainer-internal document, is cited for provenance, and will not resolve in the public tree. There is no disclosure question left to research here. Two mechanical drifts are already corrected inside the record: the preset owner key is `identity.user_id` at `api/app.py:4169`, `:4217`, `:4247` and `:4282`, not the username; and two of the four preset route rows are non-empty, with the true statement being that none of them states the owner rule.

**One sentence in the shipped documentation is FALSE, and it sits inside the blockquote that IS the public statement of the data rule.** `docs/SECURITY.md:707` asserts "Monitoring dashboards stay global." Executed, not read: `pytest tests/test_connection_event_scope.py -k topology_and_events_are_filtered` passes, asserting a scoped operator's channel list, connection list and event list are all narrowed, with its unscoped twin in the same run as the positive control. The code says so too -- `api/app.py:1670` filters channels on the scope predicate, `:1684-1701` suppresses shared-outbound rows and filters inbounds, `:2336` and `:2401` scope events and active alerts, and `:4458-4468` refuses to traverse into a shared outbound. The sentence is inherited verbatim from an internal design document where it was a decision the code later outgrew. Two lines above it, `docs/SECURITY.md:704` enumerates four scoped permissions for a set that spans at least seven -- the completeness-claim liability SDS-3.6 names.

**The gap is an order of magnitude larger than one object family, and the first census understated it further.** Per-route data-scoping rules are enforced in code and stated in almost no route-map row, and the console's route map is STRUCTURALLY incapable of stating one: `docs/SECURITY.md:547` is a four-column table, and a parse of all 87 console rows found every row four-cell with zero stating a data rule, against a positive control of 35 of those same rows mentioning step-up or pacing. Adversarial review then broke the engine-side census on its own terms: it was derived by AST over `messagefoundry/api/app.py` alone, while `docs/SECURITY.md:306` -- the counting basis in the very artifact under grade -- states that `create_app()` builds 105 route objects, 67 in `app.py` and 38 in `api/auth_routes.py`. Replaying the same predicate reproduces the app-module number exactly and returns 14 more in the auth module the census never touched. The scan is also blind inside the file it did scan: the approvals release, the stats socket and `DELETE /me/sessions/{id}` all score zero because their bodies name none of the helper primitives, yet all three enforce real data rules -- the self-approval refusal compares a stored requester against a REASSIGNABLE username (`api/approvals.py:122`, `api/app.py:2780`), which is a second instance of the exact key-integrity class this codebase has already been bitten by twice; and the stats socket carries a per-PROPERTY rule, one global field beside a channel-scoped one in the same frame, which is the properties case the verb explicitly ranges over.

**The honest path is to make the data axis DERIVED, the way the function axis already is, and to correct the false sentence first.** Extend the single shared route walk -- deliberately one implementation, consumed by both the drift guard and the authorization sweep -- to emit a per-route descriptor of RULE KIND, KEY ATTRIBUTE and DENIAL SHAPE, resolved by exact AST node resolution rather than substring (a first pass substring-matched a helper name and produced three false positives, which is the cheapest possible demonstration that a name-presence scan is not an instrument), over BOTH route modules, with a taxonomy able to express a requester-versus-approver rule and a per-property split. Then extend the drift guard, whose parser today locates the permission and gate columns by header name and never reads the extra-constraints cell at all -- measured, zero occurrences of the scoping primitives across the whole 1769-line suite against 95 occurrences of "permission" as the control, which is why the suite is green while the doc carries a false data sentence. Two mitigations the repo already knows to demand: a planted-mutation control in the existing house pattern, and a FLOOR on the number of data-rule rows found, because the walk's own docstring prescribes flooring after a refactor once made every route read as ungated while the guard stayed green.

**Still not an honest pass:** adding sentences describing the preset and channel scoping and calling the cell closed -- and its sharpest form is not ungated prose in general but prose scoped to the RESIDUAL rather than the VERB, which would satisfy every word of the current record while leaving the rest of the surface silent. Nor pasting "per-channel scope" into the silent cells: those routes do not enforce the same rule -- one answers 403 through a control guard, one answers 404 deliberately before any update or audit row, one is a flat 403 for a scoped caller, and two silently filter and never refuse -- so uniform boilerplate would trade one defect for a subtler one and a presence-only gate would certify it forever. Nor treating the gate as the pass: for a documentation requirement the documentation is the control and the gate only keeps it true. And nor quietly deleting the false sentence rather than replacing it, which removes a falsehood and also the only public statement about monitoring-plane scoping, converting one failure into another while reading as progress in a diff. This item's second disqualifier is MIS-AIMED as written and must not be carried forward: deleting the `docs/security/` pointer is not the move, because the target exists and the policy sanctions provenance citations that do not resolve publicly -- re-pointing the source comment at the public section gives the reader MORE, not less, and "supplying what it points at" would spend a build publishing an internal design document to satisfy a source comment. Proposed work, all unallocated and named by subject: the monitoring-scope correction, stating BOTH halves -- that the topology, event, alert and graph reads are narrowed for a scoped caller and a shared outbound is suppressed, AND that the aggregate metrics counts remain global; the per-route data-rule derivation over both route modules, resolved at the point of decision; the bidirectional extra-constraints comparison with its planted mutation and row-count floor; the rows the gate then demands; the key-attribute work, which spans the thirteen self-service routes covered by one sentence whose members' keys diverge plus the self-approval rule, not just two keys; a per-route data descriptor for the console plane rather than a single inherited sentence, which would be false the day it was written because a console route already decides channel scope in its own body; the derived not-restricted table, covering at least the channel-unrestricted audit read and the log tail; a cross-scope pass in the existing authorization sweep, which today runs no object-level pass at all; and re-pointing the source comment at the public section, amending the re-score trigger in the same pass so it names the rule resolving rather than the path.

## 1152. research an honest pass for ASVS 8.2.2 -- object-level authorization on the uploads family, which carries PHI and no owner check

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **6/10** · Difficulty **4/10** · _quick win_. The PHI-bearing half is fixed in shipped code, so the cross-operator enumeration, the content oracle and the two-step injection path are gone (app.py:3749, :3941-3971). What remains is the principal-narrowing axis nothing else closes -- identity.py:38 still defaults to every channel -- plus the pageless GET /uploads against the master-test-plan clause, with per-user scoping available as an awkward workaround (value 6). The remainder is a default flip with its first-run console handling plus pagination across API and console, tested but not touching the store (difficulty 4). _(was 9/10 · 5/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **8.2.2** (L1) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that data-specific access be restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items, to mitigate IDOR and BOLA. **As filed**, one PHI-bearing object family had no object-level authorization at all: `GET /uploads` listed every user's files unfiltered, and browse and delete took a `file_id` straight through to `get_meta`/`read_bytes` with no channel and no owner check.
> **UPDATE 2026-08-11 -- THE UPLOADS HALF IS BUILT; THE ITEM STAYS OPEN.** Owner-only plus a `files:access_any` Administrator override, keyed on the immutable `uploader_id` (`Identity.user_id`), owner-ratified and recorded in [ADR 0134](adr/0134-offline-uploaded-logs-viewer-connection-decoupled-upload-browse-resend-deletion-phi-at-rest-posture-stdlib-multipart.md) Amendment A. All four routes now enforce it, including resend's SOURCE file (it previously checked only the TARGET inbound). So the three specific defects named above are fixed in the shipped code and the paragraph above describes the pre-fix state, not the current one.
> **WHY IT IS NOT CLOSED, and none of these is a formality.** (1) The principal-narrowing axis is UNTOUCHED: `Identity.allowed_channels` still defaults to `None` (`auth/identity.py:38`) = every channel. (2) This item's own acceptance says **"Both halves need answers; neither alone closes the cell"** -- one half is answered. (3) ADR 0134 Amendment A satisfies only the SECOND clause of the master-test-plan's exit criterion 12; `GET /uploads` remains pageless, so the first clause is open. (4) The scorecard carrying the 8.2.2 verdict lives outside this repo and is not re-scored by this work.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P1. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity (as filed, and CORRECTED 2026-08-11 -- the original wording overstated the read):** on a first deployment, any operator holding the uploads permission would have been able to enumerate every other operator's uploaded files. **No route returned a file's body** -- browse returns metadata only. What the surface actually exposed was (a) cross-operator enumeration, (b) a CONTENT ORACLE, since browse accepts arbitrary `content`/`field_path` searches run against another operator's DECRYPTED PHI and returns `matched`/`scanned` counts plus per-message `message_type`, `control_id` and size, and (c) an INJECTION PATH THAT YIELDS BODIES IN TWO STEPS -- resend checked `can_access_channel` on the TARGET inbound and never the SOURCE file's owner, so a scoped operator could inject another operator's messages into an inbound they were authorized for and then read them as ordinary messages. Mitigated even then by step-up, the PHI read-hop guard, PHI read pacing and needle-shape-only auditing. **"Including their bodies" was wrong as a description of the routes and propagated from this row into three downstream messages before it was caught** -- the two-step path is real, the one-step read never existed. Fixed in the shipped code as of 2026-08-11 (see the update above).

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA)."

**What holds it short.** Two separate things, and only one is a switch. **Still open:** the principal-narrowing axis ships off -- `Identity.allowed_channels` defaults to None (`auth/identity.py:38`), meaning every channel. **Answered 2026-08-11:** the uploads family had no owner check in any configuration and no channel dimension to scope by, so the channel axis could not reach it even when narrowed; it is now scoped by OWNER instead, which needs no configuration and therefore protects a default install. The owner identity was already persisted as a bare username (`UploadMeta.uploader` at `uploads.py:107` as filed) and is now `UploadedFileMeta.uploader_id`, the immutable `Identity.user_id`, with `uploader` retained as the display label.

**The research question -- HALF ANSWERED.** What is the correct authorization model for an uploaded file? The engine's whole data-scoping vocabulary is the channel, and an upload is not bound to one, so the research had to decide what a file's resource attribute even is -- uploader identity, the inbound it was injected into, both, or something the model does not yet express -- and whether owner-scoping is right for an operational console where a colleague may legitimately need to inspect a file after a shift change.

**ANSWERED 2026-08-11 (owner-ratified):** the resource attribute is **uploader identity**, bound to the immutable `user_id` and not the username, with the shift-change case served by an explicit `files:access_any` Administrator override rather than by widening the default. The channel axis was rejected on the ground that `allowed_channels` defaults to every channel, so a channel-scoped rule would protect nobody on a default install -- a control resting on a false premise. **Bound on that answer:** re-keying onto `user_id` does NOT close a `sAMAccountName` recycled in the directory without a MessageFoundry `delete_user`, because `_upsert_ad_user` adopts the surviving mirror row and re-binds its id; that needs the directory-immutable binding tracked as **#1143**.

**STILL UNANSWERED, and it is what keeps this item open:** narrowing `allowed_channels` by default carries a first-run cost, because new non-admins and unmapped AD users would see an empty console until scoped, which reads as broken RBAC on day one. Both halves need answers; neither alone closes the cell.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Flipping the `allowed_channels` default and rescoring. The triage is explicit that it narrows the channel axis and does not close the cell, because uploads carry no channel dimension -- the verdict would move on a change that does not touch the binding defect. Re-declaring uploaded files as something other than "data items" is the other tempting move and does not survive contact with the requirement's text or with the fact that those files carry message bodies.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 80 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no item naming them in `docs/BACKLOG.md`. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. An honest pass is REACHABLE with a build, and this item's TRAP has lost its stated ground while surviving on its second.** The uploads paragraph was already retracted and re-verifies retracted: the three upload-store accessor sites in the API (`api/app.py:3769`, `:4012`, `:4101`) are each preceded by an authorization call at `:3751`, delete is preceded at `:4144`, and the listing filters at `:3959`. But the trap says a default flip does not close the cell BECAUSE uploads carry no channel dimension -- and uploads no longer need one, they carry a configuration-free owner check on the immutable `Identity.user_id` (`api/app.py:3717`, `:3751`). Reason three for staying open is likewise no longer this cell's reason: a prior ruling recorded that the pageless uploads listing is a resource-consumption gap, not an object-authorization one. And "what holds it short" is incomplete in both directions -- two further limbs are live and named by neither this item nor the record.

**The live blocker is that "every channel" is what the schema does when nobody says anything.** `Identity.allowed_channels` defaults to None (`auth/identity.py:37-38`) and the predicate returns True unconditionally when it is None (`:76-78`); the resolver returns None for a NULL column (`auth/service.py:222`); the column is declared "NULL = all" (`store/store.py:1651`); and `create_user`'s INSERT does not list the column at all (`store/store.py:7733-7749`), so every account is minted permissive. A shipped test pins that permissive default by name (`tests/test_channel_rbac.py:296-306`). All 18 predicate call sites in `api/app.py` therefore narrow nobody on a shipped install. The store needs no new predicate for a deny-by-default end state: `_append_channel_scope` already renders an EMPTY scope as `1=0` (`store/store.py:1279`, mirrored in both server backends).

**Two limbs nobody has been measuring, and the second is the sharper one.** `GET /me/security-events` restricts a per-user object family on a REASSIGNABLE username -- `api/auth_routes.py:471` passes `identity.username` into `auth/service.py:2649`, which reaches `SELECT ... WHERE actor = ?` at `store/store.py:7470-7472` against a table with no immutable-id sibling column (`store/store.py:1586-1595`), mirrored in the console at `routes/audit.py:33-39`. On a first deployment a deleted-and-recreated account carrying the same username would inherit the departed operator's authentication-event history. And `POST /connections/{name}/flag` (`api/app.py:1999-2025`) is the one by-id route on an otherwise fully channel-scoped family with NO per-object check at all, while all eight siblings carry one (`:1970`, `:1979`, `:1988`, `:2028`, `:2078`, `:2127`, `:2196`, `:2349`) -- and it is a write that persists into `connections.toml`. Its route-map row states no per-channel constraint, so the documentation does not disclose the inconsistency, and its console twin (`routes/connection_writes.py:102-133`) inherits the omission verbatim. Separately, `_upsert_ad_user` (`auth/service.py:1322-1335`) resolves by account name and re-binds a surviving mirror row's user id, because the AD principal carries no directory-immutable identifier -- the federated path shows the correct shape by contrast, matching on issuer and subject together.

**Scope review corrected one box that was graded verified and is false.** `GET /metrics` renders an unscoped Prometheus exposition: `render_metrics(engine)` (`api/metrics.py:533`) and `gather_snapshot(engine)` (`:212`) take no identity, and measured, `grep -cE "allowed_channels|can_access_channel|Identity" messagefoundry/api/metrics.py` returns 0 against a positive control of 127 for the same pattern in `api/app.py`. The exposition emits per-connection received, errored, delivered, dead-lettered and queue-depth series keyed by connection and destination, under a permission every built-in non-administrator role holds -- so on a first deployment a channel-scoped operator would enumerate every connection in the estate plus its volumes, including the shared-outbound topology that three sibling collection routes deliberately withhold from that same principal with code comments saying so. A by-id guard-token scanner cannot see it, which is why the parity test below must cover COLLECTION routes as well.

**Still not an honest pass:** flipping the scope default and re-scoring on that alone. It is one of six builds and explicitly insufficient -- though it is fair to say it is the load-bearing one, and if the record ever shows it landing alone, the trap fired. Nor re-declaring the directory as outside the set of values authorization reads: the code is harsher than the item knew, because the group-to-channel resolver has exactly ONE engine consumer, on the login path (`auth/service.py:1304`), against a positive control of TWO for the group-to-role resolver (`:1235` login and `:1439` reconciler) -- so the reconciler re-diffs roles and never channel scope, and the very limb the trap names as the reason not to scope the directory out is the limb nobody has been measuring. Nor citing the store-level owner-scoping test as the execution evidence the re-score trigger asks for: it drives the store with literal owner strings, never constructs an identity, and would stay green on exactly the recycling case. And nothing here is a purpose purchase -- the scope predicate occurs zero times across the pipeline, transport and parsing packages against 44 occurrences of the channel identifier in the pipeline alone, so no clinical message is NAKed or dropped by any of it; the cost is a console that shows an unprovisioned operator nothing, which the affordance below exists to make legible. Proposed work, all unallocated and named by subject: the explicit channel-grant work, retiring the NULL-means-all encoding in favour of a grant somebody typed and making an absent scope deny, carried through the identity predicate, the scope resolver, the AD sync's wildcard collapse, the setter, user creation and the API model; the unprovisioned-operator first-run affordance in the console, deliberately NOT a start-time refusal, which would make a fresh one-operator install unstartable for the same verdict; the audit-actor immutable-id work, folded INTO the hash chain following the existing conditional-element precedent rather than hung off it, since attribution an attacker can rewrite without breaking tamper-evidence would be worse than none; the connection-flag object check plus a parity test covering by-id AND collection routes on channel-bearing and owner-bearing families; the metrics-exposition scoping, dropping shared-outbound series entirely for a scoped caller, or a written scope-out inside the record naming the requirement that owns it; the directory-immutable identity binding, or its explicit written relocation, since silence is not an accepted third option; and the test inversion, replacing the test that pins an unscoped non-administrator's full access with one asserting a freshly minted non-administrator reaches nothing until granted, plus identity-level owner-scoping tests exercising a deleted-and-recreated same-username account.

## 1153. research an honest pass for ASVS 8.2.4 -- adaptive controls inside a live session on a single-host loopback deployment

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P3.** Value **3/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _money pit_. The one in-session contextual signal still ships off and is documented in the shipped code as never changing an authorization decision, and the allowed-networks list still ships empty with a recorded inert-behind-NAT limit, so the existing-session half of the requirement rests on nothing at the shipped bind. Value 3 because no signal changes an authorization outcome in any configuration, so what is bought is a cell rather than a closed exposure; difficulty 6 because the honest answer needs an owner boundary decision first and the four attribute classes the verb names are largely unavailable to an on-premises single-host engine, with time-of-day gating on a 24-hour clinical service actively harmful. _(was 3/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **8.2.4** (L3) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks for adaptive controls based on environmental and contextual attributes -- time of day, location, IP address, device -- applied both when a consumer starts a new session AND during an existing one, as defined in the application's documentation. The session-start half ships on; the in-session half rests on a single signal that ships off.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P3. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no present product effect at the shipped bind. On a first deployment behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy, a session hijacked mid-life would trigger no contextual re-check, since the one signal that could fire is off and no signal changes an RBAC allow or deny in any configuration.

**The pinned verb.** "...adaptive security controls based on a consumer's environmental and contextual attributes... These controls must be applied when the consumer tries to start a new session and also during an existing session."

**What holds it short today.** Session start is covered (login limiters, lockout, `require_mfa: bool = True`). In session, the sole contextual signal is `admin_new_ip_step_up`, shipping False (`config/settings.py:1729`), with `allowed_client_networks` empty (`:3556`); even enabled it cannot fire on a single-host loopback session (`auth/service.py:1857` early-returns) and it never changes an authorization decision. Of the four attribute classes the requirement names, only IP is consumed at all -- `docs/SECURITY.md:1167` says so under "Attributes not consumed at this release".

**The research question.** The triage classifies this `needs-owner-decision` and adds a caveat that cuts against its own cost estimate: the flip is free at the shipped loopback bind but not on the posture the method assesses, where `api/security.py:181-183` resolves the admin's real workstation address behind a declared trusted proxy and NAT churn becomes live. So the boundary is an owner call, and the research must sit inside it: what could an honest pass consist of for an on-premises engine that binds loopback by default, where location and device attributes may be genuinely unavailable and time-of-day gating on a 24-hour clinical service may be actively harmful? Whether the requirement can be met without any signal ever changing an authorization decision is the sharpest sub-question.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Editing `docs/SECURITY.md` to narrow what the application "defines" so the shipped controls match the documentation. The requirement's phrase "as defined in the application's documentation" makes that the obvious lever and it is exactly the move the honest-pass bar rules out -- the documentation is the thing measured, not the thing tuned. Flipping `admin_new_ip_step_up` alone is not a pass either: the triage records it leaves the cell partial, and it fires on one attribute of four.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 80 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no item naming them in `docs/BACKLOG.md`. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. The cell NEEDS AN OWNER RULING -- on THREE questions in order, not one -- and this item's severity sentence is confirmed while its framing of the levers is short by one.** The item names `admin_new_ip_step_up` as the sole in-session contextual signal; the record names two, and the second is enforced in pure ASGI middleware on EVERY request including the stats socket and the static mount (`messagefoundry/api/client_networks.py:5-7`, `:158`), so it is an in-session control too. That matters, because the item reads as though one flip were the only lever when in fact BOTH are dead on the shipped bind for the SAME structural reason -- each folds loopback -- and that shared cause, not the count of levers, is what this cell turns on. Anchors have drifted: the knob is `config/settings.py:1808`, the allow-list is `:3647`, the early return is `auth/service.py:1970`, and the not-consumed paragraph is `docs/SECURITY.md:1257`.

**The measurement, with a two-sided instrument.** The only decision-read of a per-session environmental baseline is `auth/service.py:1978`, and it is unreachable twice over on a shipped install: the knob early-returns at `:1970` against a default of False, and even flipped, `_same_host` (`:1929-1940`) folds `127.0.0.1` and `::1` into one host, with the docstring saying the fold keeps the loopback default a genuine no-op. The network gate ships empty (`config/settings.py:3647`) and `messagefoundry/netaddr.py:80-89` allows loopback unconditionally and with no knob -- a deliberate, documented lock-out defence for credential-less on-box clients. Time of day, geolocation, device posture and user-agent are all absent across the engine, the console and the extension, each measured with a positive control that fired in the same run. And no consumer-environment attribute changes a resolved permission set anywhere: the shipped source says so twice, at `config/settings.py:1803-1804` and `auth/service.py:1963-1964`.

**Scope review found the surface was enumerated over the CONTROL PLANE only, and the product's own documentation contradicts that.** `docs/SECURITY.md:1126` -- inside the exact section that satisfies this verb's documentation limb -- reads "every one consumed at this release, on the control plane AND the data plane", and the second table beneath it tabulates data-plane rows in the same closed action vocabulary. On the code side, `peer_ip_allowed` (`messagefoundry/netaddr.py:42`) is called from five listeners -- `transports/mllp.py:1485`, `tcp.py:495`, `x12.py:537`, `http_listener.py:691` and `dicom.py:283` -- and `netaddr.py:95` states in source that the loopback carve-out lives in the OTHER function and deliberately not here. So the structural argument that every contextual control keys on an address loopback collapses is a property of one function on one plane, generalised to the engine. Consequently the in-session limb is REALISED on the data plane: `transports/dicom.py:283` evaluates the peer address per object inside an already-negotiated association and returns a not-authorized status before any durable commit. Two construction gates additionally match the second half of the shipped-default rule by refusing to start when the precondition is absent (`pipeline/wiring_runner.py:6963-7008`, `transports/dicom.py:199-209`) and were never graded.

**The three questions, in order.** First and prior: does this verb's "consumer" range over ingest peers, given that the documentation the verb defers to currently places them inside this exact inventory? If yes, the residual is a control-plane statement presented as an engine statement, the data-plane peer controls must be graded on their own terms, and any build must cover both planes. If no, the documentation over-discloses relative to the assessed scope and that needs recording, because the documentation limb is currently earned by a document describing more than the matrix grades. Only then: is the verb's parenthetical a coverage FLOOR or exemplary? Under the floor reading the ceiling is partial permanently and the reason is structural rather than budgetary -- on a single-host bind the consumer has no location distinguishable from the engine's, and every geolocation path needs an operator-supplied database the product cannot ship. And third: which posture does the shipped-default rule grade for this cell -- the bare loopback bind, or the one posture the assessment method names, behind a declared TLS-terminating reverse proxy, where `api/security.py:173-186` has already resolved the operator's real workstation address? Note that question changes whether the address-keyed signal is CAPABLE of firing; on the record's own terms it does not change the verdict without new code.

**Still not an honest pass, and the tempting move has moved.** Flipping `admin_new_ip_step_up` is disqualified for the item's reason and for a stronger measured one: on the bind the shipped-default rule grades, THE FLIP CHANGES NOTHING, because `_same_host` folds both loopback forms so the flipped control still returns False on every request a stock install will ever see. It is not a weak pass; it is a null edit dressed as remediation. Removing the loopback fold so the two forms "differ" would make the absence claim stop being writable by FABRICATING a signal, and the shipped comment at `auth/service.py:1931-1934` records that the fold exists so a dual-stack box presenting one form on one connection and the other on another is treated as one host. And a fourth trap this item does not name, which is now the cheapest move available: the engine ALREADY ships a complete timezone-aware, IANA-validated time-of-day and day-of-week window evaluator at `config/models.py:336-436`, with two live consumers in the pipeline, neither an authorization decision -- wiring it into the auth path would manufacture a time-of-day contextual control for almost no code. Disqualified twice: it would ship off like every schedule does, and shipping it ON requires a shipped DEFAULT WINDOW, and there is no defensible default window for the operator console of a twenty-four-hour clinical service, which is the product-purpose disqualifier in its sibling form. A softened challenge-instead-of-deny variant does not escape it, and the learned-hour variant is a behavioural baseline with a cold start and is the attribute class the documentation explicitly disclaims. That finding also exposes a guard defect worth fixing on its own: the recorded time-of-day absence pattern matches NONE of that evaluator's spellings, so a gate built on the engine's own evaluator would pass the absence check silently -- the zero is real and it is spelling-specific in a tree that demonstrably contains the thing. Proposed work, all unallocated and named by subject, the first three independent of every ruling above: a CI guard pinning the "attributes not consumed at this release" list at `docs/SECURITY.md:1257-1259` against the measured absences, so narrowing that paragraph reds the suite the way the per-row thresholds at `tests/test_security_doc_drift.py:359-375` already do -- this is the mechanical defence against the exact trap this item names and it does not exist today; widening the shared time-of-day absence pattern so it can see the engine's own window evaluator; correcting the stale in-source rationale at `messagefoundry/__main__.py:1933-1935`, which justifies the shipped default as preserving a not-applicable keystone that no cell holds, a false premise sitting in a distributed artifact a future assessor will read as authority; then the decision packet for the three questions; and, gated on those, the session client-context anchor with its compared field NAMED and its discriminating power measured -- on a single-operator host an owner-valued attribute collapses to a constant for exactly the reason diagnosed in the address signal, so the anchor must key on process identity and must carry a measurement that could come back "constant" -- the confine action for a mismatched anchor placed at the request dependency beside the existing precedent, the sessions-table context column across all three backends because a process-local anchor is wrong across restarts and under engine sharding, and a feasibility spike on resolving the ASGI peer port to an owning local process.

## 1154. research an honest pass for ASVS 8.3.2 -- directory-sourced authorization changes that lag, fail open, and have neither named mitigation

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P3.** Value **4/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _money pit_. The 300 s directory reconciliation interval is unchanged at config/settings.py:1904 and its validator at :2085-2091 constrains only the range, so no alert-on-action-while-unauthorized and no revert exists and the requirement's alternative arm is entirely unbuilt. Value 4 because the engine-owned half is already strong (opaque tokens, per-request identity re-resolution, revoke-on-mutation) and what would be built is alerting and revert over a lag in data the engine does not own; difficulty 6 because both named mitigations need definition before either could be built, and revert has no meaning for delivered clinical messages. _(was 4/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **8.3.2** (L3) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that changes to values on which authorization decisions are made apply immediately, and where they cannot, that mitigating controls alert when a consumer acts while no longer authorized and revert the change. Engine-side values do apply immediately; directory-sourced ones lag the reconciliation loop, and neither named mitigation exists.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P3. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment, a principal whose directory group membership was revoked would keep acting on the old permissions for up to `[auth].ad_session_recheck_seconds` (300 s, `config/settings.py:1817`), longer if the first pass is inconclusive, and indefinitely while the domain controller is unreachable -- the reconciler needs two consecutive failed passes to conclude an absence and fails open in between.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that changes to values on which authorization decisions are made are applied immediately. Where changes cannot be applied immediately... there must be mitigating controls to alert when a consumer performs an action when they are no longer authorized to do so and revert the change."

**What holds it short today.** The engine's own half is strong: opaque server-side tokens rather than self-contained ones (`auth/tokens.py:5`), full per-request identity re-resolution (`auth/service.py:1520`), and revoke-on-mutation so a permission reduction bites at once. The gaps are all on data the engine does not own: the 300 s directory loop, the fail-open posture on an unreachable DC, no alert on an action taken while no longer authorized, no revert, and the `/ws/stats` feed re-checking on a 3 s cadence (`api/app.py:321`) rather than per frame.

**The research question.** Is "applied immediately" reachable at all for a value that lives in someone else's directory, and if not, what would the requirement's alternative arm actually take here? Both named mitigations need definition before either could be built: what counts as detecting "an action performed while no longer authorized" once the reconciler catches up, and what "revert the change" means for an integration engine whose actions include delivered clinical messages that cannot be un-sent. The fail-open behaviour on an unreachable DC is a separate sub-question with its own product cost -- failing closed would take an operator's console offline during a network partition.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Shortening `ad_session_recheck_seconds`. A smaller lag is still a lag, and the requirement's first arm says immediately; buying the cell by tuning the interval also raises directory load with no principled stopping point. Re-declaring directory group membership as outside the set of "values on which authorization decisions are made" is the other available move, and it fails on the code -- those groups resolve to roles and channel scope, which is precisely what the authorization decision reads.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 80 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no item naming them in `docs/BACKLOG.md`. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. CONTESTED -- and this item's load-bearing sentence is FALSE in three places, each of which was already false at the commit the record was verified against, so these are misses rather than drift.** The item says the engine's own half is strong and the gaps are all on data the engine does not own. (1) `set_ad_group_map` (`auth/service.py:2942-2946`) and `set_ad_group_scope_map` (`:2948-2955`) rewrite the group-to-role and group-to-channel-scope maps through step-up-gated routes (`api/auth_routes.py:843-874`) and revoke NOTHING, while every sibling mutator does -- `set_roles` at `:2726`, custom-role update and delete via `:2845-2851`, `set_channel_scope` at `:2885`, disable at `:2702`, password reset at `:2869`. The scope setter's own docstring at `:2951` says "Takes effect on each AD user's next login", and that sentence was in the same file the record graded. (2) `ApprovalGate.approve()` (`api/approvals.py:116-137`) re-executes a captured operation with no re-validation of the requester's current authorization; `guard()` (`:67-100`) captures no permission set and persists the requester as a bare username at `:90`, inside a 72-hour window (`config/settings.py:3321`). The SIGNED risk-acceptance register row for this same cell names that arm explicitly and calls the fallback clause unbuilt in every configuration, so the record's residual is NARROWER than the signed register row for the same cell and this item inherited the narrower one. (3) The severity sentence is wrong in BOTH directions: two strikes apply only to an ABSENCE (`auth/reconcile.py:154-160`), a group change that alters the role set revokes on the FIRST present pass with no strikes (`:161-177`), and a removed group mapping only to a CHANNEL SCOPE is never picked up at all -- measured, the channel resolver has exactly one engine consumer, on the login path (`auth/service.py:1304`), against a positive control of two for the role resolver (`:1235` login and `:1439` reconciler) -- so that case is bounded only by the 12-hour absolute cap or the next login.

**Four builds are required under either reading and none is this item's named trap.** Revoke-on-mutation parity for the two AD map editors, matching the parity every other authorization-value mutator already has, plus a channel-scope re-diff in the reconciler as a third revocation reason counted against the same mass-revoke breaker budget. Requester re-validation at approval release -- an immutable requester id on `pending_approvals` across all three backends, capture of the required permission set at guard time, and a refuse-plus-audit-plus-alert when the requester no longer holds it -- explicitly NOT sequenced behind flipping `[approvals].enabled`, both because an off-by-default control cannot reach a pass anyway and because the register's binding ordering rule forbids recommending that flip while the single-actor dual-control defect stands. Per-frame authorization on `/ws/stats`: `api/app.py:5140` gates the re-check on a three-second elapsed timer while `:5133` sends a frame per second, so up to three consecutive frames -- including the per-channel-scoped rendering -- are emitted from an identity resolved up to three seconds earlier. And a bounded age on the extension's offline AI-policy cache (`ide/src/aiPolicy.ts:80-88`), where a cached PERMIT is returned with no age bound whenever the engine is unreachable, persisted across restarts; the sticky-deny asymmetry is correct and must not change.

**Scope review added a fifth surface of a kind the matrix already grades elsewhere.** `GET /messages/export` resolves the identity once at the dependency and then, inside a streaming generator (`api/app.py:3189-3204`), loops over the selected ids with a store round trip each and re-tests `identity.can_access_channel(row["channel_id"])` per row against the CAPTURED snapshot, for a limit accepting up to 100000 -- the code's own comment at `:3193-3194` calls that per-row check load-bearing, which makes the staleness of the value it tests material rather than incidental. `GET /audit/export` is the same shape at lower stake. So the socket build does not close the limb "outright", and any claim that the engine holds no cached authorization decision anywhere is false while these stand.

**What the two reviews split on, and why it is a decision rather than more research.** The research offered the owner a fork: does "applied immediately" bind the application to the propagation latency of an upstream directory it does not own, or to the application's own use of the value once it holds it -- with the second branch producing a pass. The second review argued that branch IS this item's second disqualified move wearing a temporal hat: it does not argue the group is outside the set of values authorization reads, it relabels the engine's own materialized copy as the authoritative record, which removes the directory value from the set by construction rather than by argument. I verified the code claim underneath it. `auth/service.py:1237` is `await self._store.set_user_roles(user.id, role_ids, assigned_by="ad-sync")` -- the engine PERSISTS the directory-derived roles into its own table with an explicit directory-provenance tag -- and `_build_identity` at `:1765-1766` opens with `role_ids = await self._store.get_user_role_ids(user.id)`, so every request resolves against that copy; `_sync_ad_channel_scope`'s own docstring (`:1295-1298`) says the same, describing itself as persisting the AD-group-derived scope so it is durable for later requests, mirroring the role sync. So the engine's role store IS a cached copy of an authorization value that outlives the value's change -- the parenthetical's own named failure mode -- and the four builds do not touch it, because the first makes the map EDITOR revoke, which is a different value from group MEMBERSHIP. That correction stands and is not negotiable. What it does not carry is the leap to a flat "cannot pass": settling the interpretive question is reserved for a reading of fetched chapter prose at the tagged release, which the research names as the only thing that could settle it and did not fetch. So the fork survives and must be put ASYMMETRICALLY -- the reading that would yield a pass is already rebutted by this item and by the code; is there anything in fetched chapter prose that reopens it? Until then the worse verdict stands.

**Still not an honest pass:** shortening the reconciler interval. Its first form is already spent, since the default moved from zero to 300 (`config/settings.py:1904`) and is CI-pinned, so the available move is tuning it further -- which fails for this item's stated reason and for a measured one it could not have known: the per-pass bind budget is 200 principals (`config/settings.py:1914`, `auth/reconcile.py:108-119`), so above that estate size shortening the interval does not shorten the worst-case rotation at all, it only raises directory load. Re-declaring directory group membership as outside the set of values authorization decisions read, which now includes the relabeling above. Landing the engine-owned builds and re-scoring on those alone, which is the sharpest trap here precisely because those builds are real and correct -- they change the residual and do not settle the verdict, and the write-up must say so in the same sentence that reports them. Wiring the zero-consumer `directory_reconcile_alert` property into the alert sink and calling the alert limb satisfied: it genuinely has zero production consumers (positive control -- the reconcile entry point has a real caller at `api/app.py:5465`), so wiring it is a real improvement and would make an absence grep stop returning zero, and it signals a mass-revoke BREAKER TRIP, a misconfiguration, never a consumer acting while no longer authorized. Arguing the directory limb away because the AD feature ships off, which the method rejects by name because every off-by-default control removes its own trigger. And making the revert limb reachable by shrinking the action set -- holding message-plane operations for one reconciler interval so anything done in the stale window stays reversible -- which buys the verdict with the product's stated purpose, since a 300-second delay on a dead-letter replay or a resend on a clinical integration engine is a patient-safety cost paid to move a cell. One correction to the ceiling argument: "revert is unreachable" is established for the MESSAGE plane, where a delivered message cannot be un-sent, and the admin plane is revertible from state the engine already records on a hash-chained audit (`auth/service.py:1244-1248` records from-and-to on a role resync), so pleading unreachability for the whole action set does not meet the rule that requires naming the change and saying why it is impossible. Proposed work, all unallocated and named by subject: revoke-on-mutation parity for the two AD map setters; the channel-scope re-diff in the reconciler; requester re-validation at approval release; per-frame authorization on the stats socket; re-resolution inside the streaming export loop, or a written and defended ruling that one bounded request is one authorization decision, since taking one position for the socket and the other for the export by silence is itself the defect; a bounded age on the extension's offline policy cache; the stale-authorization-action alert, which requires converting the reconciler's last-probed ledger from a monotonic clock to wall clock to join audit rows and registering a new type in the closed, CI-pinned alert allow-list; admin-plane revert of changes made inside the stale window; and correcting the three in-source comments that still say the reconciler defaults to zero while it ships 300, plus re-anchoring the six drifted evidence lines.

## 1155. research an honest pass for ASVS 10.1.1 under the owner ruling that a default-off OIDC feature is a partial

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _money pit_. No product effect and the enablement boundary is an owner ruling rather than a defect, but the same question governs at least 10.1.2, 10.2.1, 10.2.2, 10.5.1 and 10.5.4, so answering it once carries more than one cell and holds value at 5. Difficulty stays 6 because the two custody deltas the residual names, an operator-declared cleartext relaxation under ADR 0153 and the ECH sidecar's loopback bearer hop under ADR 0139, are cross-cutting rather than record work, and the honest outcome may still be that no pass exists. _(was 5/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **10.1.1** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that tokens reach only the components that strictly need them. What holds it short is not token custody but enablement: the owner ruled on 2026-08-05 that a feature shipping off is a rule-5 partial, and the relying party ships off at `messagefoundry/config/settings.py:1880`.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P3. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no product effect. On a first deployment the token-distribution controls the residual enumerates would all be in force; this is a scorecard-accuracy and method question, plus two narrow custody residuals worth a second look.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, when using a backend-for-frontend pattern for browser-based JavaScript applications, access and refresh tokens shall only be accessible for the backend."

**What holds it short today.** The scorecard residual records the verdict as an owner-ruled correction from pass, with zero engine code changed: rule 5 reads that the control exists but ships off, and OIDC does. The derivation under it still stands, and it names three things the research should not lose: an operator-declared `cleartext_accepted` relaxation (ADR 0153) can re-open a cleartext bearer hop through a forward proxy, the ECH sidecar (ADR 0139) puts a live bearer on a loopback cleartext hop, and only the asymmetric SMART client carries a 10.1.1-labelled test assertion.

**The research question.** Given the owner ruling stands as a boundary, what would an honest pass on this cell even look like? The unknowns are whether the method admits any route to pass for a feature that cannot honestly ship on (`settings.py:2133` refuses `oidc_enabled` without `ad_enabled`, and six further site-supplied values follow), whether the two custody deltas above can be closed so the residual is clean regardless of the enablement rule, and whether the test-coverage asymmetry is worth closing on its own. This question is shared with 10.1.2, 10.2.1, 10.2.2, 10.5.1 and 10.5.4; answer it once.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Enabling OIDC by default to move the cell - that reverses the owner's own ruling to buy six cells, and the config validator refuses to load it anyway. Nor is re-wording the method's rule 5 so default-off stops reading partial: that is editing the document the requirement is measured against.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 70 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no live-ledger item citing the cell id at all. The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. Outcome: the ceiling is partial and no build reaches pass -- which this item names as a valid finding -- but the surface is four OAuth enablement axes wide rather than one, and an in-scope engine package that handles ID Tokens was never opened. The scope lens refuted the surface matrix and the proposed build; the cheap-flip lens upheld the verdict on all six of its attacks.**

**THIS ITEM'S RESEARCH QUESTION WAS ANSWERED BY THE OWNER AFTER IT WAS FILED, TWICE.** `docs/ASVS-ASSESSMENT-METHOD.md` section 1.1a (owner ruling 2026-08-16) makes rule 4 strict and pre-rejects by name both arguments this cell would have to run -- "the feature ships off but every control inside it is unconditional" is rule 5, and the vacuity argument is rejected because a property predicated of an object the shipped default never creates is not satisfied. Owner Ruling 1 of 2026-08-17 then accepts the federated-login family as permanently partial and closes rule 4's second limb for it: a gate demanding those site-supplied values would refuse to start for every site that does not use federated login. That ruling is also the seventh entry the 2026-08-08 research-items audit recorded as missing, so this item's "answer it once for all six" instruction now has a holder. Neither ruling is applied to the record yet, which is why the cell still reads as if the question were open. Anchor drift: this item's `settings.py:1880` is at `messagefoundry/config/settings.py:1942`.

**THIS ITEM'S "NOT TOKEN CUSTODY BUT ENABLEMENT" SENTENCE IS TRUE IN SUBSTANCE AND WRONG IN SCOPE.** This verb ranges over every OAuth token the product handles, and `[auth].oidc_enabled` governs only one of FOUR independent enablement axes. The other three are per-connection outbound client legs with nothing to do with federated login: the asymmetric SMART Backend Services provider (`messagefoundry/transports/smart.py`, enabled by `smart_token_url`), the symmetric OAuth2 client-credentials provider (`messagefoundry/transports/http_auth.py`), and `FhirLookup()` composed with `with_smart_backend` (`messagefoundry/config/wiring.py:494-571`, minting at `messagefoundry/transports/fhir.py:829`), which is a distinct connection kind with its own spec, executor and opener table. So Ruling 1's stated premise -- the cells whose SOLE binding limb is that federated login ships off -- does not describe this cell. Its DISPOSITION survives intact either way, since the cell is permanently partial on the rubric gate regardless; but applying the ruling verbatim would retire two live, buildable residual items along with the unreachable one.

**THE ONE CONFIGURATION UNDER WHICH THE VERB IS FALSE, and it is independent of federated login.** `messagefoundry/transports/rest.py:479-516` refuses a named credential on a cleartext http hop at the assessed posture, and its own docstring at `:492-503` records that `cleartext_accepted` "deliberately reaches the credential hops too" and crosses with a loud audited WARN, while `tls_hop_attested` crosses silently through `_enforce_shipped_hop` (`rest.py:399-448`). Method section 1.1a is explicit that a warning is not a refusal and a signed relaxation is never a pass. On a first deployment a site declaring either would put a minted OAuth bearer on a segment every intermediary can read.

**THE PROPOSED WITHDRAWAL IS NOT EXPRESSIBLE WHERE THIS RESEARCH FIRST POINTED IT, AND THE CARVE-OUT IT WOULD PRESERVE IS THE WRONG ONE.** `refuse_cleartext_credential_hop` receives `credential: str` as a display string and carries no mintedness parameter, and its wrapper `refuse_cleartext_credentials` (`rest.py:519-548`) collapses every Authorization header to the single label "credential (Authorization header)", so making the refusal unconditional for a MINTED bearer requires a new discriminator threaded from at least seven construction sites (`rest.py:1261`, `soap.py:452`, `fhir.py:357`, `fhir.py:831`, `smart.py:135`, `http_auth.py:153`, `http_auth.py:376`). PHI-body hops are `refuse_cleartext_egress` (`rest.py:551+`), a different function; what actually shares this seam is other CREDENTIALS -- dicomweb's static bearer (`messagefoundry/transports/dicomweb.py:313-317`), static Basic, the SOAP UsernameToken and body secrets (`soap.py:528`, `:605`), and the proxy credential chain (`http_auth.py:376`) -- and the ADR 0153 declaration must be explicitly retained for those. Note also that `refuse_cleartext_credential_hop` fires at CONNECTOR CONSTRUCTION, which ADR 0031 isolates into a degraded connection rather than a refusal to start; that placement question is real and separate.

**AN IN-SCOPE ENGINE PACKAGE WAS NEVER OPENED, and the instrument is why.** Every absence measurement keyed on the literal `access_token`, while this verb's subject is "tokens" -- which in this product includes the OIDC `id_token`. A count of `access_token` under `messagefoundry/verify/**` returns ZERO rows while a listing of `oidc` under the same path fires on two files in the same run. `messagefoundry/verify/federation.py` carries 22 `id_token` references and backs a shipped, documented CLI (`messagefoundry/__main__.py:772-784`, `messagefoundry/verify/runner.py:178-261`, `docs/testing/VERIFY.md:44`) whose documented workflow instructs an operator to capture a live `id_token` to a FILE ON DISK and hand it to a second process. That is squarely inside "not persisted" and "sent only to components that strictly need them". The tool is offline and emits claims rather than the token (`federation.py:373-381`), so it may well be a defensible exception -- but it must be graded and given handling, lifetime and deletion guidance the shipped doc row currently omits, not left ungraded. Equally unenumerated: minted bearers are injected at five delivery sites across three files (`rest.py:1470`, `soap.py:792`, `fhir.py:547` -- the connection-test probe, which mints a real bearer -- `fhir.py:603`, and `fhir.py:943`/`:1008`), and the gate call is present and correct at every one, so that is an evidence gap rather than a control gap.
