Second, dropping RS256 and RS384 from `SignatureAlgorithm` outright, justified by there being no deployments, is the item's disqualified move: the zero-deployment rule deletes OUR migration and notice costs and says nothing about whether a partner's verifier accepts PS256, and `config/models.py:481-489` records that an outbound JWS is verified by the receiver out-of-band per partner contract. The item's own unknown about which counterparties actually verify PSS or ECDSA is the blocker, and it must not be dropped.

**The ruling is two questions.** Does "weak padding schemes" reach SIGNATURE padding as well as key transport? And -- prior, and reaching well beyond this requirement -- does an off-by-default WEAKNESS block a pass the way `docs/ASVS-ASSESSMENT-METHOD.md` section 1.1a rules an off-by-default CONTROL does? That section rules the control direction at length and is silent on the weakness direction, and the symmetric reading looks forced because its stated reason for rejecting the vacuity argument transfers verbatim: every opt-in connector removes its own weakness, so the argument buys every cell and grades none. Both readings converge on `direct.py:359`, where the options are to fund a CMS writer emitting `id-RSAES-OAEP`, to retire the connector, or to accept a mixed posture -- which under the method is a signed relaxation and therefore a recorded partial, never a pass. One cost correction for the packet: `pyasn1==0.6.4` and `pyasn1-modules==0.4.2` are already in `requirements.lock`, and `rfc5652` and `rfc4055` expose the needed structures, so the real gate on that path is the HISP interop unknown, not hand-written ASN.1 labour. **Still not an honest pass:** any padding gate whose acceptance test is a mutation at a settings field, because `direct.py:344` hardcodes its call and `:359` has no parameter to refuse -- mutate the signer instead. Proposed work, unallocated and by subject: the probe disposition (a residual argument, or a narrowing with a server-side acceptance test, never the narrowing alone); the IDE cipher pin plus correction of its decision comment; the WebAuthn advertised-algorithm restriction, gated on a lab measurement of which workforce authenticators enrol without RS256; the XML-DSig accept-set restriction stated as a positive allow-list over digests AND schemes, since `parsing/xml/signature.py:70` passes no configuration; SSH key-type support, since `transports/remotefile.py:454` can load only an RSA key and every SSH RSA signature algorithm is PKCS#1 v1.5; the DIRECT signer padding change gated on an interop measurement, which is already on the record as contested and asserted without one; the unhardened-context sweep, since sixteen contexts are built and seven hardened; the DIRECT content-cipher upgrade, measured AES-128-CBC by omission; and the two SMART defaults missing from the record.

**Researched 2026-09-04 at HEAD `a2eef0f37`. The version disagreement is SETTLED at 50.0.0, the triage was right and the scorecard's 49.0.0 is stale, and at 50.0.0 the two DIRECT sites are confirmed to differ in kind exactly as this item says.** `requirements.lock:262` pins `cryptography==50.0.0`, `uv.lock:458` agrees, and the importable module reports `50.0.0` on CPython 3.14.6. `pyproject.toml:64` carries only the floor `>=48.0.1`, which is what a reader mistaking a floor for a pin would report; the floor is not the version in play. Everything below was introspected against the installed 50.0.0 rather than read from documentation.

**All nine anchors have drifted, and the stale numbers do not fail loudly.** Re-verified at HEAD: PKCS1v15 signing is `signing.py:246` (was `:212`) and the verify-side mirror is `signing.py:273` (was `:239`); `add_signer` with no `rsa_padding=` is `direct.py:363` (was `:344`); `add_recipient` is `direct.py:378` (was `:359`); `with_signing`'s RS256 default is `signing.py:507` (was `:473`); `OutboundSigning.algorithm` is `config/models.py:517` (was `:486`); the SMART default is `smart.py:110` (was `:108`), its `connections.toml` string fallback is `smart.py:394` (was `:304`) and the `with_smart_backend` default is `smart.py:433` (was `:342`). Control, and it is the point: every one of the seven old numbers still resolves to a line, and each holds unrelated text -- `signing.py:212` is a docstring line about EC curves, `direct.py:344` is `await asyncio.to_thread(self._send, payload)`, `smart.py:108` is `client_id: str`. A re-scorer checking these by line number reads plausible code and never learns the anchor moved. Positive control on the grep instrument itself: `PKCS1v15` returns two engine hits and four test hits tree-wide, against a deliberately absent token returning zero in the same run.

**The API surface at 50.0.0, introspected.** `PKCS7SignatureBuilder.add_signer(certificate, private_key, hash_algorithm, *, rsa_padding: padding.PSS | padding.PKCS1v15 | None = None)` -- the keyword is exposed, keyword-only, and defaults to `None`. `PKCS7EnvelopeBuilder`'s entire public surface is `add_recipient(certificate)`, `set_data`, `set_content_encryption_algorithm` and `encrypt`; `add_recipient` takes one positional certificate and there is no key-encryption seam anywhere on the type. `PKCS7EnvelopeBuilder.__init__` calls `ossl.rsa_encryption_supported(padding=padding.PKCS1v15())` and raises `UnsupportedAlgorithm` when it is false, so PKCS#1 v1.5 support is a precondition of the type CONSTRUCTING -- the item's prior wording holds verbatim at 50.0.0. One change nobody has recorded: `ContentEncryptionAlgorithm` is no longer an enum at 50.0.0, it is the typing union `type[AES128] | type[AES256]`, so it is passed the class itself and any code written against a `.AES128` enum MEMBER will not run. That matters to the proposed DIRECT content-cipher upgrade and to #1169, both of which touch this type.

**Measured end to end on generated RSA-2048 certs, reading OIDs out of the emitted DER, with eight controls that all fired.** Arm 1 rebuilds `direct.py`'s exact shipped call and the SignedData carries `rsaEncryption` (1.2.840.113549.1.1.1). Arm 2 adds only `rsa_padding=PSS` and `RSASSA-PSS` (1.2.840.113549.1.1.10) appears. A byte-scan cannot say WHICH field carries an OID, so the discriminator is a count: `rsaEncryption` occurs twice in arm 1 and once in arm 2, and the embedded signer certificate on its own accounts for exactly one -- its SubjectPublicKeyInfo -- so the field that changed is the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm and not something incidental. Arm 3 rebuilds the shipped envelope: key transport is `rsaEncryption` and the content cipher is `aes128-CBC` (2.16.840.1.101.3.4.1.2), confirming the AES-128-CBC-by-omission finding. Arm 4 sets `set_content_encryption_algorithm(AES256)` and the content becomes `aes256-CBC` while the key transport does not move. `id-RSAES-OAEP` (1.2.840.113549.1.1.7) is absent from BOTH envelopes, and the scanner's ability to find an OID it is given was controlled separately against `id-envelopedData`.

**The verdict on each site, and they must stay apart.** `direct.py:363` is a CODE CHOICE and is fixable today with one keyword on a call the pinned library already accepts -- what gates it is partner interoperability, not the library. `direct.py:378` is a LIBRARY LIMIT: no argument, no seam, and PKCS#1 v1.5 demanded before the builder will construct. No engine-side change reaches it. Any fix claiming to close both is wrong, and so is any finding that reports them as one defect. Two consequences follow that the record does not carry. First, the closed enum has no `PS384` member (`config/models.py:489-494` is RS256, PS256, ES256, RS384, ES384), so the SMART arm has no PSS counterpart at SHA-384 at all -- dropping RS384 forces ES384 and therefore a P-384 EC key, which is precisely the cost the triage priced, and it is a structural fact rather than a preference. Second, `direct.py:498` registers a destination only and no source, so the engine verifies nothing on this surface; a partner rejecting PSS would surface as a delivery failure at the receiving HISP, with no engine-side signal distinguishing it from any other SMTP-level failure.

**What I could not establish, stated as a gap rather than guessed.** The partner field data this item names as unknown (a) remains unknown, and it cannot be established from inside this repository. Three things would have to be known before any signature-padding flip: whether a given receiving HISP's CMS verifier accepts an `RSASSA-PSS` SignerInfo, where RFC 5751 makes PKCS#1 v1.5 mandatory-to-implement for S/MIME and PSS (RFC 4056) optional, so a fully conformant receiver may refuse it and be right; whether a given SMART token endpoint accepts ES384, which the Backend Services profile makes mandatory-to-support but which "mandatory in the specification" does not make implemented; and, for `OutboundSigning`, nothing at all, because `config/models.py` records that the receiver verifies out-of-band per partner contract, so there is no discoverable set even in principle. The repository holds no partner inventory, no interop corpus and no captured counterparty responses, and per section 0 there are zero deployments, so there is no field traffic to sample either -- the absence is structural, not an omission. A site would have to enumerate its own trading partners, obtain each verifier's capability statement, and run a signed test message through each partner's test environment before switching. I made no padding change: the prior "not reachable" ruling is the only ruling on the record, it authorizes nothing, and a shipped signing default is a security-posture decision with partner consequences that section 0's zero-deployment rule does not transfer to.

**Handoff for the Tracker seat, engine-side evidence by path.** The re-score needs no vault content to act on. Refresh the four cell anchors to `signing.py:246`, `signing.py:273`, `direct.py:363` and `direct.py:378`, and the three default anchors to `signing.py:507`, `config/models.py:517` and `smart.py:110`, adding the two SMART sites still missing from the record at `smart.py:394` and `smart.py:433`. Correct the recorded library version from 49.0.0 to 50.0.0; the residual that turns on it should be re-read, since it was written against a version that is not the one pinned. The key-transport limb at `direct.py:378` is measured unreachable within the pinned library, so a pass on this cell cannot be reached by configuration and the honest dispositions are the three this item already names -- fund a CMS writer emitting `id-RSAES-OAEP`, retire the connector, or record a signed relaxation, which under the method is a partial and never a pass. The two ruling questions stand unchanged and unanswered.

## 1169. research an honest pass for ASVS 11.3.3 -- a strict-ciphertext read that refuses an unmarked cipher column

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **7/10** · Difficulty **6/10** · _big bet_. A stripped marker would, on a first deployment, read back as plaintext instead of failing, so the integrity property the AEAD writer provides would be silently absent on that row, and the cell additionally carries the re-homed DIRECT S/MIME unauthenticated AES-128-CBC surface with no other cell to defer to. Difficulty 6 stands because strict mode must decide per-column versus global scope across dozens of decrypt call sites in three backends, and must define the mixed-marker state that arises inside a single install when encryption is enabled after rows exist or a value is purged. _(was 7/10 · 6/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **11.3.3** (L2) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb asks that encrypted data be protected against unauthorized modification. The cipher's read path returns an unmarked value straight through -- `if not stored.startswith(MARKER_PREFIX): return stored`, `messagefoundry/store/crypto.py:751-752`, re-read at 166634c9 and still live.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment a cipher column whose marker had been stripped would read back as plaintext rather than failing, so the integrity property the AEAD writer provides would be silently absent on that row.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm."

**What holds it short today.** The writer side is strong: AES-256-GCM is the only registered at-rest algorithm, `_parse` fails closed on an unknown marker version or an unsupported `alg`, and a v2 blob pasted into another cell fails the tag through AAD binding. The read side is where it goes: an unmarked value is accepted as "legacy plaintext (pre-encryption) or a purged/blank value" per the in-code comment. The scorecard records that the sealed strict-ciphertext read the acceptance bar required never shipped, and separately re-homes the DIRECT S/MIME EnvelopedData surface here -- unauthenticated AES-128-CBC, whose CMS signature is a digital signature, not a MAC. This cell's residual is one sentence and was last verified 2026-08-01 at `f8d11685`, older than the rest of the V11 family.

**The research question.** What would a strict-ciphertext read have to refuse, and what breaks when it does? Unknowns: whether any legitimate row can still be unmarked once a key is configured, and whether the two cases the code names -- legacy pre-encryption rows and purged or blank values -- are distinguishable from a stripped marker at read time; whether strictness is per-column, per-table or global; and what a mixed-marker store does across the transition. A separate question for the DIRECT half: can the enveloped body be authenticated at all within the pinned library. Start by re-verifying the cell against the current tree, since the residual predates it.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Rescoring on the AEAD-only writer evidence while leaving the read passthrough in place. The verb is about protection against modification, and a reader that accepts an unmarked value is exactly where that protection is lost. Deferring the DIRECT surface to 11.3.5 is also unavailable -- that cell already deferred it here.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 43 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all (measured as zero occurrences of the cell id across `docs/BACKLOG.md` and the closed archive). The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. This needs an OWNER RULING -- and the ruling as currently framed must be re-put before it is taken.** This item's core claim survives verbatim: `messagefoundry/store/crypto.py:756-757` is `if not stored.startswith(MARKER_PREFIX): return stored`, measured by execution to return a forged plaintext unchanged from a keyed cipher, in the same run as two controls that both fired (a mutated ciphertext raised, and a valid blob decrypted under another cell's AAD raised). Three corrections. The cited lines moved -- `:751-752` is now `:756-757`, and the recorded anchor at `:752` is a blank line at HEAD `fc54d169`. "The cipher's read path" is THREE sites, not one: the store cipher, its byte-identical twin at `store/crypto_transit.py:111-112` for the `mfenc:v3` provider, and the same passthrough reached through `messagefoundry/uploads.py:355-357` and `:364-366`, which is not a database column at all but a pair of FILES per upload -- measured by execution, a hand-written plaintext sidecar was accepted and returned a fully populated metadata object with file id, filename, uploader and uploader id all attacker-chosen, while `_scan_metas_sync` at `:399-401` swallows every exception into one generic warning. And the consequence is understated: an unmarked value is not merely read back, it is LAUNDERED, because `reencrypt_to_active` selects anything not already under the active key -- plaintext included -- and rewrites it as `cipher.encrypt(cipher.decrypt(stored))` (`store/store.py:2707-2732`, `:2784`), so the next `rotate-key` converts a substituted plaintext into a genuine cell-AAD-bound ciphertext after which no evidence of the substitution survives.

**The control the record says never shipped, shipped -- on the sibling surface.** `pipeline/dr_backup.py:671-680` refuses to verify a plaintext `.mfbak` when a store key is configured, calling it a possible downgrade, with `_looks_encrypted` at `:811-819` as the structural twin of the marker test and `[backup].allow_unencrypted` shipping FALSE at `config/settings.py:3398`. Two sibling surfaces, one line each, opposite decisions. That asymmetry is the finding, and it makes the build a PORT rather than a design. Placement answers the item's open question: strictness is naturally GLOBAL-PER-CIPHER, because the two `Cipher` implementations are only ever handed values from covered cells, so a refusal at that seam covers all 31 decrypt call sites across three backends AND the uploads store without threading anything -- and no read path pre-checks the marker and bypasses the seam, the only `is_encrypted` call site being `crypto.py:321`, which runs AFTER decrypt. A per-column dial would be a second definition of coverage that can drift from `_CIPHER_COLUMNS`. The acceptance bar can also be corrected DOWNWARD: the persisted "sealed" flag the 2026-07-22 disposition demanded is unnecessary, because the invariant it would encode is re-established at every keyed open by `_encrypt_existing_rows` (called at `store/store.py:2077`, `sqlserver.py:2361`, `postgres.py:963`, self-guarded and idempotent), and a persisted flag can go stale where a migration cannot.

**Three preconditions must close first or the refusal fires on legitimate data, and one of the three as first reported is FALSE.** The claim that `shared_body` and `attachment_chunk` are both left unmigrated on the two server backends does not hold for the first: `INSERT INTO shared_body` occurs EXACTLY ONCE tree-wide, at `store/store.py:3409`, the SQLite backend -- positive control in the same run, the bare token appears 55, 10 and 7 times across the three backend files, so the pattern reached all three and the single writer is a real result, and both server backends state in their own comments that the table is schema-only or that bodies stay inline. The `attachment_chunk` half STANDS: I confirmed `INSERT INTO attachment_chunk` on all three backends (`store.py:3516`, `postgres.py:4701`, `sqlserver.py:7617`). The other two preconditions stand as reported: the uploaded-file store has no migration pass at all and `rotate-key` covers only `reencrypt_to_active` (`__main__.py:4119`), and the blanket exception swallow would make the new refusal invisible exactly where the plant is easiest.

**The ruling must be re-put.** The question is whether an approved DIGITAL SIGNATURE carried inside an unauthenticated CMS envelope satisfies "protected against unauthorized modification", when the verb's stated means are "preferably an approved authenticated encryption method or an approved encryption method with an approved MAC". Two things are wrong with how it is currently posed. First, the discriminator offered for the strict reading -- that AEAD and MAC make the DECRYPTOR refuse whereas a signature depends on a receiving HISP the engine cannot compel -- does not separate them, because an approved MAC is EQUALLY receiver-verified, and `transports/direct.py:437` registers a destination only with no source, so the engine verifies nothing on this surface under any construction. Second, the library ceiling is real but narrower than stated: `pkcs7.ContentEncryptionAlgorithm` is AES128 or AES256, CBC only, with no AEAD member, so RFC 5083 AuthEnvelopedData is not constructible -- but an OUTER CMS SignedData computed over the EnvelopedData ciphertext (encrypt-then-sign) constructs today with the builders already imported at `direct.py:58`, so "no AEAD available" is not "no integrity over the ciphertext available". Put the ruling with all three options and without the compellability argument, or the owner chooses between two when three exist.

**Still not an honest pass:** re-scoring on the writer evidence while leaving the read passthrough. That is more tempting now than when this item was filed, because the writer evidence got better -- `[store].aad_bind` ships true (`config/settings.py:410`, threaded at `store/base.py:1879`) and relocation detection was measured refusing, so three of four limbs read verified with clean measurements. The downgrade limb is not a weaker version of the substitution limb: substitution is a VERIFICATION with a tag to check, downgrade has no tag and only a REFUSAL can protect it. The second trap is nearly reached by anyone who measures the migration: arguing the passthrough is unreachable by any legitimate value and therefore harmless. It is false on the server backends for the attachment table, false on the uploads surface entirely, and grades the wrong thing even where true -- "no legitimate value has this shape" is an argument about inputs, not a control. Proposed work, unallocated and by subject: the strict-ciphertext read at both cipher implementations, defaulting on and registered in `security_loosenings()`; server-backend migration parity for the attachment table plus a mechanical reconciliation so a future covered table cannot ship without a pass; uploaded-file store crypto parity with a distinct logged and alerted refusal event; a review of the queue-claim `CipherError` containment sites, where a stripped payload would be absorbed as an ordinary undecryptable row at warning level; the DIRECT integrity option, costed and interop-measured; the re-put ruling packet; and a re-verification that re-anchors the stale evidence, takes delivery of the enveloped surface, adds the SSH transit hop, and sets the reviewer field this record lacks.

**PRECONDITIONS BUILT 2026-09-04. The refusal is still NOT built and still needs the re-put owner ruling — this item stays open.** Everything below was re-measured by execution against `a2eef0f37` before any code was written; every line number in the 2026-08-20 research had moved. The core claim survives verbatim: `crypto.py:756-757` returned a forged plaintext unchanged from a keyed cipher, with both controls firing in the same run (a mutated ciphertext and a wrong-cell AAD each raised `CipherError`). On the uploads surface a hand-written plaintext sidecar was accepted by a KEYED store and returned filename, uploader and uploader id all attacker-chosen, while a relocated SEALED sidecar raised — the positive control separating the passthrough from a broken test.

**A SECOND precondition as reported is FALSE, and this one is the item's own.** `attachment_chunk` was reported "unmigrated on all three backends" on the strength of its three `INSERT INTO` sites. Those sites answer *where it is written*, not *where it is sealed* — an SDS-3.8 instrument mismatch. Measured: **SQLite has had an on-open pass all along** (`store/store.py:2765-2798`), and **rotation covers the table on all three** backends. The real gap was one pass on two backends: `_encrypt_existing_rows` omitted it on `postgres.py` and `sqlserver.py` only. Both now have it, with a batch of 16 rather than the sibling passes' 500 because one row is a whole 1 MiB `DETACH_CHUNK_BYTES` slice and 500 would hold ~650 MiB resident in one transaction at store open. The `shared_body` correction **holds** and needed no new evidence: `tests/test_phi_at_rest_inventory.py` already pinned it, with the same instrument and the same SQLite-only reasoning, *before this item was filed* — so the record contained its own refutation. Not restated in the new guard (SDS-3.5).

**Precondition 2 was worse than reported and is a standing data-loss defect, not only a blocker.** The uploaded-file store had no migration pass *and* no rotation pass. Measured: after a rotation the on-disk blob was byte-identical, and once the prior key was dropped — the step `rotate-key`'s own docstring tells the operator to take — the upload raised `CipherError` permanently. `UploadStore.reseal_to_active()` now closes both transitions and `rotate-key` calls it on the store's live cipher instance (ASVS 11.3.4). **One asymmetry is deliberate and named rather than papered over:** the store seals legacy plaintext automatically at every keyed open, whereas this pass has one caller, so a first key-enable is closed only when an operator runs the command. A whole-directory crypto sweep at API startup is unbounded boot-time work and a separate decision.

**Precondition 3 closed.** `_scan_metas_sync`'s blanket `except Exception` folded a cipher refusal, a damaged file and a malformed sidecar into one identical warning — measured, three causes, three identical lines. Each class is now caught and logged separately, so the refusal this item contemplates would be visible on the surface where planting is easiest instead of reading like a routine post-rotation skip.

**A mechanical reconciliation ships with it** (`tests/test_store_cipher_sweep_parity.py`): every `cell_aad` cell whose table a backend INSERTs into must be reached by BOTH sweeps, so a future covered table cannot ship half-added the way this one did. The `INSERT INTO` scoping is load-bearing — without it the check falsely accuses both server backends over `shared_body`. **Recorded because it nearly shipped broken:** the first version matched raw source text and passed the real Postgres omission, because a comment above the missing call said the word `attachment_chunk`. Prose satisfied a check about code. It now matches only executed string constants, and both backend mutations were measured red before the fix and green after.

**Named, measured and NOT done.** The refusal, pending the ruling. The three store `_reencrypt_value` staticmethods and the uploads one are four spellings of a single seam; the leaf-module rule blocks importing the store copies, so the new one carries the same name to stay greppable. Each backend still hand-maintains its own list of composite passes — roughly 26 sites, and SQL Server has no `_CIPHER_COLUMNS` at all, so `postgres.py:856`'s "mirrors `MessageStore._CIPHER_COLUMNS`" is untrue of one backend. Driving all passes off one declaration would retire this guard and ~1,300 lines of sibling AST scaffolding, but it is ~1,000 lines in the one path **no CI leg executes** (every SQL Server and Postgres leg is keyless and returns before the sweep body), so it is a separate item. `UploadStore` is also constructed from settings in three places with a repeated `uploads_dir` gate.

## 1170. research an honest pass for ASVS 11.3.5 -- asserting encrypt-then-MAC on hops that deliberately keep CBC-SHA2 for hospital peers

> 🔢 **Re-scored 2026-08-20 -> P2.** Value **5/10** · Difficulty **3/10** · _fill-in_. The at-rest half is AEAD-only (store/crypto.py:109-111 registers AES-256-GCM alone) and the transport half is unchanged, with the deliberate six-CBC-SHA2 retention recorded at tls_policy.py:375-376 and no encrypt_then_mac reference anywhere under messagefoundry/, so nothing asserts, logs or refuses on the RFC 7366 state. Value 5 because a deploying site has a clean workaround in the shipped tls_ciphers setting (settings.py:766, forward-secrecy-validated at :935-940), leaving the default's breadth rather than an unfixable property; difficulty 3 because the item's named concrete unknown is now answered -- the stdlib exposes no negotiation state at all on this interpreter -- so the remainder is a documented finding plus the V11.3-versus-V12 scope ruling. _(was 4/10 · 7/10.)_
> Research: done 2026-08-20
>
> **Filed 2026-08-08 - not started. RESEARCH item: the goal is an HONEST pass, and "cannot honestly reach pass" is a valid finding.** ASVS **11.3.5** (L3) currently scores **partial**. The pinned verb requires any encryption-plus-MAC combination to operate in encrypt-then-MAC mode. The application's own cryptography is AEAD-only and therefore EtM by construction; what holds the cell short is the TLS surface, at `config/tls_policy.py:349`.
> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore

**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P3. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** on a first deployment, a TLS 1.2 peer that does not offer RFC 7366 would silently get a MAC-then-encrypt composition on six of the seventeen default suites, and nothing in the tree would notice.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that any combination of an encryption algorithm and a MAC algorithm is operating in encrypt-then-MAC mode."

**What holds it short today.** AES-256-GCM is the sole registered at-rest algorithm (`store/crypto.py:107`) and the `.mfbak` archive uses the same; the one composition that could have been MAC-then-encrypt was checked and is not (`audit_log` is absent from `store/store.py:2291`'s `_CIPHER_COLUMNS`). The residual holds the cell on transport: `config/tls_policy.py` deliberately does not restrict suites, and the decision is recorded in-tree at `tls_policy.py:349` -- restricting would remove "six CBC-SHA2 suites that real MLLP/DICOM hospital peers still speak". Those are MAC-then-encrypt unless the peer negotiates RFC 7366, and nothing asserts, logs or refuses on that.

**The research question.** The CBC-SHA2 retention is a stated, shipped product choice protecting interop with peers the engine exists to serve -- research must not assume it away. Under that constraint: can the engine establish that `encrypt_then_mac` was negotiated on a given hop? The concrete unknown is whether CPython's `ssl` exposes the RFC 7366 extension state at all; if it does not, the follow-on is whether an honest pass is reachable by any means short of removing the suites. A second, prior question is scope: the scorecard records a live disagreement over whether V11.3 reaches TLS suite selection or whether that belongs to V12, resolved today only by the worse-verdict tie-breaker.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Adopting the narrow reading -- scoping V11.3 to the application's own cryptography -- to score pass on the AEAD evidence alone. The scorecard already names that reading and records why it was not taken; choosing it now to move a number is re-declaring scope to dodge the verb. Pinning the six suites out without re-running the interop measurement that kept them is the mirror-image move: it buys the cell by breaking the property the default protects.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 43 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all (measured as zero occurrences of the cell id across `docs/BACKLOG.md` and the closed archive). The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. This needs an OWNER RULING on two questions, and one of this item's sentences no longer holds while another rests on a measurement that does not exist.** "`config/tls_policy.py` deliberately does not restrict suites" is false at HEAD `fc54d169`: `harden_cipher_suites` at `:362` RAISES on any non-forward-secret suite and fires at SEVEN construction sites. What it does not do is assert AEAD, and that distinction was measured with a live negative control -- executed, the gate RAISED on `AES128-SHA:@SECLEVEL=0` and ACCEPTED `ECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256`, a list that is 100 percent MAC-then-encrypt. The one shipped gate touching cipher suites is structurally blind to the exact property this requirement asks about, and so is the operator knob: `validate_tls_ciphers` accepted that same list unchanged, so a supported `[api].tls_ciphers` value makes the verb definitively false on the most exposed hop.

**The item's trap sentence needs amending, and the amendment strengthens it.** It forbids pinning the six CBC-SHA2 suites out "without re-running the interop measurement that kept them". There is no such measurement. What `tls_policy.py:373-379` records as measured is the SUITE-SET DELTA of a candidate cipher string; the clause "that real MLLP/DICOM hospital peers still speak" is an in-code assertion about the world with no cited measurement -- searched across `docs/`, `messagefoundry/` and `tests/` it returns only that line and the backlog items quoting it, against a positive control of 26 hits for `harden_cipher_suites` in the same run, and the vault carries no census either. Nor is it owner-ratified: no ruling on those suites exists in either rulings document, against a positive control of 19 occurrences of "ruling" in each. So the honest form of the trap is: pinning them out without RUNNING, for the first time, the census the rationale asserts. As filed it reads as "a measurement already settled this, do not disturb it", which lets a stale assertion function as a settled finding indefinitely.

**This item never names one of the three declared artifacts, and that artifact has the LARGER weak surface.** `ide/src/engineClient.ts:69-70` returns `{ minVersion: TLS_MIN_VERSION }` and no cipher list, feeding both request sites, with zero hits for `ciphers|secureContext|secureProtocol|rejectUnauthorized` across `ide/src` against a live positive control. Node's shipped `tls.DEFAULT_CIPHERS` explicitly NAMES six CBC-SHA2 suites and then appends `HIGH`, which pulls in SHA1-CBC and static-RSA families the engine's own gate would refuse -- on a hop that terminates at the engine or the operator's own reverse proxy, so the hospital-peer constraint this item is built around does not govern it. Pinning an AEAD-only list beside the `minVersion` already there costs zero interop.

**The runtime limb is settled negatively, and that decides the shape of the answer.** No accessor exists on either shipped runtime: scanning the TLS module and its socket types for any name containing "mac" or "etm" returns exactly one unrelated alert constant and `OP_NO_ENCRYPT_THEN_MAC` is absent, against a positive control in the same run finding five real names for "cipher" and confirming `OP_NO_TICKET` present. The product also reads a negotiated suite NOWHERE. So the verb cannot be satisfied by observation on any TLS hop, and the only route is to EMPTY THE ANTECEDENT -- which is achievable on most of the surface and, on one hop family, a product decision. **But the enumeration was seeded from two TLS-shaped instruments** (a `harden_cipher_suites` call-site census and an `SSLContext` sweep), so it missed the one shipped protocol that is not TLS: `messagefoundry/transports/remotefile.py:396-448` drives paramiko with NO `disabled_algorithms` -- measured zero tree-wide against a positive control of 17 `paramiko` hits in that file -- and SSH negotiates a cipher and a SEPARATE MAC by construction, with encrypt-then-MAC available only as distinct `*-etm@openssh.com` algorithm names. That is squarely inside the verb and is governed by no hospital-peer rationale. A second miss falsifies the "exactly two connector families" narrowing: `transports/http_listener.py:419` builds its inbound TLS via `_mllp_ssl_context(s, server=True)`, so a shipped data-carrying inbound hop carries the same six suites, is not an MLLP or DICOM peer hop, and is labelled "MLLP listener" inside the very seam a per-connector policy would key on -- which would silently extend the peer carve-out to it.

**The two rulings.** May the six suites be removed from the MLLP and DICOM contexts? Yes empties the antecedent on the last hop family and the requirement is satisfied by the shipped default; no makes the terminal state a recorded partial keyed to exactly two families, which is far better than today's record. The owner must be told the premise is unmeasured, and the packet must name what evidence is available BEFORE a first deployment -- published conformance statements and vendor TLS documentation -- because with zero deployments there is no site to census. Second: does this chapter reach TLS suite selection, or does that belong to the communications chapter? The narrow reading passes today on the AEAD evidence alone; taking it mid-research to move a number is this item's own named trap, while ruling it as a STANDING interpretation applied across the section before looking at any one cell is a legitimate act of method. **Still not an honest pass:** logging the negotiated suite name and calling the requirement satisfied -- a genuine improvement, since nothing reads a negotiated suite today, and the suite name is compatible with BOTH compositions, so shipping it and re-scoring records a verdict on an instrument that cannot answer the question asked. One build constraint, measured and easy to get wrong: raising `minimum_version` to TLS 1.3 does NOT change what `get_ciphers()` returns -- the enumeration still lists all six CBC-SHA2 suites -- so the honest predicate is "no non-AEAD suite is NEGOTIABLE" and must read the version floor alongside the enumeration, or it fires falsely on the strongest possible configuration. Proposed work, unallocated and by subject: the IDE cipher pin plus its comment correction; an AEAD assertion on the shared suite seam with a per-connector policy and a label that does not conflate the inbound HTTP listener with MLLP; reaching the ten unasserted first-party contexts with a guard against an eleventh; the operator cipher-string AEAD validator; the SSH algorithm disposition; the peer suite census; the absence-corpus extension past Python; and the negotiated-suite read-out, labelled as a read-out and never as an order assertion.


**OWNER RULING 2026-08-22 -- split three ways; only one third needs a ruling at all.** The packet framed one hospital-peer interop judgement. The re-scoping found **33 distinct composition sites spanning the 45 hop rows of the CI-enforced communications inventory**, across four protocol families, and the interop rationale reaches only TLS on MLLP and DICOM. (1) **SSH is ordinary in-house work, not a ruling:** drop two non-EtM MAC names from a frozenset the product already maintains, and pass a `"cipher"` key beside the `"mac"` key it already passes. Take it. (2) The **MLLP and DICOM** interop question stands on its own merits as the packet intended. (3) **LDAPS, Vault and the SQL Server TDS hop** choose their suites inside `ldap3`, `hvac` or ODBC Driver 18, where the engine has no reach -- those rows get a terminal state. A single uniform policy was rejected because it would commit the engine to a guarantee it cannot keep on nine of the rows.


**BUILT 2026-08-22 -- and the build found that the CONTROL ALREADY ON MAIN WAS INERT.** That second
part matters more than the first and is why this note leads with it.

**The inert control.** `_SftpClient._connect` passed `disabled_algorithms = {"mac": ...}`. paramiko
reads **`"macs"`**. Its `Transport._filter_algorithm` does `self.disabled_algorithms.get(type_, [])`
and is called with `"ciphers"`, `"macs"`, `"keys"`, `"pubkeys"`, `"kex"` and `"compression"` -- so a
singular key matched nothing, `.get` returned the empty default, and every weak algorithm stayed on
the wire. paramiko neither validates the keys nor warns about an unknown one, so nothing reported a
problem. **The MAC restriction shipped as decoration from the day it landed, and any ASVS 11.4.1
claim resting on it was unsupported.**

Proved by a REAL handshake, not by reading: both ends real paramiko 5.0.0 over a socketpair, driving
the shipped `_connect` with only `SSHClient` replaced by a recorder, against a server pinned to
`3des-cbc` and `hmac-md5`. The handshake **COMPLETED** and negotiated exactly those. Positive control
in the same run, the same derived deny-lists under the plural keys: negotiation **REFUSED**
(`IncompatiblePeer`). Good-input control, plural keys against a default server: completed on
`aes128-ctr` and `hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com`.

**Why no test caught it, which is the reusable part.** The tests read `["disabled_algorithms"]["mac"]`
-- the same wrong key production wrote -- then recomputed the subtraction by hand against a fake.
Test and code agreed on a fiction. Their "cannot pass vacuously" guard was built for the wrong
failure mode: it fires on an EMPTY deny list, the renamed-attribute case, while a WRONG KEY produces
a fully populated deny list that paramiko silently ignores. **A test that models a library's
semantics instead of invoking them cannot see a disagreement about the interface.**

**What now ships.** The keys are plural. `_APPROVED_SFTP_MACS` drops the two Encrypt-and-MAC names,
keeping only the two `-etm@openssh.com` entries, because composition order rather than hash strength
is what this cell asks about. A new `_APPROVED_SFTP_CIPHERS` allow-list admits the two AES-GCM and
three AES-CTR names and excludes the four CBC and 3DES ones paramiko 5.0.0 would otherwise propose
(CVE-2008-5161 for CBC; Sweet32 and roughly 112-bit strength for 3DES). Allow-list, not deny-list, so
forgetting to approve a future algorithm EXCLUDES it -- wrong in the safe direction.

**The regression guard runs everywhere, including where paramiko is absent**, which is what this
repository's CI test legs actually use. It pins the exact key set the connector passes and asserts
each key is one paramiko consults. Restoring the shipped singular keys turns four tests RED; three
further mutations (single key reverted, cipher arm deleted, a CBC name approved) each turn it red
too, with zero vacuous.

**Residual.** The live fixture-fidelity check still skips where the `[sftp]` extra is absent, so the
literal key set is pinned locally but compared against the real library only where it is installed.
Nothing here touches the TLS/FTPS context in the same module, which was already hardened.

> Verdict: research
> Closing-act: scorecard-rescore
**Cluster:** Security / ASVS remediation research. **Priority:** P2. **Verdict:** research.
**Severity:** no present exploitability is claimed for either site -- SHA-1 in HMAC has no practical break and BLAKE2b is sound. The gap is conformance to the named list, which is what an L1 requirement measures.

**The pinned verb.** "Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose."

**What holds it short today.** ~~The TOTP primitive is RFC 6238 HMAC-SHA1 with no SHA-256 or SHA-512 option, and the enrolment URI advertises `algorithm=SHA1` (`totp.py:170`).~~ **[FALSIFIED 2026-08-12 by PR #325 (`0ace6bb6`) -- struck, not deleted.** `auth/totp.py:84` is `_TOTP_DIGEST = hashlib.sha256`; `:85` DERIVES `_TOTP_ALGORITHM` from it so the two cannot be edited apart; `:91` reads *"SHA-256 since 2026-08-11, not RFC 4226's SHA-1"*. **Neither cited token exists.** The research question it framed -- *app support is the blocker and nobody has measured it* -- is **MOOT**: it shipped as a hard cutover with the authenticator cost accepted. **This is a RE-SCOPE, not a close: the BLAKE2b limb is untouched and remains the live question, so the SP 800-131A contested-reading paragraph now bears ONLY on BLAKE2b.]** The de-identification seed is a keyed BLAKE2b with a 128-bit digest, twinned byte-identically at `tee/anon/keying.py` and formally inventoried at `scripts/security/crypto_inventory_check.py:86`; BLAKE2b is not on the NIST approved list. A third SHA-1 use, `auth/policy.py:150`, is marked `usedforsecurity=False` as the HIBP corpus index. No MD5 implementation exists; the token appears once as a rejected value in a test asserting `config/wiring.py:3885` refuses `ws_password_type='md5'`.

**The research question.** SHA-1 is what makes TOTP universally interoperable, so the unknown is real authenticator-app support for SHA-256 TOTP across the apps a hospital workforce actually uses -- RFC 6238 permits it, app support is the blocker, and nobody has measured it. Separately and independently: is the keyed BLAKE2b doing a cryptographic job this verb reaches, or is it, like the HIBP index, a non-cryptographic use? Settle that before touching it. Third, prior to both: the scorecard records a contested reading -- NIST SP 800-131A Rev 2 still permits SHA-1 for HMAC until 2030 -- so establish which list "approved" binds to, because that answer changes the TOTP verdict and does not rescue BLAKE2b either way.

**What would NOT be an honest pass.** Switching TOTP to SHA-256 without app-support evidence -- that moves the cell and locks users out of their own second factor. Swapping BLAKE2b for a listed hash purely to clear the inventory scanner, without deciding whether the seed is in the verb's reach, clears the number without answering the question.

**Source:** filed 2026-08-08 from the ASVS ledger-coverage sweep, which found 43 of the 108 partial and fail cells carried no backlog item at all (measured as zero occurrences of the cell id across `docs/BACKLOG.md` and the closed archive). The scorecard is the record of record for the verdict; this item tracks the research toward changing it.

**Researched 2026-08-20. Reachable with a build -- and the surviving half of this item is FALSE IN ITS REASONING, which is the most consequential finding here.** One half is already struck in the ledger: commit `0ace6bb6` (2026-08-11) moved the TOTP digest to SHA-256 at `messagefoundry/auth/totp.py:84`, with `_TOTP_ALGORITHM` DERIVED from it at `:85` so the computation and the advertisement cannot be edited apart. The other half -- "the de-identification seed is a keyed BLAKE2b ...; BLAKE2b is not on the NIST approved list" -- is true of the NIST list and IRRELEVANT to the pinned verb. The V11 chapter says in its own words (fetched at tag `v5.0.0`) that the standard "provides more in-depth technical information about the requirements in Appendix C ... includ[ing] algorithms and modes that are considered 'approved' for the purposes of the requirements in this chapter." In that appendix's general-use hash table BLAKE2b is status **A** with an **empty Restrictions cell**, under the bullet that such algorithms are additionally approved for HMAC, KDF and RBG -- while the restricted rows (SHA-224, SHA-512/224, SHA3-224, SHA-1) each carry "Not suitable for HMAC, KDF, RBG, digital signatures" and BLAKE2b does not. So the site the record says now decides this requirement is APPROVED, and it is graded against the wrong list. A corroborating consequence: the same appendix lists argon2id as approved for password storage, and argon2's core permutation IS BLAKE2b, so a NIST-only reading would have the standard mandating a KDF built on a disapproved primitive. This is exactly the failure `docs/ASVS-ASSESSMENT-METHOD.md` section 2.1a warns about -- a claim about what the standard counts as approved is a claim about chapter prose, which the pinned corpus structurally cannot check, so it came back clean for three successive assessors. SHA-1 is likewise **L**, not D, so the opt-in WS-Security digest at `transports/soap.py:672` does not trip the unconditional clause.

**The site that DOES decide it is negotiated, not called, and it was invisible to every instrument used so far.** `messagefoundry/transports/remotefile.py:438-447` calls `client.connect(...)` with NO `disabled_algorithms=` -- measured zero tree-wide against a positive control of `set_missing_host_key_policy|SSHClient(` firing in the same file -- and paramiko 5.0.0 (pinned at `requirements.lock:565`) has `_preferred_macs` including `hmac-sha1`, `hmac-md5`, `hmac-sha1-96` and `hmac-md5-96`. Appendix C marks HMAC-MD5 **D**. So the shipped SFTP connector PROPOSES an HMAC over a disallowed hash, and a server that selects it gets it, on a use case the verb names by name and in a clause that admits no default-off escape.

**It is one of THREE such classes, and I re-measured the other two on the supported interpreter.** HTTP Digest authentication: `messagefoundry/transports/http_auth.py:401` returns a bare `urllib.request.HTTPDigestAuthHandler(pwmgr)` with no algorithm restriction, wired into three connector openers (`transports/rest.py:1316-1329`, `transports/fhir.py:402-404`, `transports/soap.py:443-461`), plus `rest.py:881` for the proxy twin. CPython 3.14.6's handler source reads `algorithm = chal.get('algorithm', 'MD5')` -- the SERVER's challenge chooses, and the default when it omits the parameter is MD5, which is the common RFC 2617 case. That is strictly worse than the SFTP case, where the weak MAC is one proposal among several. SMTP authentication: five engine sites call `smtp.login(...)` with no mechanism restriction (`pipeline/alert_sinks.py:433`, `transports/direct.py:403` and `:425`, `transports/email.py:285` and `:307`), and `smtplib`'s source reads `preferred_auths = ['CRAM-MD5', 'PLAIN', 'LOGIN']` with `_have_cram_md5_support` measuring True -- so an HMAC-MD5 response is tried FIRST. Neither class needs an optional extra; both are pure standard library, shipped in the wheel.

**The build, and one correction that must land with it.** Record "approved means Appendix C status A, not the NIST list" as a standing definition, once, with the verbatim chapter sentence. Constrain the SFTP algorithm proposal, stated as a positive ALLOW-LIST rather than a deny-list so a future library addition is excluded by construction, with a test asserting the effective MAC set contains no `md5` or `sha1` member AND a positive control asserting the set is non-empty (a deny-list test that passes against an empty set proves nothing). Constrain or delete the HTTP digest option and the SMTP mechanism selection -- deletion is the simpler correct end state and with zero deployments it costs nothing. Pass an explicit signature configuration at `parsing/xml/signature.py:70`, which today passes none, restricted to approved digests AND schemes: the pinned library's default accept-set admits SHA-224 and SHA3-224 (both L, explicitly "not suitable for ... digital signatures") and also RSA-PKCS#1-v1.5 and DSA, both **D** in the appendix's signature table. And delete `ws_password_type='digest'` rather than defend it, which retires the last SHA-1 with a cryptographic job and removes a live rule dispute from the record.

**Still not an honest pass:** swapping the de-identification hash for a listed one. That is no longer merely a scanner-clearing move, it is a WRONG FIX -- it would change every derived seed and move every surrogate mapping in every dataset built under it, to replace one approved hash with another approved hash. The standing recommendation to do it should be withdrawn. And re-scoring on the Appendix C correction alone is the live trap: it moves the verdict on a corrected READING while an HMAC over a disallowed hash remains in the set the shipped SFTP connector proposes. The correction is necessary for the pass and is not any part of what the pass rests on. Two more, both available and reasonable-looking: declaring the SFTP connector out of scope because paramiko is an extra (the connector is shipped engine code; the extra governs installation, not the algorithm choice, and the unconditional clause has no default-off escape); and adding a settings knob so an operator can restrict the MACs (a control you have to configure is never a pass). One contest to record rather than reassign: the same appendix's general-use preamble disqualifies a sub-254-bit digest output for new designs in any collision-resistance-requiring application, and `anon/keying.py:30` sets a 16-byte digest -- state that beside the MAC-table question in the residual rather than pushing it to another requirement whose verb reaches only signatures and data integrity. Proposed work, unallocated and by subject: the SFTP algorithm allow-list; the HTTP digest constraint or deletion; the SMTP mechanism constraint at all five sites; the XML verification accept-set over digests and schemes; retirement of the opt-in weak-digest token option, re-cutting the recorded absence positive control in the same change if and only if the last `hashlib.sha1` call goes with it; the standing definition of "approved"; withdrawal of the replacement recommendation; and replacement of the library-call-shaped absence claim with an instrument that measures each third-party surface's EFFECTIVE algorithm set.


***THIS ITEM'S OWN PRESCRIPTION IS UNSAFE IF FOLLOWED LITERALLY. DO NOT JUST RESTRICT THE MECHANISM LIST.*** Raised by the building lane, which stopped rather than build it, and re-verified here at every coordinate.

**The gap is real:** five sites call `smtp.login()` with no mechanism restriction -- `pipeline/alert_sinks.py:433`, `transports/direct.py:403` and `:425`, `transports/email.py:285` and `:307`. On the supported interpreter `smtplib` offers `['CRAM-MD5', 'PLAIN', 'LOGIN']` with **CRAM-MD5 first**, so an HMAC over MD5 is attempted at every site.

***AND THE NAIVE FIX TRADES A CONFORMANCE DEFECT FOR A CREDENTIAL EXPOSURE.*** **`PLAIN` and `LOGIN` send the password; `CRAM-MD5` does not.** Restricting to the approved mechanisms is only safe on an encrypted channel, and this engine has an unencrypted one:

- `email_use_tls: bool = True` (`config/settings.py:2888`) -- **default true, but configurable**
- `alert_sinks.py`: `if use_tls: smtp.starttls(...)` -- and **`if username is not None: smtp.login(...)` sits at the SAME indentation**, verified, so **login runs whether or not TLS was negotiated**

**With `email_use_tls=false` and a username set, restricting the list puts a cleartext password on the wire where a challenge-response had been.** *Closing an 11.4.1 gap by creating a credential exposure is strictly worse than leaving it open.*

**DISPATCHER RULING: restrict to `PLAIN`/`LOGIN` AND refuse to authenticate at all on an unencrypted channel.** Both halves, or neither.

**The shape is not a new invention -- this repository already does it in four places.** `alert_sinks.py` refuses a plaintext `http://` webhook target unless an explicit dev escape is set, citing *no insecure fallback*, and its own comment names the pattern as shared with **LDAPS, SQL Server and MLLP**. *Use that mechanism rather than minting a fifth variant; confirm the existing escape's semantics cover an SMTP surface before reusing its name.*

**Zero deployments makes the breaking change free, and that is the only thing it makes free.** It is why there is still time to get this right, not a reason to ship the weaker half first.
